Title: SMS of Death: Android under attack, an invisible SMS can block calls and emergency services
Context: A threat to communications availability SMS of Death demonstrates how a cyberattack doesn’t necessarily have to involve information theft, code execution, or device control to...
Full Text:
SMS of Death lets attackers crash Android call services with a hidden, zero-click message, blocking phone calls, even emergency calls too.

A specially manipulated SMS message is enough to crash Android’s phone service, interrupt ongoing calls, and temporarily render the smartphone unusable. The attack requires no interaction from the victim and can even compromise the ability to contact emergency services.

The vulnerability, dubbed the SMS of Death, is bringing renewed attention to the security of the messaging system in Android smartphones. The issue, documented by independent researcher Mark Blaszczyk, allows a remote attacker to cause a disruption in phone service by sending a single, specially crafted WAP Push message.

WAP Push (Wireless Application Protocol Push) is a particular message transmitted over the mobile network, generally in the form of a binary SMS, which contains structured data and is processed automatically by the smartphone without requiring user intervention. Unlike a traditional SMS, it can carry notifications, links to Internet resources, and configurations for mobile services.

The most worrying aspect is the execution method. It’s a zero-click attack, in which the recipient doesn’t have to open the message, select a link, or authorize any action. The content is automatically processed by the operating system and can cause the process responsible for phone functionality to crash.

The vulnerability affects “WapPushOverSms“, an Android framework component located in the “frameworks/opt/telephony” path, responsible for interpreting and managing WAP Push messages received by the device.

The technical cause lies in the incorrect handling of a numeric value used during message interpretation. Specifically, the “decodeWapPdu()” function, the researcher explains, reads the length of the WSP header through a value encoded as “uintvar” , initially returned as a 64-bit number. The value is subsequently converted to a 32-bit integer without prior range checking. This operation can transform a seemingly valid number into a negative value, which is then used to determine the size of an array. The consequence of this is a “NegativeArraySizeException” exception, thrown when Android attempts to allocate a negative-sized array. The exception is not handled correctly in the processing path and causes the “com.android.phone” process, responsible for telephony functions, to terminate.

The researcher demonstrated that a five-byte WSP header can generate the value “-2147483648“, which is sufficient to trigger the issue. Therefore, it is not necessary to transmit particularly large amounts of content to cause the issue.

“A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000. Cast to a signed 32-bit int, that is -2147483648. Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone:” reads the analysis.

An invisible attack that also interrupts emergency calls

The message is transmitted as a data SMS via the WAP Push channel on port 2948. Unlike a regular SMS, it isn’t displayed in the message inbox and doesn’t generate a user-recognizable notification. The sender’s number isn’t normally visible in the conversation, and when the device receives the message, Android automatically starts processing it. A crash in the phone process causes a temporary loss of connectivity and interrupts active voice calls, including those to emergency services.

According to the researcher’s published evidence, each message processing can cause a disruption in telephone service lasting about one to two seconds, during which the component is rebooted. However, the problem can become much more serious if the message is processed repeatedly.

One of the most significant aspects of SMS of Death is the ability to transform a simple crash into a persistent Denial of Service condition. The malicious message can remain in the incoming SMS queue and be reprocessed during subsequent delivery attempts. The telephone operator’s retransmission mechanism can also contribute to a repeat of the event, causing further service disruptions.

The researcher reports observing intermittent crashes for up to a week after receiving a single message. Sending around twenty specially crafted messages can render the device unusable for an extended period. In more severe cases, the phone process can continue to crash during system startup, triggering a condition similar to a boot loop. Recovery may require using the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) on a computer, directly intervening in the queue of messages waiting to be processed. For a typical user, this is far from a simple procedure.

A threat to communications availability

SMS of Death demonstrates how a cyberattack doesn’t necessarily have to involve information theft, code execution, or device control to have significant consequences. In this case, the target is phone service availability, a crucial feature especially when contacting emergency services. The ability to interrupt communications without any user interaction makes this vulnerability particularly sensitive. To reduce exposure, it’s important to check the Android security patch level installed and apply available updates, paying particular attention to devices no longer receiving manufacturer support.

Testing conducted by Mark Blah has shown that the issue is reproducible on several devices, including the Google Pixel 9 and Samsung smartphones from the Galaxy and Galaxy A families. The vulnerable code appears to be present on Android versions ranging from Android 12 to Android 17. However, the availability of the fix is ​​not uniform across all generations of the operating system.

According to documentation published by the researcher, Google has distributed a fix via the October 2026 security update for Android 14, 15, 16, and 17. Older devices, such as those running Android 12 and 13, may remain exposed if they do not receive corrective updates.

It's assigned CVE-2026-58882 and a Critical severity in the November 2026 Android Security Bulletin. We've had it listed as one of the patches included in our security preview releases since our 2026072901 release which you can see in the release notes:https://t.co/tBoWBpALw1

Title: Hackers Steal About $2.7 Million From Polymarket Traders via Hijacked DebugBear Script
Context: They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script
Full Text:
Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company.

Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour.

The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors.

Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script.

DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking.

Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's.

How the Script Took the Money

The code reuses the access a signed-in trader already has in an open Polymarket page, Hudson Rock found after reviewing the file without running it. It reads account details that Polymarket keeps in the browser, including a set of trading API keys.

Those API keys alone cannot place an order on Polymarket, because orders also need a wallet signature. Hudson Rock found no part of the code that sends the keys, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to the server it reports to.

Instead, the code searches the page for the part of Polymarket's site that places orders, and for the signer that approves the account's transactions.

It then takes one of two paths. For accounts that sign in with their own crypto wallet, it moves the trader's positions straight to the hackers' wallet. For accounts that sign in via email, it sells positions at ever-worse prices and then moves the money out.

In both paths, the code asks the account's own signer to sign its requests and hands them to Polymarket's relayer, which submits them. Hudson Rock said a signing request alone does not prove a trader signed without seeing a prompt. The wallet provider may still ask the trader, refuse, or apply its own rules for the session.

The wallet written into the code received its first funds at 17:10 UTC and its last at 18:02 UTC, according to Ohey's blockchain trace. In that time, it collected 28.6 million POL tokens and positions from 33 wallets.

At 18:19 UTC, those 28.6 million POL were worth about $2.64 million at DefiLlama's price of $0.0922, DefiPrime calculated. The figure covers only the POL, not the positions.

The wallet sent all 28.6 million POL on to three other addresses between 18:28 and 18:38 UTC, its transaction history shows.

Polymarket's Response and Refunds

Polymarket posted its first status update about unauthorized activity in user wallets at 17:38 UTC. At 18:05 UTC, it said its exchange was in cancel-only mode, with relayer actions paused.

The company said it removed the script "within the hour." It also cleared every cache, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It has referred the case to law enforcement.

By October 30, 689 of the 726 affected wallets had been refunded in full, and the remaining 37 were being paid as they were checked. Polymarket is also paying $1.19 million to about 5,500 wallets that lost money during the trading pause or had positions taken. In all, it is returning $3.9 million to traders.

Traders do not need to file a claim. Polymarket's status page links a form for anyone who thinks their amount is wrong or that they should have received a payment.

What Sites and Traders Can Do

DebugBear has told customers of its RUM product to remove its embed code from their websites. The address that served the malicious file, cdn.debugbear[.]com, had no DNS record when The Hacker News checked on November 1.

Polymarket said it is putting third-party scripts back in place with extra checks, such as a stronger Content Security Policy (CSP), pinned versions, and sandboxing.

Hudson Rock's advice for sites that load outside scripts:

Keep unneeded third-party code off pages where users trade or sign.

Where a file can be pinned, use Subresource Integrity (SRI), which lets the browser reject the file if its contents change. A security policy that simply allows a trusted CDN does not check the files that CDN serves.

Check what code on a signed-in page can ask the signer to do.

Hudson Rock's advice for traders is to reject any signing request they did not expect.

Title: NetamLoader Malware Targets Government Windows 10 Systems in Asia via .NET Injection
Context: The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what has been described as a "highly sophisticated infection chain" targeting government organizations in Asia.

The activity, detailed by Kaspersky this week, targeted a custom Windows 10 build used exclusively by government entities in Asia and involves the deployment of a previously undocumented .NET assembly-loading framework codenamed NetamLoader.

The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Nor is it clear if the intrusion compromised more than one system and allowed the hackers to steal any sensitive information.

The Russian cybersecurity company said the artifact was detected in the first half of 2026, packaged inside a Windows cabinet archive (CAB) file placed in a directory that stores Windows operating system update packages.

It's suspected the operation involved a supply chain attack, in which bad actors compromised a trusted third-party vendor to gain access to downstream users who rely on its services or software.

The sample in question features a ".config" file that employs AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. AppDomainManager injection is an adversarial technique used to load arbitrary payloads by hijacking .NET Framework's AppDomainManager mechanism when a .NET application starts.

Put differently, the approach targets .NET Framework's application-domain initialization to achieve code execution. The end result is the same as DLL sideloading: to run malicious code inside a legitimate application's process so as to fly under the radar.

According to Kaspersky, the CAB archive containing the .config file was placed in the path: "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24," with its contents extracted and dropped into "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\."

Infection chain: Stage 1

The exact delivery vehicle for the CAB archive remains unknown. Present in the archive are seven files, four of which are legitimate components of Patch My PC, an endpoint management software -

fabric.config

Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll

PatchMyPC-Enum.dll

PatchMyPC-Models.dll

PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe

PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config

Resources.resx

None of the files with the exception of "Resources.resx" embed malicious code. The infection chain plays out as a two-stage process as follows -

The execution of "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe" serves as the launchpad for several payloads. It abuses AppDomainManager injection to parse "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config," resulting in the execution of "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll."

Once loaded, "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll" finds "fabric.config" located in the same directory and parses its contents to load "Resources.resx."

"Resources.resx" contains "multiple layers" of encoded, compressed, or encrypted payloads, such as XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data, which are decoded and loaded by the component before it.

Infection chain: Stage 2

A brief description of these payloads is listed below -

XAML-1, a loader for an embedded payload, XAML-2.

XAML‑2 initializes the second stage of the attack chain by loading two compressed and Base64‑encoded XAML files: XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2. XAML-2-1 is used to bypass Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI).

XAML-2-2 contains two parts, a .NET module (aka .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (aka JSON-1).

JSON-1, the JSON payload that contains two components: JSON-1-c, which stores command-and-control (C2) server configuration, and JSON-1-p, which contains a Base64‑encoded file (.NET 2 Plugin) and a collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3.

XAML-2-2 loads .NET 1 Loader, which then serves as a decrypting, assembling, and loading for XAML‑3, reports the status to the C2 server, and deletes malicious files extracted from the CAB archive, along with CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to cover up the tracks.

XAML-3, the XAML payload that runs within "dllhost.exe" and is designed to decode, decompress, and load .NET 2 Plugin.

.NET 2 Plugin, a .NET assembly that loads the C2 configuration, gathers system information from Windows Registry, checks if the current host process is "dllhost.exe," waits a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes before issuing its first request to the C2 server ("openaigpt4v[.]com"), and enters into a periodic polling loop to fetch an XAML file and execute it in an isolated AppDomain.

"If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed," Kaspersky explained.

Telemetry data gathered by Kaspersky has identified a single victim in Asia, with NetamLoader designed to attack a Windows 10 build customized for government-only use. Although the targeted Asian country was not disclosed, signs are that it's likely China, as Microsoft offers a bespoke version called Windows 10 China Government Edition specifically for the Chinese government and state-owned entities.

Earlier this August, Bloomberg reported that China's Ministry of State Security had ordered some government agencies to stop using the "Government Edition" in favor of Chinese-made Linux distributions as part of an effort to reduce its dependence on foreign technology.

"Beijing's instruction stemmed from data security concerns," Bloomberg said, citing "people familiar with the matter." No additional details were disclosed at the time.

"In today's geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority," Kaspersky concluded.

"The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process."

Title: Northflank security breach leads to abuse of customers' AI API keys
Context: Wiz says attackers involved in some of these incidents have specifically targeted environment variables containing AI service credentials, which can be exploited through a...
Full Text:
Cloud application hosting platform Northflank is warning customers to rotate all credentials and secrets stored on its platform after a security breach led to unauthorized use of customers' AI API keys.

Northflank is a cloud platform that allows developers to deploy and manage applications, containers, databases, and AI applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.

The company disclosed a security incident on October 30, warning customers to immediately rotate their environment variables and API keys after receiving a threat alert from cloud security company Wiz.

Soon after, Northflank told all customers to assume their environment variables had been decrypted and that the secrets stored within them were stolen.

"Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys," Northflank warned in an October 30 update.

Applications commonly use environment variables to store sensitive information, including database passwords, cloud service credentials, authentication tokens, and API keys.

If exposed, these credentials can be used to breach other customer services, potentially leading to data theft or unauthorized charges through API keys.

Northflank later confirmed that multiple customers had reported unauthorized use of AI API keys stored on the platform.

"Users have reported unauthorised use of AI API keys supplied to the Northflank platform," the company said.

"If you have not already rotated your user-provided secrets stored in Northflank, please do so immediately."

Customers were also advised to review their AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity and report suspicious usage to Northflank and their AI providers.

According to Northflank's published incident timeline, Wiz warned them about the breach at 11:43 UTC on October 30, which the company's engineers reviewed one minute later.

Northflank quickly responded with a network policy patch, followed by additional patches at 12:50 UTC and 13:05 UTC. The company also requested assistance from Wiz's incident response team.

The company has not disclosed how attackers gained access to its systems, how many customers were affected, or whether attackers stole or abused credentials other than the reported AI API keys.

As part of its response, Northflank enabled credential rotation for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, and Redis.

The company also enabled audit logs for all customers, including those using free accounts, to help them investigate any suspicious activity.

Northflank continues to advise customers to rotate secrets stored in workloads, secret groups, and global secrets, and to disable public access to add-ons where enabled.

BleepingComputer contacted Northflank with questions about the breach, its impact on customers, and whether stored credentials were accessed or stolen, but has not received a response.

Black October

The breach comes amid a series of attacks targeting AI development platforms, which security researchers believe are valuable targets because they store API keys that can be used to access expensive AI services.

In a report titled "Black October for AI Developer Platforms," Wiz identified at least nine security incidents affecting AI development platforms during the month, including Northflank, Railway, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI.

The Railway incident also involved potential exposure of decrypted customer environment variables, while OpenCode disclosed exposed AI API keys. Warp reported a breach that exposed AI agent logs and user telemetry data.

Wiz says attackers involved in some of these incidents have specifically targeted environment variables containing AI service credentials, which can be exploited through a practice known as LLMJacking.

LLMJacking involves using stolen credentials to access AI models using another organization's API keys, generating massive API charges or allowing the stolen access to be resold.

In two cases investigated by Wiz, compromised enterprise credentials were used to make approximately 2.5 million Amazon Bedrock API calls, generating approximately $100,000 in AI usage.

The researchers also discovered infrastructure linked to services reselling access to AI models, although they could not link those operations to the initial breaches or large-scale abuse.

Wiz has not confirmed that all nine incidents were conducted by the same attackers. However, many of the incidents involved attempts to steal AI API keys.

Northflank also referenced Wiz's research in its incident updates, noting that customer reports of unauthorized AI key usage may be tied to the attacks seen by the researchers.

Title: Chainalysis discloses data breach from "offensive agentic techniques"
Context: Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers...
Full Text:
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis has disclosed a security incident after attackers used what it describes as "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its internal systems and tools.

The company says some customer information was accessed, including names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels, but claims there is no evidence that sensitive investigation data or authentication credentials were exposed.

Chainalysis says attackers accessed internal systems and tools

Chainalysis provides blockchain analytics tools used by law enforcement, government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, and financial institutions to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering.

On Friday, roughly 5:14 PM ET, Chainalysis published a security incident disclosure along with the full text of the email sent to affected customers.

The disclosure says the company detected an external actor using "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools earlier this month, and has since been patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems.

The accessed data includes user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels for users provisioned on the platform.

Chainalysis is still determining which records were accessed for each organization and will provide a detailed breakdown once that analysis is complete.

A Chainalysis spokesperson confirmed the incident to BleepingComputer and said the company is working with external cybersecurity experts. It is also using large language models (LLMs) to support a broader security review of its platform.

"Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens," the company said, adding that the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance theft.

Customers are advised to enable two-factor authentication (2FA) and watch for unexpected password reset requests, authentication prompts, and scammers impersonating Chainalysis, particularly those offering fund recovery or recruiting services.

What are "offensive agentic techniques"?

Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers had access.

It is unclear whether the attackers used existing agentic offensive security frameworks, such as ARTEX, or custom-built AI agents capable of autonomously identifying vulnerabilities, exploiting them, and chaining together subsequent actions.

ARTEX has recently been used by threat actors, including in the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, according to Microsoft.

The term "agentic" generally describes AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks with limited human intervention, potentially allowing attackers to automate portions of the intrusion process rather than relying on traditional hands-on exploitation.

A relentless week of security incidents

The Chainalysis disclosure comes amid a relentless week of security incidents affecting the cryptocurrency and technology industries.

On Friday, Binance linked the roughly $6.3 billion theft, now the largest crypto heist on record and attributed to North Korean state-backed hackers, to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.

Separately, hardware wallet maker Trezor warned of a suspected cryptocurrency-stealing implant reported in a Trezor Safe 5 device sold by a Southeast Asian reseller. The implant can reportedly read the recovery phrase shown on the device's screen and transmit it over a mobile network.

Meanwhile, a malicious version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor extension marketplace, planting persistent SSH backdoors on developers' machines.

Chainalysis says it will share further updates with affected customers as its investigation progresses.

Title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
Context: Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.

Title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
Context: The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator
Full Text:
VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.

If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.

This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

Endpoint

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions

Default model

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6

Fallback chain

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash

Temperature

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output

Request format

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection.Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash.

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host.Figure 6. The organized collection targets.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”).

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.

Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.

Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

Title: Syrian Hacker Gets Prison Time in US After Over a Decade on the Run
Context: A Syrian man tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA) has received a 42-month prison sentence in the US, more than 12 years after he was first charged
Full Text:
A Syrian man tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA) has received a 42-month prison sentence in the US, more than 12 years after he was first charged.

Ahmad Umar Agha, who used the online handle Th3Pr0, was sentenced on Thursday by a federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia. According to the Justice Department, he evaded US authorities for more than a decade.

Prosecutors say the hacking conspiracy Agha took part in was directed by figures close to Bashar al-Assad, among them the head of Syria’s General Intelligence Directorate. The scheme began as early as August 2011 and continued until January 2024.

The DOJ described Agha as a central figure in the operation. He compromised around 47 targets, a mix of Western news outlets, companies, NGOs, and government bodies in the US and allied countries.

Among the intrusions highlighted by prosecutors was the 2013 takeover of the Associated Press’s Twitter account. Agha used it to publish a fabricated report claiming that President Barack Obama had been hurt in two blasts at the White House. The fake post triggered a flash crash that briefly wiped $136 billion off the combined value of the Dow Jones Industrial Average’s component stocks.

Agha also gained access to the company hosting the Marine Corps’ recruiting website and sent its traffic to an image calling on Marines to defy their orders.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

He twice went after the White House’s social media presence by targeting the email credentials of White House employees. In one case he obtained them, but his attempt to use that access to dupe other staffers into handing over the accounts did not work.

The intrusions left many victims with large bills for cleanup and security overhauls. A firm providing online publishers with content, advertising, and outbound links lost around $35,000 per day for about six months. A global NGO spent roughly $250,000 on new network monitoring tools, retrained more than 800 employees, and upgraded its security, with total losses of $480,000.

Agha and his alleged accomplice, Firas Dardar, were first charged by criminal complaint in June 2014. The case was unsealed in March 2016, when the FBI put both men on its Cyber’s Most Wanted list and offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to Agha’s arrest.

A grand jury indicted the pair in May 2018. Dardar has yet to be caught.

Agha’s appearance in a federal courtroom in November 2025 was first reported by legal news outlet Court Watch. The DOJ’s announcement does not explain how or where he was taken into custody.

Title: A Shared ChatGPT Link Could Run Attacker Code in Your Session and Read Private Chats
Context: A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at...
Full Text:
A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at the security firm Parameter showed.

The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category.

The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared via its public link. It could be sent the same way as any real shared chat: by email, as a chat message, as a support ticket, or as a social post.

The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version of the attack, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once. In a later version, Parameter set the page to open Preview on its own, so opening the link was the only step.

What the Attacker Could Do

Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server controlled by the researchers.

The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly, rather than copying what happened to be on the screen. Because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. "Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account," the researchers wrote.

The work was a controlled test. Parameter does not report any real-world use of the flaw, and ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users.

How the Link Broke Out of Its Sandbox

Here is how the chain worked, according to Parameter. ChatGPT can turn a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page through a feature called Preview. Because that page can hold any code, ChatGPT runs it in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, where it cannot read the main ChatGPT page around it.

That sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation.

The shared chat also contained an interactive graph, and drawing it loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page. Loading MathLive left a listener running there that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard.

A message passed between browser frames is safe only if the receiver checks who sent it. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender, and that the message was allowed to carry raw HTML. The Preview could then reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page.

That HTML built a new frame that the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com. A script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it.

ChatGPT's content security policy limits where a page's scripts may come from. It blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube, which is why that step worked.

What OpenAI Fixed, and What Users Should Do

Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on.

The researchers traced the problem to three design choices that lined up:

MathLive acted on a message that changed its settings without checking which frame had sent it.

That message was allowed to carry raw HTML as keyboard-layout data.

The HTML could create a frame that was not sandboxed and inherited the chatgpt.com identity.

The YouTube step was only the final workaround, not the cause. Blocking it alone would still leave an untrusted Preview able to push HTML into the main site.

ChatGPT users do not need to do anything. The fix is on OpenAI's side, with nothing to install or reset.

Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix. OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report.

Title: Cloudflare Reports 18.2 Million Network-Layer DDoS Attacks in Q3, Up 38%
Context: Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday
Full Text:
Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday.

The web infrastructure and security company said it autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer (L3) DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests in the third quarter of 2026. That amounts to 197,400 attacks per day, or one attack every 0.44 seconds.

In comparison, a total of 13.2 million and 10.0 million L3 DDoS attacks were recorded in Q2 and Q1 2026, respectively. The increase has been linked to DDoS-for-hire booter or stresser services that are responsible for hundreds of thousands of attacks.

"Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%," the Cloudforce One threat intelligence team said in its quarterly DDoS Threat Report shared with The Hacker News.

An interesting trend is the decline of hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps by 69% from the previous quarter – going from 805 attacks in Q2 to 251 in Q3 – likely as a result of law enforcement actions against AISURU, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad earlier this March.

Still, the threat remains far from completely neutralized, given the emergence of new variants like Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot, Cloudflare warned.

Another notable shift is the decline in Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) floods, while DNS amplification jumped 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks.

The most targeted industries include media, production, and publishing; information technology and services; gambling and casinos; computer software; and telecommunications providers.

The U.S., China, Indonesia, the U.K., and Türkiye emerged as the most attacked countries during the time period, with Canada and Israel entering the top 10 ranking, fueled by attacks targeting Canada's retail, telecommunications, and marketing sectors.

On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails.

Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete.

Attack chain overview

A malicious artifact associated with the Cursor Marketplace incident included a JavaScript function that executed before the extension’s expected code. When the module loads, this function can use Node.js APIs to collect host information, modify files, and execute operating-system commands. The following sections describe capabilities and attempted actions based on our analysis of the injected code.

Attack chain

The loader first collects host reconnaissance. It then attempts to install an SSH key, enable SSH, create a reverse tunnel, and configure persistence. A delayed callback subsequently attempts to send host details. The following sequence reflects code execution order; it does not prove that every step succeeded on every host.

Module loading and reconnaissance collection. The injected function executes before normal extension initialization and collects host and user information.

SSH access preparation. The loader appends an embedded public key and attempts to enable the local SSH service.

Reverse forwarding. An embedded tunnel identity authenticates an outbound connection that requests forwarding to the workstation’s SSH port.

Platform-specific persistence. Scripts and startup configuration are written to relaunch the connection.

Host reconnaissance reporting. After the access and persistence setup attempts, a delayed callback attempts to transmit the previously collected host details and selected environment-variable names.

Figure 1. Attack chain reconstructed from the injected code.

The loader uses embedded components and built-in system tools to establish persistent access without downloading another executable. It suppresses command output and silently catches errors to conceal failures and malicious activity, while the extension continues functioning normally to avoid alerting users.

Host reconnaissance collection

The loader collects the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, home directory, working directory, and global Git email. It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP, keeping up to forty matches.

The callback sends matching environment-variable names, not values. This reveals potentially sensitive configuration categories but does not demonstrate theft of the secrets stored in those variables.

Collection occurs during module loading. The collected details are retained for the delayed reporting callback described after the persistence stage.

SSH authorization and tunnel identities

The loader uses two SSH identities with distinct roles. One public key authorizes access to the workstation’s user account, while a separate private key authenticates the outbound connection to the tunnel server. First, the loader checks the user’s authorized_keys file for the comment svc-telemetry. If the marker is missing, it appends an embedded Ed25519 public key. That creates an authorization entry for whoever holds the corresponding private key, subject to the local SSH server’s configuration.

Next, it decodes a separate private key for the outbound connection. The initial copy is written to a hidden temporary file named .stk_ followed by ten hexadecimal characters derived from the hostname and home directory. SSH receives that file through its -i option and connects using the remote account tunnel.

The public-key material is redacted but the format is similar to the following:

ssh-ed25519 [REDACTED PUBLIC KEY] svc-telemetry

Protocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwarding

The tunneling SSH process is launched with the command line containing the following arguments:

-N -R '*:0:localhost:22'

It requests a listening port on the remote SSH server and forwards connections through the tunnel to port 22 on the victim’s loopback interface. The remote port value 0 asks the server to allocate a port; it does not change the local target from port 22. The -N option tells SSH not to run a command on the tunnel server.

This design starts with an outbound connection from the workstation rather than waiting for a direct inbound connection to it. The loader disables ordinary host-key checking, bypasses the normal known-hosts file, sets keepalives, and avoids interactive prompts. On Unix-like systems it prefers autossh, falling back to ssh; on Windows it uses a hidden PowerShell loop. The loops wait sixty seconds after SSH exits before retrying.

Figure 2. Terminal-style SSH command configuring an outbound reverse tunnel from a server-assigned remote port to the workstation’s local SSH service on port 22. Host-key verification is disabled, and the identity-file path is redacted.

A running SSH process does not necessarily mean the attacker gained access. Both the attacker’s server and the victim’s workstation must allow the connection, and server settings determine whether the tunnel is publicly reachable. Cursor reports that errors and administrator-permission requirements blocked SSH access on most macOS and Windows hosts. However, the malware could still attempt to plant its SSH key, establish persistence, and report host information.

Platform-specific startup persistence

The loader writes platform-specific scripts and startup configuration outside the extension directory. The following table summarizes these mechanisms and their associated artifacts. The code attempts to configure persistence, but the presence of an artifact alone does not establish that the startup mechanism ran successfully.

Platform

Startup mechanism

Key artifacts

macOS

User LaunchAgent with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive

User-crontab @reboot entry

On Unix-like systems, the .smt script reconstructs the persistent .smtk identity when it runs, then starts its own SSH retry loop. On Windows, the loader writes the identity and batch script directly.

The startup objects use names such as SysMon and com.apple.sysmond, which resemble monitoring components. Behind these names, their configured actions invoke the generated scripts that maintain reverse SSH forwarding.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Run advanced hunting queries below to identify affected systems and investigate systems where users installed or automatically updated anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313 and 2.1.312 through the Cursor Extension Marketplace. Review extension-installation records and correlate endpoint, network, file, process, and authentication telemetry with the published indicators. Preserve the extension package, modified SSH authorization files, generated keys and scripts, and startup configuration before cleanup. Isolate devices with evidence of loader execution or backdoor installation.

Remediation actions

After evidence collection, check the affected user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on macOS and Linux for the attacker-controlled key labeled svc-telemetry. On Windows, check both %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys and C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys, where present. Confirm the key against the fingerprint in Indicators of Compromise before removing the exact unauthorized entry. Preserve unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development configuration. A missing marker alone should not replace review of the installation, process, network, and persistence evidence.

Remove the trojanized extension and confirmed malicious persistence after evidence collection. Inspect each startup object’s configured action before removal; names alone are not sufficient to distinguish malicious objects from legitimate monitoring software.

macOS: Unload and remove the malicious user LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist and remove its associated ~/.config/.smt script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Linux: Remove the malicious user-crontab @reboot entry referencing ~/.config/.smt, preserving unrelated entries, and remove the associated script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Windows: Remove the malicious SysMon scheduled task, the Startup-folder sysmon.cmd fallback, and associated %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd and %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk files.

All applicable platforms: Stop confirmed malicious SSH and retry processes and remove their temporary .stk_ identity files after collection.

Cursor published platform-specific checks and remediation scripts in its security notice. Review the scripts and execution requirements before use, then verify that no listed artifacts remain. Cleanup does not replace investigation of device activity during the exposure window.

Removing or updating the extension does not remove artifacts written outside its installation directory. Remove confirmed unauthorized SSH keys, tunnel identities, scripts, and startup entries separately. Cursor’s reported server takedown does not remove artifacts already present on a device.

Follow-up Investigation and recovery

Review telemetry after the extension loaded for SSH key acceptance, tunnel processes, local SSH sessions, command execution, and file activity. Rotate credentials and revoke sessions from a known-clean device when telemetry indicates credential access or when device trust cannot be restored. Rebuild the device when required by the investigation and verify that the tunnel and startup artifacts do not return after login or restart.

To reduce the risk of malicious extensions and extension-based supply chain attacks, organizations using Cursor should apply the relevant controls in Cursor’s security-hardening guidance, including restricting extensions to approved publishers and configuring an extension installation cooldown to delay installation of newly published versions. These measures can help limit exposure to malicious releases.

Advanced hunting queries

The following queries use the Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting schema and the time range selected in the portal. A result is an investigative lead, not proof of compromise.

Title: Yoba Malware Hides a Crypto Miner Behind Legitimate OpenAI and Anthropic Binaries
Context: “The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first...
Full Text:
Yoba malware uses fake ChatGPT and Claude apps to sideload malware through signed installers and deploy a cryptocurrency miner.

Check Point Research has spent two months tracking a campaign it calls Yoba, which uses the popularity of AI tools to spread a custom malware chain. The attackers build fake GitHub projects that pose as AI desktop applications such as GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus. The projects look convincing and run on real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them seem legitimate to potential victims.

“These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload.” reads the report. “In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.”

The lure is simple. Each project has a repository, a GitHub.io page describing the software, and a ZIP release with the malware. The repositories show no fake stars or forks, yet they still rank among the top Google results, most likely through SEO poisoning that optimizes titles, descriptions and hosting domains.

The first repository appeared around July 2026, but the first malicious releases landed only on August 30 and 31, and a third followed about five days later on September 4. Each repository uses a different Outlook address, and commit times point to UTC+4, UTC-4 and UTC+3, which Check Point reads as a deliberate attempt to hide the actor’s real time zone.

Here’s the trick that gives the report its title. Each ZIP holds a legitimate signed executable from OpenAI or Anthropic, named Setup.exe, next to a malicious winmm.dll. The signed program loads the DLL on its own, a technique known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.

The ZIP files were not even password-protected. Attackers often use passwords to prevent security tools from automatically unpacking and scanning files. However, these binaries already had very low detection rates because they used anti-sandbox and other techniques to avoid analysis. The DLL’s compilation date is another clue: it was built on the same day it was added to the archive, unlike the legitimate files around it.

The dropper, called YobaDropper, checks the environment before running. It calculates a hash of the name of the program that launched it and continues only if the name is Setup.exe. This means that sandboxes that run the DLL on its own will fail this check. When that happens, the process does not exit. Instead, it sleeps 200,000 times for 5.5 seconds each, a total of about 12.73 days.

The malware also avoids victims in CIS countries by checking the keyboard layout. It excludes Russian, Belarusian, Tajik, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Georgian, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Turkmen, Uzbek, and Tatar. Interestingly, Ukraine, which has often appeared in similar exclusion lists, is not included.

Next, the malware requests administrator privileges. If the user does not have them, it displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” and exits. The victim must then restart it with administrator rights.

Once it has the required privileges, the malware creates a folder called WMProcess under ProgramData. It copies the legitimate WMPDMC.exe file from System32 into this folder and places the second-stage payload there under the name wmpdui.dll.

The malicious code achieves persistence by using a scheduled task dressed up as Microsoft. The author is set to Microsoft Corporation, the description says it collects device metadata for Windows Media Player, and it starts three minutes after boot as Local System. The task launches the legitimate program, which sideloads the malicious DLL.

The second stage, YobaLoader, shares code with the dropper, which points to the same developer. It only runs under WMPDMC.exe and uses a different seed for its hashing than the dropper does, which separates the stages and weakens hash-based detection. Its job is to find its payload without a classic command server.

It goes to a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub, and downloads the channel’s profile picture. The last 50 bytes of the image seed a domain generator that builds names from word lists in the form adjective-noun-verb-number on dedyn[.]io. Change the picture and the operator gets a new domain.

Then it asks Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS service for a TXT record on that domain. The reply is signed, and the loader checks the signature before decrypting it, which gives a link to a payload on Catbox. Check Point says this reliance on DoH and common hosting aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway protections, and the campaign avoids dedicated command-and-control infrastructure, using Telegram, Tor, Catbox and DoH instead.

The operator can choose how the payload runs. It can inject it into svchost.exe, save it as an executable after removing the Zone.Identifier mark, or run it as a hidden PowerShell script while bypassing execution policies.

“Finally, the injected payload into svchost.exe is an XMRig 6.26.0 miner with a hidden command line targeting a TLS-enabled onion mining endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. It can unpack and start Tor 0.4.9.12 plus lyrebird 0.8.1, monitor user-input activity to pause mining, and conditionally load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based mining optimization.” continnues the report.

The miner uses Tor to connect to an encrypted mining server. It can start its own Tor components, use about 85% of CPU threads, and pause mining when the user is active. It resumes after 240 seconds of inactivity and can load the WinRing0 driver to optimize mining performance.

However, YobaLoader is not limited to cryptocurrency mining. Its DNS tasking system allows operators to deliver any PE executable or PowerShell payload, meaning future attacks could distribute other malware families.

Earlier versions appeared in June 2026. They used Cursor.exe for sideloading, a startup shortcut for persistence, and excluded only Russia. They also used .aber[.]ir instead of dedyn[.]io and included anti-debugging and anti-VM checks that later versions dropped.

Check Point believes the attackers may have Russian origins and mainly operate in the UTC-4 time zone, but this is an assessment, not a confirmed attribution.

Defenders should look for suspicious WMPDMC.exe copies under ProgramData, fake Microsoft scheduled tasks, Telegram-related traffic, DNS lookups for dedyn[.]io through dns.google, and unexplained high CPU usage.

“The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.” concludes the report. “Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Title: A Supply Chain Attack Put Malicious Anthropic Claude Extensions on Thousands of Devices
Context: “Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first...
Full Text:
The AI software-development platform Cursor, which is owned by SpaceX, had a malicious Anthropic Claude Code extension for Windows, macOS, and Linux live in its integrated development environment extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on Thursday. The company says the rogue extension was downloaded by “at most 5,000 users.” Cursor briefly shut down the extension marketplace while it investigated the situation, which the company says did not impact any other extensions.

The tainted extension was designed with a backdoor to give attackers access to victim devices—the type of implant that malicious hackers often use as a stepping stone to deeper control inside a target network. Cursor published remediation steps on Thursday for the roughly 5,000 affected targets. A saving grace of the situation, though, was a flaw in the malware's design that blocked it from fully establishing itself on the vast majority of targets.

“Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first researchers to spot the malicious extension after detecting it on a customer's Mac.

What is still unclear is how the malicious extension made its way into the Cursor marketplace at all. Some researchers initially speculated that it came from a compromised Anthropic system. But Cursor said in its Thursday security alert that “these malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.”

Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted on X on Friday: “We’re working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn’t build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected and this only impacts Cursor users.”

David Dworken, who works on security at Anthropic, posted on X shortly after, explaining that “this did not involve a compromise of any Anthropic systems … We were not involved with building, publishing, or hosting this.”

Cursor did not return WIRED's request for comment about how the malicious upload happened and whether it was the result of a breach at Cursor.

Title: “Are We Exposed?” What CISOs Need to Know About Their Software Risk
Context: Curl When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer
Full Text:
Recent events have once again highlighted the need to quickly answer the question, “Are we exposed?”

We now face threats to businesses and governments from vulnerabilities and compromises in three fundamental components used in software development: Curl, PHP, and LiteLLM.

Curl

When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer. With libcurl embedded in many enterprise environments – from backend microservices and container runtimes to automated CI/CD pipelines and shell scripts – this vulnerability carries potential systemic risk. The core threat centers on high-severity flaws disclosed in October 2026, notably a high-severity HTTP/2 use-after-free issue (such as CVE-2026-92392) where a malicious upstream server handling an upload can corrupt client-side memory and, under specific conditions, trigger remote code execution or application crashes on the machine initiating the transfer. Because libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for HTTPS URLs when the server supports it and applications rarely inspect what libcurl does under the hood, development stacks and automated deployment pipelines that have not upgraded to a fixed version can remain exposed to hostile external endpoints.

LiteLLM

Regarding LiteLLM, JFrog Security Research detected the problem within 2 hours, and the errant LiteLLM package, version 1.107.0, has already been removed from PyPI. Reflecting the open-source community ecosystem’s continually improving maturation, the package maintainers have already published a report. But from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on October 21, 2026, software developers, agentic agents, or your build systems could have downloaded that package from PyPI, and affected Docker images remained available until 14:20 UTC. The ripple effect of a compromised package or vulnerable component getting into an environment doesn’t just impact the developers or security team. It also impacts IT Ops and, down the line, auditors. Every change impacts the whole organization. Executives, the business decision makers who determine where to invest and allocate resources, need a way to understand where they sit in this maturity. Do they have complete visibility or not?

PHP

In the case of PHP, two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), were disclosed and referred to publicly as PHP2Shell. The bugs can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, according to public advisories. Within days, news outlets reported on the vulnerabilities, and CISA issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately, including CNBC and the BBC, CISA.

“Are We Exposed?”

When a CISO wrestles with the question of “Are we exposed?”, their triage process should focus on these key issues:

Is it really a threat?

Where is it being used?

What is the business impact?

Do I have a reporting or disclosure obligation under rules or standards that apply to my organization, such as those of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), PCI DSS, or, for product manufacturers, the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)?

Did we block it?

How do we fix it?

The CISO’s ability to answer these questions with confidence depends on how well they’ve integrated their tools, people, processes, and security program to provide that visibility and respond quickly to security incidents. The ability to do this, in turn, is a reflection of the maturity of their overall security program and how well they can protect, monitor, and govern the full gamut of software development operations – whether it’s on the developer’s workstation, in agentic workflows, or implemented directly by AI coding agents.

A true assessment of your organization’s abilities to determine your strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats is critical to providing a full 360 view of your risk posture.

Hands-On Assessment Experience

As a CISO, I’ve done these assessments on a number of occasions, for both new deployments and as an ongoing protective measure to help keep the business protected as new threats and vulnerabilities evolve.

These assessments should be broadly based and take into account business objectives, employee capabilities, workflows, data usage, and the maturity of the infrastructure. Covering these bases should give you an accurate compass of where you are and where you need to improve.

This should, of course, include your tools, but should not lead to one of the classic mistakes organizations make, which is over-focusing on tools, simply because they’re the easiest thing to measure. The other areas mentioned above are easy to overlook, but extremely important to a realistic assessment, as tools without the right people and processes won’t achieve the objective of protecting your business.

JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment

Based on JFrog’s experience working with many of the Fortune 100 customers and through the expertise of our in-house security research team, we’ve actually built our own Security Maturity Assessment. It lets organizations self-assess their software supply chain security program maturity across 11 domains, based on their answers.

I strongly recommend taking a few minutes out of your busy day to complete the questionnaire, as it assesses the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and risks in your software development operations and could help you identify where to start when it comes to ensuring you can truly answer the question: “Are we exposed?”

Takeaways

The question of “Are we exposed?” can be complicated and difficult to assess, but recent high-profile security incidents don’t give CISOs the luxury of taking days to come up with a reply. Corporate executives and board members need fast, accurate answers.

Having complete visibility into your people, processes, workflows, tools, and dependencies gives you the leverage to protect your business under the pressure of the latest attacks.
