Title: The Binance Breach | What Can be Reached and Why it Matters
Context: What we know is that the attacker allegedly used access to reach an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, highlighting how standing...
Full Text:
What you will learn

How standing privilege turns one compromised engineer laptop into financial loss, and how just-in-time access, scoped workload identities, session recording and external authorization decisions help contain the damage.

On October 29, 2026, Binance reportedly suffered a $6.3 billion theft with preliminary findings pointing to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as a possible entry point.

Binance hasn’t published its root cause yet, and we won’t try to diagnose it for them.

What we know is that the attacker allegedly used access to reach an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, highlighting how standing privilege can turn a compromised device into a path to financial loss.

Binance says it has found no evidence of a private key leak, and that further investigation uncovered additional points of breach. Its CEO has said the attack was more than misuse of a single engineer’s permissions. Blockchain analysts at TRM Labs concluded that the attacker most likely got Binance’s own signing system to sign transactions of the attacker’s choosing. If those findings hold, the keys inside the infrastructure should be safe.

The attacker borrowed the authority of the systems trusted to use them. This is a common pattern we see in the field and will continue to see until just-in-time and zero standing privilege are the norm. Developers cannot be excluded from this security posture.

Engineering laptops routinely carry kubeconfigs, cloud sessions and SSH keys because they are convenient and frictionless. Production workloads carry identities that can move money, change data or alter infrastructure. Anyone who can get a shell inside a workload inherits that workload’s identity. Developer-targeted social engineering, including fake job interviews with malicious “coding tests,” is a well-documented technique used by the North Korean group that analysts have linked to this incident.

The useful question isn’t whether an engineer’s laptop can be compromised, because eventually one will be, the useful question is “What can that laptop reach without anyone else knowing or approving?” Every organization should be asking that question, especially with the advent of AI-assisted attacks. Imagine Black Hat chaos monkey in your org.

The answer “nobody touches production” is incorrect because engineers still have to fix things at 3am.

The right answer is good access design, and that looks like this:

no standing access to systems that can provide value (e.g., production)

elevation that is fast, short-lived, scoped to the task, and either approved or visible to the team

sessions that are recorded and watched for activity that doesn’t match the stated purpose

workload identities scoped so that infrastructure access doesn’t automatically confer transaction authority

authorization decisions made outside the workload requesting them, so a compromised service can’t approve its own actions

While this is not a guarantee against a patient, well-resourced adversary, it will put up a significant defense in the event of an eventual “assume breach” scenario. Binance’s final report may also surface factors that no access control would have addressed. But together they turn one compromised endpoint from a path to the treasury into a contained incident.

The same principle applies to AI agents, which increasingly operate with delegated credentials in production.

PS: Betting $1 that during an interview, the engineer was asked to install something to complete a challenge...

Title: Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor
Context: The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a
Full Text:
Anthropic's official Claude Code extension for the Cursor VS Code Marketplace was hijacked and swapped out for a malicious version with a persistent backdoor.

The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a.m. GMT to 8:35 p.m. GMT, on Oct. 29, according to Cursor's disclosure. Any software developers who downloaded or updated Claude Code in their Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) during that time would have received a malicious version 2.1.313, which pilfered sensitive data from infected machines and, in a minority of cases, could have allowed attackers persistent, privileged access to users' systems.

Cursor stated that "at most 5,000 users were affected," and that they will be contacted about the incident directly.

Separately that same day, researchers described an unrelated exploit in Cursor, allowing attackers to deploy arbitrary code to developers' machines via Cursor's built-in browser.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Cursor did not immediately respond to an inquiry from Dark Reading regarding both of these stories.

Cursor's Claude Code Conundrum

For some, the notion of a compromised "extension" might evoke browser extensions, which are so frequently vulnerable, suspicious, and outright malicious that cybersecurity news concerning them tends not to evoke much panic, even in extreme cases.

Extensions in coding environments are a different beast. "IDE extensions are scarier than browser extensions because, unlike browser extensions, they are designed to have the same level of permissions as their host," Gal Weizman, security researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading. "They can run code, access the filesystem, fire network requests and more."

On Thursday, an attacker tried to leverage the power afforded by coding environment extensions by sneaking a 66-line loader on top of the real extension's legitimate code. According to an analysis from the community threat intelligence platform OpenSourceMalware, everything about the extension remained the same besides this lone edit to its extension.js file.

As soon as the extension loaded — without need for the user to establish a Claude conversation — the new file is revved up. It attempts to add an attacker-controlled key to victims' SSH configurations, with the goal of establishing reverse tunnels that act as a backdoor into the compromised systems.

The malicious extension also attempts to make those connections persistent by registering background processes — for macOS systems, a LaunchAgent; and for Windows, scheduled tasks running with system privileges, plus a fallback Startup script. This whole business was doomed from the start, Cursor wrote, since turning on the local SSH service requires administrative privileges, which the Claude Code extension only possesses in "highly unusual circumstances."

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

Victims weren't totally out of the woods, though, as the malicious code also exfiltrated system information via separate Web requests. Stolen data was limited to hostnames, usernames, operating systems (OS), OS architectures, home directory paths, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git emails, and public IP addresses.

Cursor Contains Compromise

Cursor's public disclosure suggests that the security incident was its own, not Anthropic's. The malicious version "was not developed by Anthropic," the SpaceX-owned company reported.

In response to the discovery, Cursor took a variety of steps to protect itself: rotating its keys, checking for tampering in other extensions, and taking its marketplace temporarily offline and rebuilding it. It also worked with the relevant cloud hosting provider to take down the attacker's malicious infrastructure.

Cursor did not specify how the intrusion occurred in the first place. While acknowledging that it's not yet known what happened here, Weizman explains, "Historically, the most common way extensions and plug-ins get hijacked is through theft of locally stored credentials that allow publishing new versions of these packages."

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

"Enabling 2FA for publishing such extensions is an excellent way to significantly mitigate such risk in the future. Relying on an access token as the only gate for pushing such critical software significantly increases the risk of this happening," he says.

More Security Concerns for Cursor, AI Assistants

On the same day of the Anthropic Cursor attack, Weizman published separate research detailing weaknesses in the browsers built into top desktop AI assistants today, which could be exploited to devastating effect. His test cases included Claude Desktop, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Cursor. Cursor has arguably the worst issue of the bunch.

In his experiments, Weizman's team created a clean-looking website, with a visible HTML chip concealing a malicious shell command in its attributes. Then they opened up the site in a built-in Cursor browser. "When the command hit Cursor's safety sandbox and was blocked, the agent — on its own, with nothing in the page telling it to — switched the sandbox off and tried again. The control worked. The agent talked itself out of using it," Weizman wrote in the report.

The attack didn't work universally across all models. When it did work, the browser escape allowed the researchers to deploy an arbitrary app to their test victim's computer. And just like the malicious Claude Code extension, the app ran with the victim's full permissions. Cursor did not respond to Forever Security's disclosure, but the company quietly patched the issue on Oct. 1.

“IDEs are becoming more agentic. They're being given agentic capabilities, which can introduce dangerous architecture. It can be very risky when things go wrong," Weizman says.

"Here we've had two examples of that: built-in browsers, and what happened with Claude Code, both of which impacted Cursor," he concludes. "And because of the rapid pace at which this is happening, security isn't necessarily keeping up."

Title: Warning: Romance Scammers Are Targeting US Citizens For Money Laundering
Context: Threat actors are using romance scams to trick U
Full Text:
Threat actors are using romance scams to trick U.S. citizens into acting as money mules, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Journal cites the example of Garrick Stafford, a 50-year-old Texas man who lost $65,000 and unwittingly laundered $50,000 for an international crime ring after falling for an online scammer posing as an attractive woman.

Notably, Stafford was texting with the scammer all summer before the individual first asked for money, claiming that she needed $150 to pay her cellphone bill. Stafford immediately recognized this as a red flag and blocked the individual. Months later, however, he unblocked her, and they began texting again.

“Stafford still isn’t sure why he didn’t cut her off for good after that first request for money, but by Christmas that year, he realized he missed her,” the Journal says. “Once they reconnected, though, the asks only grew. Several thousand dollars for a seminar in digital design. Seed money for an antiques business. Medical costs for her sick mother.” In addition to asking Stafford for his own money, the threat actor’s primary objective was to use Stafford’s bank account to launder money stolen in separate scams.

“Whenever a payment arrived in Stafford’s account, Sarah would frantically press him to move the money into various crypto wallets—sometimes requiring him to leave work,” the Journal says. “He briefly set up other accounts, but banks, suspecting illegal activity, would soon freeze them. Still, Sarah always had a reason why she couldn’t open her own accounts or make the transfers herself—citing bad credit or a move to London from Miami. In all, Stafford said, about $50,000 moved through his account or others she had him set up, while another $100,000 in bad checks she sent him bounced.”

A police detective in South Carolina eventually notified Stafford that he was being scammed, and “Sarah” turned out to be a married couple in Nigeria who used AI to respond to his texts.

John Breyault, vice president of the National Consumers League, told the WSJ, “Romantic interest is a very strong emotion. Scammers recognize this and devote a lot of time to develop the trust needed to exploit the victim.”

The Wall Street Journal has the story: https://www.wsj.com/us-news/romance-scammers-turned-a-texas-man-into-an-unwitting-money-mule-b440be36

Title: Crim spent $7K+ on AI services in extortion attacks, then left evidence for all to see
Context: “We found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined
Full Text: A n0n ransomware operator tried to break into 23 organizations across 14 countries, but couldn't secure its own front door, leaving its server exposed with all of its methods on view. The criminals used a mix of new (AI) and old (stolen credentials) tooling during their data-theft spree, and in some cases not only stole and encrypted files, but also deleted data and backups, eliminating victims’ ability to recover their information. And despite the fear and hype around the breachpocalypse, with AI finding and developing exploits for critical vulnerabilities affecting most organizations across the globe, these crooks did not exploit a single bug to gain entry into any of their victims’ IT environments. “In every documented compromise in this investigation, access relied on weak or stolen credentials,” said Ensar Seker, chief information security officer of threat intelligence firm SOCRadar. “What stands out is the combination of AI-assisted development and very conventional entry points,” Seker told The Register. “We found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined.” The gang breaks into organizations at scale using widespread Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) scanning and automated FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing. To access US-based IT managed services provider ChiBiTek, the crew used a 15-thread residential SOCKS5 proxy pool to test credentials (ip:port:user:password) against FortiGate portals (GET /remote/login). The operators also gained entry using exposed cloud credentials and reused hosting portal sessions. In one case linked to e-commerce site Fanatics, SOCRadar found that n0n used an exposed AWS access key with permissions to list, read, and delete objects in S3 buckets. The criminals then used this key to pull data from 40 S3 buckets, with up to 110 GB per bucket, and ultimately deleted data, including bank-transaction archives, and purged keys across 12 sensitive buckets. AI-assisted extortion While the threat hunters didn’t find any evidence of a fully autonomous attack system, the ransomware operator did use AI to assist with these intrusions, incurring more than $7,216 in AI usage costs by October 22. Specifically: the criminal or criminals used OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, configured with 154 model entries across seven providers. Models included Gemini, Mistral, Nemotron, Llama, Claude, GPT-5.x, Grok, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Qwen, and many, many others, some with safety training removed and others marketed as “uncensored” models. “The operator used AI to write and debug hundreds of scripts. That shows how AI can help an attacker turn basic access into a broader, tailored operation,” Seker said. “The destructive behavior is equally significant,” he added. “The operator did more than steal and encrypt files: in some cases, it deleted data and backups, and in one case changed firewall policies to block traffic. That creates a recovery problem that a decryption key alone cannot solve.” SOCRadar’s threat hunters found the operator’s workspace - a publicly accessible Python HTTP file server hosted in Sweden at 185.157.161[.]148 on port 8877 - last month, and documented the exposed directory in snapshots on September 25 and 26. “Across those snapshots, we identified 1,719 files, including attack scripts, ransomware source code, extortion infrastructure, and an AI coding agent environment,” Seker said. “This gave us visibility into the operation behind the victim listings, including how the operator prepared attacks and handled stolen data.” Meet n0n It also provided a close look at n0n, a newcomer to the data-theft and extortion game that has claimed 108 victims since it emerged last month. On October 12, the group added 38 maritime, port and logistics organizations across 18 countries to its leak site in a single batch. Researchers have linked at least 21 of them to customers of South Korean maritime software provider CyberLogitec, although the software provider has not confirmed an intrusion. The crooks set an October 19 deadline for the maritime firms, with ransom demands ranging from $400,000 to $28 million, payable in Bitcoin. After the deadline, however, none of the 38 listings were marked “settled” and none of their payment addresses showed any transaction. All affected organizations’ stolen data was published. While a handful of the gang’s claimed victims have been marked “honored - data destroyed” on n0n’s leak site, indicating the victim orgs paid the ransom demand, SOCRadar hasn’t validated any transactions on-chain. In its profile details, the security shop rates the gang a 10 out of 10 for "aggressiveness" and a zero out of 10 for “lethality.” The group is believed to be based in Russia, although the server uncovered by SOCRadar, which it attributed to a single operator or small team, didn’t provide any definitive geographic or national attribution. Every case that the exposed server documented followed the same lifecycle, moving from initial access to establishing persistence and credential collection via hidden admin accounts disguised as services, covert proxies, credential and session-token theft, mailboxes and emailed multi-factor authentication codes. The crooks then collected sensitive data and sent everything to the operator’s central storage with the attack impact shifting between data-theft, encryption, destruction, and network disruption, depending on the targeted organization. After breaking into Transcom, a Netherlands-based financial services provider, the crims sent a secondary ransom alert directly to PayPal's security team, even though the compromised data was only on Transcom's network. Stupid mistakes and n0n security basics Finally, the crims send ransom notes, post a countdown clock on the leak site, establish negotiation rooms and emails for victims - and then leak the stolen files or destroy backups when the organizations don’t pay up. In some cases, and to apply increased pressure on victimized companies, n0n also broadcasts automated countdown warnings to businesses’ service providers, clients, and media outlets. Despite its aggressive tactics, the operator in this case - as with other stupid criminals The Register has gleefully documented in earlier stories - still struggles with basic security hygiene. “There is a striking gap between operational ambition and security discipline,” Seker said. “The operator invested thousands of dollars in AI services while leaving its own workspace exposed. The locker also contained hardcoded encryption keys, with evidence suggesting reuse across victims. An operation can have serious destructive capability while still making fundamental mistakes.”®

Title: Chinese Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX to Target Over 200 Organizations Worldwide
Context: "It orchestrates multiple LLM backends to autonomously perform reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and exploitation, significantly lowering the technical barrier for...
Full Text:
Chinese state-sponsored threat actors have been observed using a Go-based artificial intelligence (AI)-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX in attacks aimed at high-value targets simultaneously.

The activity has been attributed by CrowdStrike to a China-based "targeted intrusion adversary" it tracks under the moniker Vapor Panda (previously VexatiousTemper). First identified in February 2021, the hacking group overlaps with a threat cluster detailed by Trend Micro as Earth Estries.

"Agentic tooling like ARTEX enables this scale of expansion at speed, allowing a small team to pursue a wider target set than manual operations would support, rather than a wholesale shift away from the adversary's established access-development mission," CrowdStrike said in a Thursday analysis.

Starting October 17, 2026, Vapor Panda is said to have used the AI tool against more than 200 distinct organizations across the world, including foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S.; and telecommunications providers in multiple regions.

Some of the notable targets listed by CrowdStrike are listed below -

Foreign ministries of two Latin America-based countries, Central America, and Asia

A Middle East-based interior ministry

A European country's foreign ministry, presidency, and prime minister's office, along with defense, justice, finance, and intelligence entities

19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors

Telecommunications providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines

Post-exploitation activity has been confirmed at nine organizations, allowing the attacker to deploy BLOODALCHEMY, a derivative of ShadowPad, followed by credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance.

Vapor Panda is also said to have conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning activity against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe.

Central to the operation is the use of ARTEX with DeepSeek and an as-yet-unknown, subscription-based commercial large language model (LLM) to conduct the intrusions at scale, leveraging an army of planner and worker agents that coordinate with each other in pursuit of a common goal to move from initial access to host reconnaissance and lateral movement.

A human operator in the loop oversees the operation, directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and enumerate endpoint sensor coverage.

"In a single intrusion, Vapor Panda's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, indicating the scale of the automated activity and implying far higher consumption across the operation as a whole," CrowdStrike said.

Unlike some campaigns that used to assist with individual digital break-ins, the use of ARTEX is at a much higher level to run multiple engagements concurrently, with the human operator only stepping in to steer the agents to accomplish their objective, while taking steps to bypass endpoint defenses.

Analysis of the recovered transcripts highlights the use of ARTEX in combination with tried-and-tested approaches -

Chaining an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion and an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service. This is followed by obtaining a role that can issue administration commands to thousands of instances before escalating access to recover an enterprise administrator account.

Deploying web shells, abusing an unauthenticated orchestration service to obtain root access in a production container environment, reading Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, and leveraging resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account.

Supplying the agent with a set of authentication keys that had not been rotated since 2022, which then uses those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes. In the next phase, the agent uses VPN configurations recovered from a user's sent mail, along with a VPN client key originating from a purported May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network.

"Across these engagements, the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel, spanning web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure," CrowdStrike explained. "They shifted to alternative approaches when a path failed. This breadth likely enables a single operator to apply a wider range of techniques against more targets at once than would be feasible through manual operations."

The development comes as ARTEX has witnessed broad adoption among threat actors in a short span of time, prompting its developer Li Puhua ("Autumn-27") to take it closed source.

"It orchestrates multiple LLM backends to autonomously perform reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and exploitation, significantly lowering the technical barrier for conducting complex intrusion campaigns," Zscaler ThreatLabz said in a report published earlier this month.

One of Many Panda Threat Clusters

The disclosure also coincides with the emergence of four previously undocumented China-linked state-sponsored threat groups known as Hollow Panda, Overcast Panda, Titan Panda, and Veiled Panda, which have targeted a broad range of sectors across the world for intelligence gathering and intellectual property theft.

Overcast Panda, described as "one of the most operationally sophisticated and persistent threats facing organizations with personnel traveling to China," has been linked to close access intrusions in which the adversary has deployed their proprietary FlowCloud backdoor on victims' devices via direct physical access when those targets were in the country.

FlowCloud is launched by means of DLL sideloading, with its components designed to fly under the radar and resist forensic analysis. Command-and-control (C2) is accomplished through legitimate cloud infrastructure in an attempt to further conceal their presence.

"FlowCloud itself is a sophisticated, purpose-built tool uniquely associated with Overcast Panda," CrowdStrike said. "Once deployed, FlowCloud provides the adversary with persistent, covert remote access to the target device, enabling keylogging, screen capture, file collection, and credential harvesting."

Titan Panda, on the other hand, has been observed targeting legal billing software by exploiting a hard-coded Internet Information Services (IIS) machine key vulnerability in Intapp Time Server to achieve remote code execution across law firms.

The attacks, first detected in April 2026, led to the deployment of an in-memory framework called IceGiant to carry out reconnaissance, persistence, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. The threat actor is assessed to be operational since at least 2021, compromising several legal organizations in North America for over two years.

"How Titan Panda obtained the default machine keys is unknown, though IIS compromise of a legal entity running Intapp Time Server may have exposed the hardcoded keys in the application's configuration file, enabling ViewState deserialization attacks against any organization running default installations," CrowdStrike said.

Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion

Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity

Why the response outcomes differed

Actionable investigation methods

Learn More

Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths.

Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication).

This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations.

In this blog, we analyze the shared attack chain, the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate-abuse paths, and the different response outcomes. We also provide investigation methods, mitigation recommendations, Microsoft Defender detection guidance, and advanced hunting queries to help defenders identify and interrupt this access path. The activity described here is not attributed to a specific threat actor.

Activity overview

Risk to enterprise environments

AD CS can turn a certificate request into a durable authentication path. An attacker who obtains an authentication certificate for a privileged user or machine account can use that certificate independently of the initially compromised password. Resetting the user’s password or reimaging the first workstation does not revoke an issued certificate or invalidate Kerberos tickets that have already been issued.

Two AD CS abuse techniques are central to these incidents:

ESC1 – certificate template abuse: A low-privileged requester abuses a misconfigured authentication-capable template that permits requester-supplied identity information and broad enrollment, allowing the requester to obtain a certificate for a privileged account.

ESC8 – NTLM relay to Web Enrollment: An attacker relays a user or machine account’s NTLM authentication to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint that lacks relay protections, then requests a certificate as the relayed identity.

Attackers can use Microsoft Teams to impersonate IT support personnel and persuade users to approve a remote session, gaining hands-on-keyboard access without a conventional malware attachment.

Portable or renamed runtimes such as Python, Bun, and Java can execute attacker-controlled scripts from user-writable locations while retaining legitimate file metadata.

Automated disruption is most effective when every compromised identity and device remains eligible for containment; exclusions can preserve the attacker’s path.

Attack chain overview

Both incidents followed the same initial sequence: help desk impersonation through Teams, a user-approved Quick Assist or other remote-support session, archive transfer and extraction, portable runtime execution, and host and AD CS discovery. The certificate technique and response outcome then split into two distinct branches.

Figure 1. Both incidents followed a shared entry and execution pattern before diverging into two AD CS abuse paths. Case 1 used an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template to obtain certificates for privileged identities. Case 2 used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8. The response outcomes differed based on containment coverage and removal of the active execution point.

Shared initial access and execution pattern

Teams helpdesk impersonation and remote access

Both incidents began with Teams phishing messages and calls that impersonated support personnel. The social engineering persuaded a user to establish an attacker-controlled remote session, primarily by guiding the user to open Quick Assist and provide the connection code. This gave the attacker hands-on-keyboard access to the workstation. Across the broader activity, organization-themed onmicrosoft.com tenant names and support-oriented display names were used to make the external contact appear familiar.

Figure 2. Example Teams call displaying External and Scam suspected indicators. These labels are important user-facing signals during support impersonation attempts.

The remote session was the decisive transition in the attack. Immediately after the user granted control through Quick Assist, the attacker used the session to place an archive in the victim’s Downloads folder. Commands launched during the session created a KB-prefixed staging directory under the user’s profile, extracted the archive into that directory, and started the included payload with a portable Python, JavaScript, or Java runtime. The payload then performed host and network discovery and began assessing AD CS.

Portable runtime staging and execution variants

The runtime and packaging varied between deployments, but the execution pattern remained consistent: an archive was placed on the device during the remote session, extracted into a newly created user-profile directory, and used to launch attacker-controlled code. In one JavaScript variant, a renamed executable retained version metadata identifying it as the Bun runtime and launched the staged loader. A separate variant used a staged Java runtime to launch a Java source file.

Figure 3. Sanitized Bun staging command. The update-themed path, renamed runtime, script operand, and remote-session context form the useful investigation pattern.

File names alone are weak indicators. The actionable pattern is a portable runtime launched from a newly created, user-writable staging directory after an unauthorized remote session, followed by script execution, discovery commands, or connections to identity infrastructure.

Figure 4. Sanitized Java staging variant. The campaign could substitute runtime and packaging choices while keeping the broader access pattern.

The Java variant confirms that runtime choice can change between deployments. The AD CS behavior in each incident should be validated through the initiating process, account, device, and certificate records rather than assumed from the presence of Bun or Java alone.

Host discovery and AD CS assessment

The staged components queried Windows version information, network configuration, and running processes. These commands are common in administration, but they become high-value signals when it is launched by a renamed runtime from an uncommon location and follow an unexpected remote-support session.

Figure 5. Host-discovery commands from the first draft. Their value comes from the initiating staged runtime, user-writable path, and preceding unauthorized remote session.

The compromised workstation also connected to domain infrastructure using LDAPS and SMB.

From this shared workstation foothold, the incidents followed different certificate-abuse paths. In Case 1, the attacker exploited an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template. In Case 2, the attacker used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8.

Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion

ESC1 certificate requests expand privilege

The first Teams-phishing wave targeted three user accounts and compromised one workstation. From the shared foothold described above, the attacker examined AD CS for a privilege-escalation path.

Figure 6. Case 1: Help desk impersonation led to ESC1 certificate abuse. Attack disruption restricted most compromised identities, but an excluded privileged account remained usable and later supported data exfiltration.

The attacker found a certificate template vulnerable to ESC1. ESC1 describes a template configuration in which a requester can supply identity information in the certificate request and obtain a certificate that supports authentication. When broad enrollment rights and weak issuance controls are combined with that setting, a low-privileged account can request a certificate representing a privileged identity.

In the first wave, the attacker obtained certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender attack disruption targeted the initially compromised user and those three certificate-compromised identities. Remote logons and Server Message Block (SMB) access were restricted and active sessions were disconnected. One privileged account was excluded from automated response, so containment did not apply to that identity.

Renewed phishing and ESC1 privilege expansion

About 90 minutes after the first disrupted session, the attacker launched a larger Teams-phishing wave targeting 16 users and compromised another workstation. The attacker again abused the ESC1-vulnerable template, this time obtaining certificates for eight additional privileged accounts.

Attack disruption targeted the newly compromised user and the eight certificate-compromised identities. More than 1,000 subsequent SMB file-access attempts and additional logon attempts were blocked, limiting the attacker’s ability to reuse those accounts for lateral movement.

DCSync, the excluded account, and data theft

Within seconds of obtaining one privileged certificate, the attacker authenticated to a domain controller and performed DCSync while containment was taking effect. Attack disruption limited additional replication and follow-on use, but the operation had already begun.

The privileged account excluded during the first disruption remained available. The attacker continued to use it for network and remote-interactive logons, reached a file server, and launched a renamed copy of Rclone using the filename SearchApp.exe. The command recursively copied data from a file-server share to an external Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) destination, used 20 concurrent transfers, selected files up to three years old, and excluded several executable, database, virtual-disk, media, temporary, and log file types.

Figure 7. Sanitized Rclone command used to copy data from a file-server share to an external SFTP destination.

The incident demonstrates that partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route.

Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity

PetitPotam coerces domain-controller authentication

The ESC1 path used in the first case was not available in this environment. Instead, the attacker used PetitPotam to send requests over the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC), causing the domain controller to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system using its machine account. The attacker then relayed that NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment without knowing the domain controller’s password.

Figure 8. Case 2: Help desk impersonation led to PetitPotam authentication coercion, ESC8 relay to AD CS, certificate-based Kerberos authentication, and customer-led device isolation.

NTLM relay reaches AD CS Web Enrollment

The attacker relayed the domain controller’s NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment. This technique is known as ESC8. It targets an enrollment web endpoint that accepts NTLM without sufficient relay protection, allowing the attacker to submit a certificate request as the relayed account.

The AD CS server authenticated the domain-controller machine account even though the connection originated from another device. That identity-to-source mismatch is a strong investigation pivot: correlate the machine account, source device, Web Enrollment request, Certification Authority (CA) issuance record, and subsequent Kerberos activity.

After authenticating to Web Enrollment as the domain controller, the attacker requested and retrieved a certificate using the Domain Controller template. The important service paths are the certificate submission and retrieval endpoints under /certsrv; isolated URL access is not malicious by itself and must be correlated with the authenticated identity, source device, process, and CA request.

Figure 9. Sanitized view of AD CS Web Enrollment activity involving certificate submission and retrieval through /certsrv, used during ESC8 certificate issuance for a relayed domain-controller identity.

Certificate-based Kerberos authentication

The attacker used the newly issued domain-controller certificate for Kerberos PKINIT and obtained a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) for the domain controller. This step converted a relayed NTLM authentication into a certificate-backed Kerberos identity.

PKINIT success is the response threshold: responders should investigate the requesting device, authenticated account, issued certificate, active Kerberos sessions, and any service-ticket use. Certificate revocation and Kerberos ticket review are separate containment actions.

Customer-led device isolation and observed outcome

Microsoft Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the workstation associated with the certificate-enrollment and Kerberos activity. The documented containment action in this case was customer-led device isolation. No further attack progression was observed following isolation.

Why the response outcomes differed

In Case 1, an exclusion left a compromised privileged account available to the attacker despite disruption of other identities. In Case 2, customer-led device isolation followed Defender alerts, and no further attack progression was observed.

Response element

Case 1: ESC1

Case 2: ESC8

Response mechanism

Microsoft Defender automated attack disruption targeting compromised identities.

Microsoft Defender alerts followed by customer-led device isolation.

Measured effect

Covered identities were restricted; more than 1,000 SMB attempts and additional logons were blocked; further DCSync activity was limited.

The workstation associated with certificate enrollment and Kerberos activity was isolated.

Containment follow-up

One privileged account was excluded from automated response and remained available to the attacker.

No further progression was observed after isolation;

Observed outcome

The excluded identity was later used for file-server access and data exfiltration.

No subsequent attack progression was documented after customer isolation.

Actionable investigation methods

The most useful artifacts are not individual commands or ports in isolation. Investigators should reconstruct the chain across collaboration, endpoint, identity, and certificate systems.

Teams and remote access: identify the external tenant, user interaction, call or chat timing, remote-session start, approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) process, and child processes created during the session.

Runtime staging: inspect newly created KB-prefixed or application-like folders, archive extraction, runtime metadata, script operands, parent-child relationships, and subsequent network activity.

Directory interaction: use network data to identify LDAPS and SMB connections, then use endpoint and directory logs to determine what the initiating process did. TLS intentionally hides LDAP query content from passive network inspection.

ESC1: review certificate request and issuance events, requester identity, subject and Subject Alternative Names (SAN) values, template name, enrollment permissions, and the first authentication performed with the issued certificate.

PetitPotam and ESC8: correlate EFSRPC activity, outbound authentication by the domain controller, the device that relayed the authentication, Web Enrollment access, CA request and issuance records, and PKINIT from the originating workstation.

Disruption and containment: enumerate every compromised identity and device, review exclusions before and during response, revoke unauthorized certificates, and assess active Kerberos tickets separately

Reduce support impersonation and unauthorized remote access

Require users to verify unsolicited support requests through a known internal channel before joining a call, sharing a screen, or starting a remote-control session.

Encourage users to pay attention to warnings in incoming messages and calls when impersonation is detected.

Review Teams external-access and federation policies. Limit external domains to business requirements and investigate newly observed organization-themed or helpdesk-themed tenants in context.

Restrict remote-support software to approved products, operators, and workflows. Alert when approved RMM tools extract archives, create interpreters, or launch scripts from user-writable paths.

Constrain runtime-based execution

Use App Control for Business or equivalent application control to restrict unapproved portable runtimes and script execution from user-writable locations.

Evaluate file identity through signer, original filename, product metadata, path, parent process, and behavior. A renamed executable can retain legitimate version information.

Test relevant attack surface reduction rules and endpoint protection policies. Do not assume controls for Windows script hosts automatically cover JavaScript executed through Bun or source files launched through Java.

Harden AD CS against ESC1 and ESC8

Follow Microsoft’s secure configuration guidance for mitigating NTLM relay against AD CS: https://support.microsoft.com/help/5005413

Review authentication-capable templates for requester-supplied subject information, broad enrollment permissions, weak issuance requirements, and excessive certificate purpose. Remove unnecessary enrollment rights and require approval where appropriate.

Inventory AD CS Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service endpoints. Remove endpoints that are not required.

Require HTTPS and enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on enrollment web endpoints. HTTPS protects confidentiality; EPA provides the channel binding needed to resist NTLM relay.

Disable NTLM on enrollment services where operationally feasible and validate Kerberos-only authentication before broad enforcement.

Use Defender for Identity AD CS security posture assessments to identify ESC1-related template exposure and insecure enrollment Internet Information Services (IIS) endpoints associated with ESC8: https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-posture-assessments/certificates

Enable certificate auditing and prepare certificate-aware response

Enable the Certification Services advanced audit subcategory for success and failure, and configure the Certification Authority audit filter to record request and issuance activity.

Preserve CA security events, CA database records, IIS or Web Enrollment logs, endpoint process lineage, identity alerts, and Teams interaction records.

If an unauthorized certificate was issued, identify its serial number and thumbprint, revoke it, publish updated revocation information, and confirm that relying systems can obtain the update.

Review certificate-based Kerberos activity and active tickets. Revoking a certificate does not retroactively invalidate TGTs or service tickets that were already issued.

Treat containment exclusions as incident decisions. If an account or device cannot be automatically contained, assign a compensating manual action and verify completion.

Advanced hunting

Use these queries to investigate related activity. Tune time windows and filters for your environment. Matches require investigation.

Teams external contact and available impersonation signals

Use these queries as investigation starting points. Validate field availability and expected values in your tenant, tune for legitimate activity, and correlate matches with incidents rather than treating a single result as proof of compromise.

Teams external contact and available impersonation signals

Find external Teams chats and available impersonation signals.

CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where Application == "Microsoft Teams" | where (ActionType == "ChatCreated" and IsExternalUser == true) or ActionType in~ ( "TeamsImpersonationDetected", "SecurityRiskInCallDetected") | order by Timestamp desc

Bun or Java execution from KB-prefixed staging paths

Find Bun or Java running scripts from KB-prefixed AppData folders.

DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName in~ ("bun.exe", "java.exe", "javaw.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine contains ".js" or ProcessCommandLine contains ".java" | where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\AppData\\Roaming\\KB[0-9]+\\" | order by Timestamp desc

Network activity initiated by the staged runtime

Find network connections initiated by the staged runtime.

DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ( "bun.exe", "java.exe", "javaw.exe") | where RemotePort in (80, 445, 636, 88) | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\AppData\\Roaming\\KB[0-9]+\\" | order by Timestamp desc

Enrollment, relay, and PKINIT alerts with their evidence

Find relay, AD CS, and PKINIT alerts with their related evidence.

AlertInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where Title contains "NTLM relay" or Title contains "Certificate Services" or Title contains "PKINIT" or Title contains "Kerberos ticket request" | join kind=inner ( AlertEvidence | where Timestamp > ago(7d) ) on AlertId

Title: Trezor warns of suspected crypto-theft implant in hardware wallet
Context: Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access
Full Text:
Hardware wallet device maker Trezor has received credible reports about a suspected hardware crypto-theft implant in a Trezor Safe 5 sold by its reseller CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia.

Although the company has not yet received the device to examine it and confirm whether there is a malicious implant, it has warned potentially affected users to move their private keys and digital assets to known safe wallets.

Trezor wallets are physical devices that store cryptocurrency private keys and authorize transactions. Safe 5 is one of its latest models and is currently available for purchase from the official store.

According to Trezor, the concerns arose after it received a report from an Indonesian user who purchased a Safe 5 device from CryptoBilis through Tokopedia in August 2026.

The user opened it and found an extra circuit board between the wallet's main board and screen, equipped with a cellular module and antenna.

Based on unconfirmed information supplied by that customer, the implant appears capable of reading information displayed on the screen, including the wallet recovery phrase, and transmitting it over a mobile network when plugged in.

CryptoBilis is the same retailer implicated in a Ledger implant incident that unfolded earlier this month, and the implants on the two devices appear to be similar in form and function.

Ledger later confirmed the compromise and asked resellers and distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to halt all sales until the investigation confirms their safety.

In response to the Ledger incident, and before it had any indication it was impacted, Trezor immediately stopped device sales through CryptoBilis on October 9, 2026. The company later announced it would restructure and tighten its reseller network globally to maintain higher levels of security.

Trezor says it is unaware of any funds being stolen as a result of a supply-chain attack, and promised to provide updates once it receives the device, which is currently being shipped to it.

Meanwhile, multiple reports of losses by Ledger users have emerged since earlier this month, and a recent Singapore police announcement added another $3,500,000 to the tally.

For now, Trezor recommends not setting up or using any device bought via CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward.

Users who have already done so are advised to move their funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Buyers holding proof of purchase may contact Trezor for a replacement device or a voucher for a new device.

Trezor underlined that weighing devices is not a reliable way to determine if they have been tampered with.

Title: New Framework Puts Ransomware Resilience for AI Systems in Focus
Context: Cybersecurity leaders can now use a new framework to find and address weaknesses that could leave their AI systems vulnerable to ransomware attacks
Full Text:
Cybersecurity leaders can now use a new framework to find and address weaknesses that could leave their AI systems vulnerable to ransomware attacks.

The tool is the Ransomware Assessment and Incident Defense Framework for AI Systems (RAID-AI) and is fully available for anyone to use online for free.

Behnaz Karimi and Yuvaraj Govindarajulu, both co-leads of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s (OWASP) AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) initiative developed RAID-AI over the past two years.

They had initially planned to introduce the framework at the ISC2 Security Congress, held in Denver, Colorado, between October 26 and 28. Unfortunately, visa issues prevented Karimi from attending.

A Manual Ransomware Readiness Assessment for AI Systems

Speaking to Infosecurity, Karimi said RAID AI focuses on ransomware attacks against AI systems, whether or not an attacker uses AI. The framework’s approach is hands-on, asking security teams to assess their own controls rather than connecting to or scanning their systems.

“Right now, we are slowly seeing that ransomware attacks targeting AI systems are happening,” Karimi said.

She highlighted a April 2025, a report by Zoran, Mitrovic head of engineering at Kintra Health, which detailed how ransomware actors used data poisoning techniques, as well as an alleged cyber-attack on Novo Nordisk in June 2026, where hackers claimed to have stolen AI models used by the pharmaceutical company.

The RAID-AI assessment covers general cybersecurity measures alongside risks specific to AI models, data and supporting infrastructure.

The framework is delivered through a web console aimed at CISOs, cybersecurity officers and security engineers.

Users assess controls manually, selecting maturity levels on a scale from zero to five. The controls are organized into general and AI-specific categories, with levels such as basic, advanced and high.

General controls include recovery, training and sensitive-data protection. AI-specific areas include data, tools and runtime.

RAID AI maps controls to two voluntary security frameworks, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) and the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Cybersecurity Performance Goals 2.0 (CPG 2.0).

It also allows users to map adversarial attacks through three attack mapping frameworks, MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE ATLAS and NIST Adversarial.

Karimi and Govindarajulu have provided comprehensive documentation, including guidelines for using the tool and an explanation of how it was developed and how maturity levels and various security scores are calculated.

Future Plans: Extend Ransomware Assessments to Agentic AI Systems

Organizations do not need to connect their internal systems or upload company documents to complete the assessment.

Therefore, the RAID-AI assessment is not an automated audit: results depend on users’ evaluations and the tool does not independently verify an organization’s security posture.

Instead, teams review their practices and enter their assessments themselves.

“Ideally bringing security managers, engineers and AI-security specialists together in workshops,” Karimi told Infosecurity.

The console displays the results in dashboards, including maturity views and mappings to other frameworks. Users can also download PDF reports that highlight weaknesses and help teams set priorities.

Karimi said the dashboard can give senior leaders a high-level overview, while technical teams use the underlying controls to guide more detailed discussions.

In the future, Karimi hopes to provide practical implementation resources, including videos and blueprints to help security engineers apply individual controls, and develop a similar tool for ransomware threats targeting agentic AI systems.

Title: Fake PDF and search tools hijacked searches for 13.4 million Chrome users
Context: Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today
Full Text:
Ads promoted browser extensions as tools to find manuals, convert PDFs, or make searches safer. But many of these extensions sent users’ search queries through servers controlled by their operators.

Socket researcher John Tuckner identified 319 extensions with an estimated 13.4 million installs over a decade. The extensions hijacked users’ default search settings and routed their searches through servers controlled by the operators before sending them to Yahoo or Bing. This gave the operators access to users’ queries and let them earn referral payments.

Socket says the extensions were promoted through ads on networks including Google Ads, promoting tools such as “manual finders,” “PDF converters,” “safe search,” and “AI search.”

The extensions were listed in Google’s official store, but most were unlisted. That means people with a direct link could visit a listing and install an extension, while ordinary searches in the store would not show it. An ad offered help with an immediate task, a landing page encouraged installation, and the official store provided a familiar place to complete it.

Search hijacking

The main risk was that operators could see what users searched for. Searches can reveal health worries, financial problems, workplace interests, or other personal matters. Socket says queries were often associated with a unique identifier, which could let the operators link a user’s searches over time.

The proxy could also choose where to send a search. Socket says this could potentially direct users to phishing or malware pages, but it did not find evidence that the extensions had done so.

What should users do?

If your searches start going astray, or you installed a search, PDF-converter, manual-finder, or security extension after clicking an ad, check what’s installed.

Review your extensions. Enter chrome://extensions in Chrome’s address bar. Remove extensions you don’t recognize, no longer use, or don’t trust. To remove one, select Remove and confirm. If you’re unsure about an extension, check it against the list at the end of Socket’s blog.

Check your search settings. In Chrome, at the top right, select More (the three-dot menu), then Settings > Search engine. If Chrome says an extension is controlling a setting, review or remove that extension. The absence of this notice doesn’t confirm that all your extensions are safe.

Run a Malwarebytes scan to check for malicious extensions and other malware that could be affecting your device.

Title: PHP2Shell Attacks Root Palo Alto Firewalls but Fail Against WordPress
Context: Threat actors have been hammering servers vulnerable to PHP2Shell for over a week, but only a few successful compromises have been confirmed to date
Full Text:
Threat actors have been hammering servers vulnerable to PHP2Shell for over a week, but only a few successful compromises have been confirmed to date.

Standing out are Palo Alto Networks firewalls, which have been rooted by a China-linked hacking group in attacks chaining PHP2Shell with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation bug.

Assisted by AI, the hackers chained two separate exploits: one specifically targeting the PHP2Shell flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS devices, and another one for Fragnesia to deploy webshells with root privileges.

Cybersecurity outfit Dream flagged the campaign earlier this week, noting that at least 25 firewalls out of a pool of hundreds were hacked. Palo Alto Networks has since confirmed the findings.

“Dream Research has reported a campaign in which attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability to gain root access. Unit 42 has independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results,” Palo Alto Networks said.

The company has rolled out patches that resolve the PHP2Shell flaws in PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1, and 10.2 for PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, and for Panorama (virtual and M-Series).

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“No special configuration is required to be affected by this issue. Active exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company notes in its advisory.

Palo Alto Networks says that by default the management interface is not exposed to the internet and urges customers to immediately restrict access to it and apply the available fixes.

“Only a small fraction of a percent (approximately .02%) of our global installed base has internet-facing management interfaces configured and was impacted. Each of these customers has been individually contacted by our teams. We will continue to investigate and provide any necessary updates as they become available,” Palo Alto Networks notes.

22.6 million exposed PHP instances

According to the company, as of October 29, its telemetry has identified over 22.6 million exposed PHP instances that are potentially vulnerable to the PHP2Shell bugs.

That is not surprising, given that PHP is widely used across servers and content management systems, including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and many others.

The mass PHP2Shell exploitation has been targeting those as well, but remained largely unsuccessful, at least when it comes to WordPress, web security firm Defiant says.

As of October 28, it was not aware of any WordPress site being compromised via PHP2Shell exploitation, although it has recorded over 77,000 related requests from more than 2,000 IP addresses.

However, Defiant points out that testing has revealed the exploits often need to be adjusted to work on targeted servers, influenced by ASLR, PHP build, running extensions, memory limits, and the server’s request handling.

“Attackers are still changing their tools. A successful attack could give them access to your site’s files, database, and passwords, so updating PHP remains essential,” Defiant warned.

A handful of IPs

Despite the broad PHP2Shell exploitation attempts, success has been attributed to very few threat actors.

According to Cato Networks, roughly 96% of the attacks it has blocked targeted CVE-2026-109618, and 41% of them attempted remote code execution (RCE), while the remaining were scanning or invalid PoC attempts.

The attempts originated from a handful of IPs in the US, the Netherlands, and Germany, repeating proof-of-concept (PoC) style requests. Most of them focused on command execution, followed by deserialization attempts.

According to Cato, healthcare organizations were targeted the most, followed by technology and security services, professional services, automotive, education and non-profit, and manufacturing, construction, and retail.

The attacks, however, were not targeted, but appeared opportunistic, as the same source was seen sending requests to organizations in the healthcare, technology, and software sectors during the same day.

WatchTowr says it has observed successful PHP2Shell exploitation from a single IP address in Germany, despite the large volume of attempts and variety of payloads.

“In every case, it executes a simple ‘curl’ command to prove exploitation was successful, and stops there, with no additional post-exploitation activity,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.

“New techniques, inventive payloads, and better appliance-specific exploits are being thrown around as more reliable exploits are worked on, and we’re likely to only see public reporting of highly targeted successful exploitation of specific edge appliances keep growing,” Knott added.
