Title: Artificial Intimacy: Love and lies in the age of AI
Context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
Full Text:
AI is becoming a third wheel in relationships, increasingly playing a role in the most intimate parts of our lives.

It shows up in the flirty first text, the polished dating profile, the therapized language we use with a partner after a fight, the strength we gather after heartbreak, and everywhere in between. For some, AI is a source of companionship itself. And even if you’re not personally an AI user, you may still be dating, loving, arguing with, or trusting someone who is.

As AI moves deeper into our relationships, it’s reshaping connection, blurring what feels authentic, and creating new ways for intimacy to be exploited.

AI is starting to replace human interaction

AI is moving into emotional territory once reserved for other people. For some, it’s no longer just a tool, but a source of support, companionship, and even romantic connection.

According to our recent research, about one in six have turned to a chatbot for companionship or emotional support. That climbs to about one in five among Gen Z and Millennials, and nearly one in four among regular AI users (those who use AI daily or multiple times a week). The more time people spend with AI, the more likely they are to humanize its role, making room for it as a friend, confidant, advisor, or even partner.

As AI takes on more intimate roles, it’s also starting to challenge the boundaries of real human relationships. More than one in three (37%) say having a romantic relationship with an AI chatbot while already in a committed relationship isn’t the same as cheating. That view is more common among men (46% versus 30% of women), Gen Z and Millennials (43% and 45%), and regular AI users (48%).

Whether the relationship is platonic or romantic, the more AI is treated like a human, the more personal the stakes become. Just like you have to be cautious when telling a human your deepest, darkest secrets, the experience is similar when using AI. Nearly two-thirds (65%) worry that private conversations they’ve had with AI could be exposed.

One survey respondent said:

“I have used a chatbot…for emotional support, and it is worrying to think those conversations could be leaked.”

The technology may be artificial, but the relationships people form with AI can feel very real. And as with any relationship, that means there are boundaries to work out, privacy to protect, and vulnerabilities to manage.

AI is creating new ways to weaponize intimacy

AI’s growing role in human intimacy also has a darker side. The same technology that can offer comfort, advice, or companionship can also be used to violate the most intimate parts of our lives.

Non-consensual image abuse, sextortion, and other forms of sexual abuse have long been part of the internet’s dark side. Generative AI has made that content easier to create. Someone trying to exploit another person no longer needs an actual intimate photo, video, or private exchange. A regular photo—or even just someone’s likeness—can be transformed into sexual content they never made, never shared, and never consented to.

Most people draw a clear line against that, but not everyone does. About one in six people say it’s acceptable to generate explicit images of someone without their permission for personal use. Another 14% are neutral, bringing the share who do not explicitly oppose the behavior to nearly one in three (31%).

Views differ sharply by age and sex:

Younger adults are more accepting of someone using AI to generate non-consensual content: nearly one in four Gen Z (24%) and Millennials (23%) say it’s okay, compared with 13% of Gen X and just 5% of Boomers+

Men are also more permissive: more than one in five (22%) say it’s okay, compared with 14% of women

Attitudes toward the behavior may vary, but the fear of becoming a target is far more widespread. Overall, nearly two-thirds of people (62%) worry someone could create fake nude or sexually explicit photos or videos of them. Women feel this threat more acutely: nearly seven in ten (69%) are concerned, compared with 57% of men.

For some, this fear has already become a reality:

One in ten say AI has been used to generate nude or sexually explicit imagery of them without permission

One in ten say someone has threatened to release AI-generated compromising or explicit imagery of them

As one respondent recounted:

“I had someone make fake nudes of me using AI on my photos from my social media and threaten to post them on Facebook…[it] made me more cautious about AI.”

The intimate material may be fake, but the fear, coercion, and potential for reputational, emotional, and financial damage are completely real.

AI is making it harder to know who you’re really talking to

The threat doesn’t stop with fabricated sexual content. AI is also making it harder to know whether the person on the other side of a screen is who they claim to be.

Humans have always edited themselves for other people. We choose the most flattering photo, write and rewrite the text before sending it, and present our most interesting selves—especially when forming new relationships. AI dramatically expands what that kind of self-editing can look like, and people aren’t shy about using it:

54% say AI helps them present the best version of themselves

47% say using AI to present your “best self” to employers, friends, or romantic partners does not present a false identity

That rises to 58% of both Gen Z and Millennials and 64% of regular AI users

But where does enhancement end and deception begin? Is an AI-polished dating profile still authentically you? What about a message you didn’t write? A photo that looks like you, only better?

There’s a flipside to using AI to make ourselves look or sound better: If we can do it, so can everyone else. And people are much less comfortable when they’re not the ones controlling the technology. Two-thirds (67%) worry that an online friend or romantic interest could use AI-generated images, videos, or other content to deceive them.

Catfishing, fake photos, and lies on dating profiles aren’t new. AI just makes the deception easier. Someone’s photos, backstory, messages, and even their voice can all be faked.

One person described leaving dating apps after realizing the person they were talking to had gone well beyond simply polishing their profile:

“[The] dating profile had fake pictures…[it] wasn’t just making true events sound interesting and more flirty, but creating completely false photos and information. Left the dating apps again and needed to reset.”

AI can distort identity in the other direction, too. It can also create a version of us we never chose to put into the world.

76% worry about someone creating a fake profile pretending to be them

70% worry about fake images or videos of themselves being created

71% worry AI-generated content could be used to damage their reputation

Relationships are built on mutual trust. AI can distort both sides of the connection: who we think the other person is, and who they think we are.

AI is quietly finding its way into the space between people

Not all of AI’s influence on intimacy is so dramatic. Much of it happens quietly, showing up in how people communicate with each other and navigate relationships:

More than one in three have used AI to help write or edit a message

About one in seven have turned to it for advice about a relationship or personal decision

One in ten say it has already changed how they date or communicate romantically—rising to nearly one in five among Gen Z

The survey responses show what this looks like in real life. For example, one respondent described using AI with their partner as a way to step outside their own point of view:

“Personally, it has helped me. We use AI in our relationship as a reflection tool, and it has sometimes helped us take on the perspective of the other.”

For another, AI helped them work through jealousy:

“So, I used to accuse my partner, and I got really territorial about them but once I talked to AI about it, they gave helpful advice and now we are stronger than ever.”

AI is also showing up in other difficult relationship moments. One person said it helped them “stay calm and communicate” when problems came up with their partner; another said it allows them “to pause and refine [their] thoughts” before responding.

Sometimes the role is simpler. One respondent said AI gives them “new romantic words” for their partner, while another said they’ve asked AI for advice on how to make their partner smile. AI’s growing role in relationships may be unsettling, but the benefits people describe are definitely there.

AI isn’t just helping people find the right words. It’s also helping them decide what version of themselves to put forward in the first place. More than one in three say it’s okay to use AI to create or improve a dating profile; nearly two-thirds aren’t opposed. One respondent described using AI as a “creative advisor” to polish their profile and come up with conversation starters.

AI doesn’t have to replace a relationship to help shape it. It can influence how people communicate, what advice they take, and how they choose to present themselves.

AI’s intimacy problem is ultimately a trust problem

From connection to deception to outright harm, the same question keeps surfacing: Can I trust what’s in front of me? And would I know if I couldn’t?

Nearly nine in ten people (88%) say AI is making it harder to tell what online content is genuinely human or real. And 84% say even convincing video evidence no longer necessarily feels like proof. That uncertainty follows people into dating and relationships, where knowing what—and who—to trust is deeply personal.

AI may make it easier to start a conversation, smooth over a hard one, or feel connected when you’re lonely. But relationships and intimacy of all kinds still come down to trust, and AI is making that trust a little harder to take at face value.

About the research

The research in this article is based on a March 2026 survey about AI, identity, and the collapse of digital trust and was conducted among 1,500 respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The research was prepared by an independent research consultant and distributed via Forsta.

Title: The web’s having a rough week. Here’s how to browse safely
Context: Attackers were exploiting two flaws in PHP, researchers disclosed a critical flaw in Brotli software used by Node
Full Text:
You recognize the website. You’ve visited it before. You may even have it bookmarked. Then it asks you to do something unusual: install an update, allow notifications, or run a command to prove you’re human.

Stop and check first. A website you trust can still display instructions you shouldn’t follow. Our researchers have documented attacks in which criminals hacked legitimate websites and used them to deliver fake verification pages that trick visitors into installing malware.

Within the same week, serious problems emerged in several parts of the web’s security infrastructure. Attackers were exploiting two flaws in PHP, researchers disclosed a critical flaw in Brotli software used by Node.js, and eight compromised security certificates raised concerns about how browsers and apps verify websites. The incidents have different causes and levels of risk, but their timing makes this an unusual cluster.

PHP is used by about 7 in 10 websites whose underlying programming language is known. Node.js is used by 7.4% of websites with an identified web-server technology, according to W3Techs. Both run websites behind the scenes, so flaws in them can put the sites that rely on them at risk. Most browsers have blocked the certificates, though updates may still be needed for other software and devices.

These problems don’t mean you need to stop browsing. But keep your software and security protection up to date, and be wary of unexpected requests.

How to stay safe when browsing

Check the website’s address, but remember that even the genuine site may have been compromised. The important question is whether the page’s instructions make sense. A familiar website may earn your visit, but that doesn’t mean you should automatically let it run software on your device.

In documented campaigns, malicious instructions appeared on legitimate, hacked WordPress websites, not just lookalike domains.

Safer. Cleaner. Ad-free browsing.

INSTALL BROWSER GUARD

A secure connection doesn’t guarantee that a page is safe, either. HTTPS protects the connection between your browser and the site. Browser protections against dangerous content are a separate layer. A page asking you to install software or enter sensitive information still deserves scrutiny, even when the connection is encrypted.

Ask yourself: “Does this request make sense for what I came here to do?”

Reading an article shouldn’t require opening PowerShell. Watching a video shouldn’t require following a website’s instructions to “repair” your computer. These are familiar themes in ClickFix attacks, which disguise malicious commands as routine verification or troubleshooting steps.

You can’t patch someone else’s web server, but you can keep the software on your own device updated. Turn on automatic updates for your operating system, browser, and applications where available, and don’t repeatedly postpone installing them. Updates fix security flaws that criminals could otherwise use to access your files or accounts.

Keep your browser’s phishing and malware protection enabled, too. Free browser extensions like Malwarebytes Browser Guard warn about known dangerous websites, malicious downloads, and clipboard hijacking. Treat those warnings as a reason to leave, not as another obstacle to get round. These checks are a useful layer of protection, but they can’t certify that every unflagged page is safe.

Use strong, unique passwords stored in a password manager, and enable multifactor authentication on important accounts. These measures help protect your accounts from unauthorized access.

If a request involves running code or making changes to your device, verify it independently. If a website claims your browser needs updating, close the prompt and check through the browser’s own settings. If it says an account or service needs attention, check through the official app, help page, or support channel that you open yourself.

Criminals often present the harmful step as the thing that will let you do what you came to do: fix the connection, enable the player, or complete the security check. The frustration of being blocked can make it tempting to follow their instructions.

Use up-to-date, real-time anti-malware protection on your devices to help stop malware from wreaking havoc or stealing your information.

Watch for unexpected content, downloads, redirects, and repeated login requests, even on familiar sites. If something looks wrong, leave the page. If you’re unsure, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard to check whether a request may be a scam and get possible next steps.

Title: Attack on email hosting provider for German far right party AfD exposed 345k accounts
Context: Have I Been Pwned confirmed the scale of the breach for the first time today, after AfD officially disclosed the September attack on its hosting provider last week
Full Text: The cyberattack on Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country’s most prominent far-right political party, exposed hundreds of thousands of confidential emails and attachments, as well as more than 345,000 unique email addresses. Have I Been Pwned confirmed the scale of the breach for the first time today, after AfD officially disclosed the September attack on its hosting provider last week. AfD said in its statement that “only a few email accounts were illegally copied,” but admitted a large amount of the data was taken from them, resulting in an extensive data breach. The emails were added to what the party described as “an activist website,” which summarised the email chains into searchable topics and has led to the publication of various revelations, such as a party co-leader’s opinions on colleagues’ “deeply problematic” racial discourse. Per a report from investigative journalist Lilith Wittmann, citing conversations with the cybercriminals responsible for the hack-and-leak job and party sources, the attack was first spotted on September 9 and started with a compromise of a poorly protected WordPress site. The same report claimed the criminals gained persistent access to the servers operated by the hosting provider, identified as AfD-owned Alternita Dienstleistungs GmbH, and exfiltrated more than a terabyte of data. No official sources have verified the hackers’ claims about how the attack unfolded. The Register contacted Alternita Dienstleistungs for its take. AfD said the owners of the affected email accounts have been notified, and that it reported the attack to security authorities. “We are deeply concerned by what has happened,” the party said in an October 20 statement. “Such a digital attack is illegal and a criminal offense. Furthermore, it is an attack on the German party system and thus on democracy. “We are extremely worried that, apparently, the content of the stolen documents was analyzed using a very rudimentary AI. This analysis focused on keywords, not the context. The alleged scandals published so far do not stand up to scrutiny – a fact that, thankfully, is being confirmed by a growing number of commentators on social media.” Among the AI-generated summaries compiled by the “activist site” are chains supposedly expressing views related to Holocaust denial, racist and antisemitic rants, the 9/11 disaster, forged documents, and more. Der Spiegel sifted through the raw files and reported that party leader Alice Weidel seemingly knew about illegal donations related to the 2017 federal elections weeks before she previously said she did. The AfD's position is that the AI summaries of the emails are not to be trusted, but it has not specifically commented on the veracity of the raw email files available for download via torrent. It did not immediately respond to our request for input, but has told reporters previously that it will not comment on whether the emails, or the stories that have been written based on them, are to be trusted. ®

Title: Samsung TVs without mics may listen through soundbars, researcher says
Context: Investigating, they claim to have found a package called “always on voice,” which uses the TV’s built-in microphone to collect sounds from the room
Full Text:
A reverse engineer claims that their Samsung smart TV has been collecting audio without their consent.

The researcher, who calls themselves “log4j,” said in an X thread that their 2025 Samsung TV was delivering ads that seemed suspiciously relevant to them. Investigating, they claim to have found a package called “always on voice,” which uses the TV’s built-in microphone to collect sounds from the room.

The software logged events such as dogs barking and babies crying, log4j said, adding that these events are counted and reported back to Samsung.

Samsung advertises similar features on some of its AI-enabled TVs. The company says its Pet Care and Family Care features use on-device AI to detect a dog barking or a baby crying and alert users. This doesn’t confirm log4j’s claims about the package or the data it reports.

However, log4j says that on TVs without microphones, the software searches for connected devices such as soundbars or Bluetooth microphones and uses those to listen instead.

The TV was also collecting geolocation data and mapping local networks, they said, adding that it ran a service on the TV that analyzes traffic on the local network.

log4j also says that the system uses a neural network tailored to a particular region to analyze your viewing habits. A neural network is a type of machine-learning model. log4j said:

“…in youtube it’s looking for videos you watch, ads you skip, progress in a video, etc.”

The tracking that’s on the record

While log4j’s claims haven’t been independently verified, Samsung has used automatic content recognition (ACR), a system that identifies what’s on screen. Earlier this year, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton settled with Samsung, getting the company to agree that it would get Texans’ express consent before collecting or processing ACR viewing data.

A class action complaint filed in New York in January also accused Samsung of using ACR to record video and audio passing through the TV. The complaint accused Samsung of using machine-learning algorithms to analyze and link this data back to consumers. This includes information displayed when the TV is used as a computer monitor, it said, adding that the information can be linked to different people using the TV. The case was voluntarily dismissed in July.

The New York complaint added:

“Samsung exploits this Sensitive Information by (a) selling targeted advertisements to its corporate advertising clients, and (b) providing it to third-party advertising companies such as Google and X (f/k/a Twitter) for targeted advertising.”

A separate class action complaint filed in California this month accuses Samsung Electronics America of not being transparent about its ACR data collection.

This isn’t the first time that Samsung has been criticized for allegedly picking up in-room audio. In 2015, privacy group EPIC filed a complaint with the FTC, accusing Samsung of recording conversations and relaying them elsewhere. The nonprofit said at the time:

“Everything a user says in front of the Samsung SmartTV is recorded and transmitted over the internet to a third party regardless of whether it is related to the provision of the service.”

EPIC identified text-to-speech company Nuance as the third party.

What you can do

We can’t confirm all of log4j’s allegations, and Samsung doesn’t appear to have commented. But there have been multiple complaints about the data smart TVs collect. You can turn off features such as ACR, internet-based advertising, and voice recognition where possible.

log4j has also raised concerns about whether monitoring services are truly off. They said:

“ACR off via your preferences menu on samsung TVs should not be assumed to actually disable ACR telemetry.

i’ve found several instances where the checks (whether deliberate or not) are either incorrectly implemented or not checked at all.”

log4j says disconnecting your TV from Wi-Fi is the best option for immediate peace of mind, though that also means losing internet-based TV features. They also suggest using an Apple TV or a modifiable Android TV box with open-source software.

Title: From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research

Full Text:
What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos. He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses.Beyond the technical grind, Ryan shares his philosophy on building a career in security without burning out. From the value of project-based learning to the importance of finding time to step away from the keyboard, here's Ryan's take on what it really means to navigate today's cybersecurity industry.

Amy Ciminnisi: Tell me a little bit about the journey that has taken you to Talos, from early on in your career through to now. How did you get here? I actually don't know that much about it.

Ryan Fetterman: I've been doing security about 15 years now, and my career was largely shaped by where I started in the DC area. I spent about a decade there. I started out in consulting and then pivoted over to research, but that was a great place to get started.

I got a lot of great experience in federal agencies and government consulting, continued my education down there, got trained up, got certifications and things like that. And that was where I got my first exposure to doing actual security operations, which is what I really stuck with. It was my first exposure to Splunk.

Querying lots of log data and building visualizations and analytics in Splunk was the first time in my career that I felt it was kind of my natural inclination. It seems like it should have been more obvious to me looking back on it, but it's something that I try to explain to people a lot. When you first get into security, there's a desire to kind of find your specialization and start working towards it. But in my experience, it's just not something that you can rush.

I met the people connected with that space, which eventually led to me going to work for Splunk. I worked on the Splunk research team, SURGe. And then after the Cisco acquisition of Splunk, I ultimately became reorganized into Talos.

AC: I'm sure there have been so many challenges, so many obstacles in your way as you're trying to do this research. Can you share one that you've faced and how it shaped your perspective on cybersecurity?

RF: Something that stuck with me was actually my first advanced persistent threat (APT) incident. Now, you can look this up. It's called Pandora Song if you search for the C2. I was in the DC area working in a federal SOC, and I was doing some of the first host-based analytics at the time, which have now become kind of the concentration of a lot of detection. Engineering and analytics are host-based, so this was kind of pioneering at the time.

I was looking at a lot of host-based sensors and writing analytics in Splunk, actually, and we had been tipped off to this incident by a third party. I was looking through the details of the incident and how the attacker was carrying out the progression of their attack...

Title: Your Attack Surface Is Growing Faster Than Your Team Can Respond
Context: As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place
Full Text:
Security teams cannot keep responding faster forever. As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place.

That requires a pivot toward prevention and a broader view of exposure. An unpatched application matters, but so do unnecessary administrative privileges, forgotten internet-facing services, or legitimate tools available to someone who never needs them. Individually, these weaknesses may attract little attention. Connected, they can create an attacker pathway to the systems and data the business depends on.

An exposure management strategy helps organizations understand these connections and act before an attacker does. For lean IT and security teams, it also offers a practical way to reduce workload: fewer opportunities for attackers can mean fewer alerts to investigate and respond to.

Why Is Exposure Management Crucial Now?

AI is putting pressure on security from multiple directions. Attackers can use it to accelerate their operations, while employees’ adoption of AI applications, assistants, and agents introduces additional access and interactions to secure.

Detection and response remain essential. However, making them carry most of the defensive burden leaves teams dependent on quickly identifying and interrupting every intrusion.

Meanwhile, many attack opportunities involve capabilities organizations already have. Bitdefender Labs’ analysis of 700,000 security incidents found that living-off-the-land techniques, which abuse legitimate tools, appeared in 84% of major attacks. Patching alone cannot address the unnecessary access that makes those techniques possible.

The challenge is operational, too. In the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 38% of security professionals cited the overhead of maintaining hardening rules and exceptions as a barrier to shrinking their attack surface.

Organizations need prevention that adapts as their environment changes and fits the capacity of the people responsible for securing it.

What Is an Exposure Management Strategy?

Exposure management is the ongoing practice of identifying, prioritizing, and reducing weaknesses attackers could exploit across an organization’s attack surface.

It extends beyond vulnerability management. Software vulnerabilities are part of the picture, alongside misconfigurations, exposed services, identity risks, and unnecessary access to powerful tools.

An effective strategy connects three activities.

First, establish visibility into relevant exposures.

Second, prioritize them using context, including the assets an attacker could reach.

Third, reduce those exposures and reassess the environment.

This is continuous work because exposure changes whenever accounts gain privileges, services become publicly accessible, or business requirements evolve. Threat Exposure Management provides a framework for organizing that repeatable process. Technology supports the program; ownership and follow-through make it effective.

How Does GravityZone Turn Visibility Into Prevention?

Bitdefender GravityZone Exposure Management combines visibility, prioritization, and adaptive hardening to help teams remove attack opportunities.

Endpoint Risk Management identifies vulnerabilities and risky configurations. External Attack Surface Management adds an attacker’s outside view of internet-facing assets and services. User risk insights and Unified Identities help teams understand accounts, behaviors, and privileges that contribute to exposure.

There is also Attack Path Analysis, which connects findings into potential routes toward critical assets. That context can change the remediation order. A medium-severity vulnerability on a privileged user’s workstation may deserve attention ahead of a higher-severity finding on an isolated system.

It also helps teams identify shared points across multiple routes, where one change could interrupt several potential paths. The analysis models connections from available findings; teams still need to assess and implement the appropriate fixes.

However, teams can add automated action through GravityZone PHASR (Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction). It learns how each machine-user combination operates and restricts unnecessary access to tools and behaviors attackers like to abuse. Hardening can adapt as legitimate usage changes.

What Outcomes Should Organizations Expect?

The primary outcome of continuous exposure management is reduced opportunity for compromise. Closing an exposed service, addressing a dangerous configuration, or restricting unnecessary tool access can remove an opening or constrain an attacker’s next move.

Better prioritization helps teams direct limited resources to the most consequential work. For example, what if an administrator account connects to several potential attack paths? Removing unnecessary access may reduce exposure across multiple systems, giving the team a clearer reason to prioritize the change.

Dynamic hardening can also reduce the manual effort of policy maintenance. PHASR allows teams to review recommendations or use Autopilot to apply them. Changes are audited and reversible, and teams can grant access when legitimate work requires it. These safeguards help teams reduce risk while managing operational disruption.

A further outcome is clearer evidence of progress. Leaders can track changes in risk posture and new or resolved attack paths, connecting security work to the routes toward important assets that have been closed.

Reducing attack opportunities can ease pressure on teams of all sizes and especially lean teams.

How Can Lean Teams Put an Exposure Management Strategy Into Practice?

Start with business priorities: the systems, identities, and services whose compromise would cause the greatest harm. Establish visibility, identify high-risk exposures, and assign responsibility for reducing them. Reassess after changes to confirm progress and identify what needs attention next.

Organizations can build on existing investments and extend their program with separately licensed capabilities, including automated patching, cloud security posture management, and GravityZone AI Visibility and Control.

The strategic goal is to make prevention, through continuous risk reduction, part of everyday security operations. This helps close attack opportunities before they become an incident.

Title: Locked and Loaded: Phishing through Fake Bids and Protected Documents
Context: Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email...
Full Text:
By Don Santos, Cofense Phishing Defence Centre

In the sales process, few emails carry as much weight as an invitation to bid. It opens the conversation that can eventually lead to revenue, and professionals are conditioned to treat it with urgency and care. Threat actors understand this, and they have learned to pair that urgency with a simple tactic: the password-protected document. Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email security tools cannot inspect the contents of an encrypted file. In this walkthrough, we break down how an important sales invitation and a "secured" document combine to set up a tricky and deceptive credential phishing campaign.

Figure 1: Invite to Bid Email Body

The campaign starts with an email titled "Project Bid Invitation - Proposal Due August 35, 2026" as shown above in Figure 1. The subject and opening message immediately signal good news: an invitation to bid for a new project. The prospect of new business has a way of lowering an employee's guard because it often encourages a sense of urgency, not scepticism. The message says more details are in the password protected PDF attachment. This is another factor that makes the campaign tricky, as it’s a simple yet remarkably effective tactic for evading suspicion. It builds a false sense of trust with the recipient, and more importantly, it allows suspicious URLs or payloads to evade detection from automated email security tools. These tools typically work by scanning a file’s contents for suspicious patterns, but encryption keeps that content unreadable until a password is manually entered, letting the payload bypass detection entirely. Invitations to bid and password-protected files are also used in legitimate business processes, imitating these makes it difficult for untrained employees to spot suspicious emails, as shown in Figure 1. Adding to the difficulty is the fact that the sender's email address itself may belong to a legitimate, previously compromised account rather than an obviously spoofed or unfamiliar domain. This adds another layer of trust, removing one of the most apparent red flags before the recipient even opens the message.

Figure 2: Inside the Password Protected PDF

If the recipient does proceed with opening the attached PDF and unlocking it, the file reveals content as shown in Figure 2: a single button styled to resemble a OneDrive document preview, prompting them to "View" or "Download" the project files. With only one possible action, there is no room for ambiguity, and the familiar OneDrive branding makes the next click feel valid and legitimate. Hovering over the button reveals the underlying URL, [hXXps://slotpastimaxwin50jt[.]online/autoproject@autoproject[.]com/index[.]php], a clear red flag, as this is not a OneDrive domain, but a redirecting URL designed to carry the recipient further into the campaign.

Figure 3: Fake Bid Document Drive

Clicking the View/Download button leads to a page that resembles a shared document drive, complete with a list of files that appear to be related to a real contract, as shown above in Figure 3. This displays an effort to be consistent with the "invitation to bid" narrative, keeping the intended target hooked and committed to see the process through. Just like a legitimate shared document page, the intended target can choose which files to download via checkbox, then click "Download Selected", continuing the illusion of a normal bid process.

Figure 4: Email Input Required

Once the "Download Selected" button is clicked, a pop-up window appears asking for an email address, as seen in Figure 4. This again mimics the behaviour of real shared document platforms, which often request a login email to confirm that only the intended recipient can access the file. Entering an email to continue redirects to the fake Microsoft login, closely resembling the real Microsoft sign-in, first asking for an email, then a password, as shown in Figure 5. Looking at the address bar reveals the URL [hXXps://mm-lasertechnik[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/1Dmw9/?key=NKsIDYXvtY], a clear indication that the victim is not on a real Microsoft sign-in page. If the victim proceeds to enter their email and password here, the credentials are sent directly to the attacker's server [hXXps://nbpn[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/nasa[.]php], completing the phish.

Figure 5: Fake Microsoft Login Page

This campaign shows how threat actors continue to weaponize everyday business processes such as invitations to bid, password-protected files, and shared document platforms, turning them into effective phishing campaigns. The best defence is a habit of caution at every stage: Was this bid expected? Does the sender's domain check out? Does the URL of the login page match the platform it claims to be? When something feels off, contact your IT or security team before entering any credentials, as a moment of caution costs far less than a compromised account. Once a threat is confirmed, analyst-controlled quarantine can extend across the related campaign, with explainable decisions and a full audit trail. Title: Worm armed 42 GitHub repos by hiding a payload too big to fail
Context: Threat hunters at SafeDep, an open source supply chain security firm, first spotted the “testmetest” npm campaign last week, identifying 18 packages linked to the same operator...
Full Text: A new Miasma-family npm worm, originally believed to be just a test with no victims, secretly armed 42 real GitHub repositories from 11 owners, hijacking accounts as early as July and using a stealthy payload built to stay hidden from GitHub and automated scanners, according to JFrog researchers. Threat hunters at SafeDep, an open source supply chain security firm, first spotted the “testmetest” npm campaign last week, identifying 18 packages linked to the same operator between October 19 and October 25, including releases containing credential-stealing malware. As with earlier npm worms, the malware is self-replicating, steals credentials, and installs a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token, the security researchers noted. The new npm worm shares code with June’s Miasma Phantom Gyp worm, and adds Mini Shai-Hulud’s token-revocation wiper. As of October 22, however, SafeDep had found no compromised third-party packages or victims. “All observed activity belongs to the operator’s own test accounts,” the team wrote. As with most happy-ending security stories, that proved too good to be true. In a Monday report, supply chain security company JFrog said its analysis proved otherwise, and found the testmetest campaign operator “had already armed real repositories belonging to established developers and organizations.” This isn’t just about timing, either, according to JFrog researchers Guy Korolevski and Yair Benamou. “The payload blobs were large enough to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise,” they wrote. How the attacks worked The attackers planted execution hooks for AI coding assistants and development tools, including Claude, Gemini, Cursor, and VS Code, alongside polymorphic wrappers measuring 12.9 to 13.7 MB that decode a hidden CI-publisher payload. Separately, the npm worm steals credentials, modifies repositories and CI configurations, and spreads through npm packages. The malware also uses a compiled native add-on to decrypt and launch a separate payload. Before executing, the loader checks for CI runners, containers, sandboxes, debuggers, and other signs of automated analysis, exiting silently when it detects them to reduce the likelihood of detection by security scanners. The researchers also found a second build that skips the encrypted file. “It forks, detaches and runs a hard-coded command that pulls a loader from a repository on the operator's own GitHub account,” they wrote. That account – CementBeetleSteeple – hosted 17 campaign repositories in total. JFrog connected this account to a shellpanel scanner, previously documented by Socket in a large-scale campaign that abused GitHub Actions in compromised repositories to exploit CVE-2026-41940 and steal server credentials. CVE-2026-41940 is an authentication bypass affecting cPanel and WHM. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in April, and cPanel has since published patched versions. “C2 infrastructure were previously reported by Socket; our findings connect them to the testmetest GitHub victim cluster through artifacts and workflows on the same hijacked owners,” the JFrog researchers wrote. They added that while they found 42 armed GitHub repositories and attempted internet-wide exploitation, they did not confirm any downstream cPanel compromises.®

In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

A new AI agent prompt injection technique exploits how coding assistants consume local instruction files, blurring the line between text documents and executable actions.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 26, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: ipuwadol via Getty Images

A new indirect prompt injection attack relies on using markdown files in an end user's downloads folder to install malware and steal credentials.

That's according to Forever Security, which recently detailed a novel AI agent attack they captured in the wild. According to a research blog post, when an attacker plants a malicious file in a user's download folder, the user's agent may treat the file as trusted instructions and execute actions based on it.

What is notable about this attack compared to other prompt injection threats found in research reports is that this was not a case where the researchers developed the attack as a proof of concept. Rather, Forever's Gal Weizman and Omer Samet wrote that the AI security firm "caught live malware on a real customer's machine, attempting a new kind of attack the industry had not documented — and stopped it cold, before any code ran."

Malicious Markdowns

As the blog post authors explained, Forever Security found a malicious plaintext file named "AGENTS.md" in a customer's downloads folder, disguised as engineering notes. ".md" is a markdown file, used to guide agent behavior, and is trusted by many AI coding agents like OpenAI's Codex or Claude Code — Forever reproduced the attack with both (the original variant targeted Codex specifically).

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Researchers were unable to determine exactly how the file got on the user's computer, though they noted that it's the kind of file that a malicious website could attempt to download onto the user's computer. Then, when the coding agent is launched in that directory, it reads the instruction file as part of its project context.

According to Forever, the malicious instructions can persuade the agent to modify its configuration and perform follow-on actions. If the agent does ingest one of these malicious markdowns, the planted file makes the agent rewrite its own configuration, opening itself up for an attacker to instruct it to install malware or share its own login tokens.

In testing, Forever said the Codex attack chain succeeded more than 90% of the time. For Claude Code, the researchers reported roughly a 50% success rate, though certain variables may have influenced this success rate. For example, Claude Code uses a different installation path from Codex, which the original attack targeted.

'Nothing to Patch'

The attack requires someone only to grant their coding agent access to their home directory downloads folder, and that the agent can interact with web content. Forever says that according to its telemetry, about half of its customers run a coding agent inside their downloads folder, and a quarter of agent sessions open a real browser.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

"There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch. An agent that follows the AGENTS.md in its folder is doing exactly what it was built to do, the same way a browser that renders a phishing page is working as designed," the blog post read. "The problem is the circumstances: a folder the web can write to, trusted as if the user filled it. So the vector stays open. It is one early example of a bigger pattern: defenses built around a human break when an agent takes the human's place."

Weizman, lead researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading that AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic "may consider making agents aware of the risk of following commands originated by files that can be dropped by websites (such as inside the Downloads folder)," but adds that the issue described by the research is "mostly beyond their security model."

In the instance captured in the wild, Weizman says the exploit worked but was then blocked from follow-on activity by Forever's real-time security product, preventing an NPM package from being installed. Forever only managed to discover the initial example of the attack in the wild, though Weizman says the company is actively searching for more attempts.

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

For defenders, Forever recommends treating the user's home-directory download location (~/Downloads) as "hostile ground for agents," as by default it's the only way web content can reach a coding agent. Users can also check for instruction files they did not write, examine agent configurations for unexpected changes, and leave approval gates and sandboxes enabled. If a red flag has been found, the researchers said organizations should assume login tokens are compromised and rotate credentials.

Title: The breach wasn't in the model.
Context: An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update. Full Text:
A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic. The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs. AI developers get a crash course in key management. A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges. Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers. Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes. Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals. Patching what matters…matters. Monday business briefing. Tim Starks from CyberScoop is discussing targeted ads as a security risk. Championship rings come with a catch.

Today is Monday October 26th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic.

Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its researchers used AI agents to gain access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than twelve hours. According to The Washington Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in third-party business software, accessing systems containing meeting transcripts, salary information, and internal Slack messages.

Anthropic confirmed the intrusion but said access was limited to certain sales, human resources, and IT systems. Customer conversations, proprietary code, and AI model weights were not exposed. The company says its monitoring detected some suspicious activity, and it disabled the affected systems and worked with vendors to address the vulnerabilities.

Cathedral, founded by former DOGE employees, conducted the research through Anthropic’s security testing program. Anthropic disputes the startup’s characterization of the national security implications and says researchers violated some program rules.

The findings highlight a familiar security problem with potentially higher stakes: even cutting-edge AI companies depend on ordinary enterprise software, with all its ordinary vulnerabilities.

The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs.

The Pentagon has quietly established a new agency dedicated to disrupting foreign military technology programs through covert operations.

According to POLITICO, the Technology Support Office, established in April, consolidates two classified intelligence programs and aims to expand capabilities including cyberattacks, supply-chain sabotage, and deception operations.

The agency reportedly employs engineers, intelligence officers, and special operations personnel to develop tools that could delay adversaries’ technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence and advanced weapons systems.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg spearheaded the initiative, which has attracted opposition from Cyber Command and Special Operations Command over competing responsibilities and resources.

Supporters argue the effort is necessary to preserve America’s military advantage. Critics worry its secrecy could enable questionable operations and undermine congressional oversight.

The Pentagon disputes POLITICO’s reporting, calling its underlying claims inaccurate.

AI developers get a crash course in key management.

A supply-chain attack affecting tens of thousands of AI developers began with a security mistake made months earlier.

LiteLLM says it accidentally published a configuration file containing a master key in May. Although the file was removed, the key was never revoked. An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update.

Security firm Wiz says the malicious package was downloaded roughly 49,000 times. Within hours, attackers were testing stolen AWS credentials for access to AI models, suggesting a possible LLMjacking operation.

LiteLLM warns anyone who installed version 1.107.0 to assume their credentials were stolen and rotate them.

No organization has publicly confirmed a resulting breach. It’s LiteLLM’s second supply-chain compromise this year.

A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges.

A Florida businessman faces federal fraud charges for allegedly charging ransomware victims millions of dollars to recover their data while secretly paying the hackers responsible.

Prosecutors say Zohar Pinhasi, who operated the data recovery firm MonsterCloud, claimed he could decrypt files without paying ransoms. Instead, investigators allege he collected more than $19 million from clients while paying hackers over $8 million. In one case, an $8,200 ransom payment reportedly became a $150,000 customer bill.

The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation exposing the alleged scheme. MonsterCloud’s clients included law enforcement agencies that believed they were avoiding payments to criminals.

Pinhasi has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

For victims already paying one extortionist, prosecutors allege MonsterCloud effectively added another.

Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers.

Dutch police have arrested two men accused of using AI-generated phone calls to steal more than $425,000 from 170 bank customers.

The scheme began with automated calls warning of suspicious account activity. Victims who pressed a button were connected to a fake bank employee, who instructed them to download an app and scan their debit cards.

The app captured contactless payment data, which accomplices used to withdraw cash from ATMs.

The suspects, ages 23 and 25, were arrested October 6. Police also seized servers, phones, and laptops.

Both remain in custody as the investigation continues.

Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes.

Four months after European law enforcement disrupted the StealC malware operation, its seller is back with a new product.

Researchers at Varonis say Stadia RAT builds on StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities, adding remote desktop control, command execution, file management, and the ability to deploy additional malware.

The Windows malware targets browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging applications. It also avoids systems configured for several Eastern European and Central Asian languages, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, and can disable portions of Microsoft Defender’s protection.

Subscriptions range from $300 to $900 a month, with former StealC customers offered a free trial.

Researchers confirmed that Stadia reuses code from StealC, illustrating a familiar limitation of law enforcement takedowns: dismantling criminal infrastructure doesn’t necessarily put its operators out of business.

Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals.

Researchers at Korea University have demonstrated a technique for extracting sensitive information from air-gapped computers using USB power-management signals.

Called SPECTER, the method allows malware with administrator privileges to encode data through changes in USB device states, without conventional network connections or USB data transfers.

Researchers demonstrated three ways to receive the signals: monitoring smartphone charging indicators, observing changes in USB peripherals, and detecting electromagnetic emissions from USB cables.

Transmission speeds were extremely slow, topping out at one bit per second, making the technique more suitable for stealing passwords or cryptographic keys than large files.

The attack also requires hardware or firmware modifications, and some configurations produced no usable signals.

Researchers suggest monitoring unusual USB power-management activity, although the effectiveness of that approach remains untested.

Patching what matters…matters.

Security teams are patching more vulnerabilities than ever, but new research suggests all that effort isn’t necessarily making organizations safer.

According to Qualys, vulnerability closures increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, reaching 473 million. Yet the percentage of critical vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after seven days actually increased.

The problem? Prioritization.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on severity scores rather than evidence of real-world attacks.

Meanwhile, attackers are moving faster. Across the most critical exploited vulnerabilities, manual remediation failed to keep pace 88 percent of the time.

Qualys recommends shifting toward intelligence-driven, automated remediation that prioritizes actual exploitation and business impact.

The takeaway: Security isn’t necessarily about patching more. It’s about patching what matters.

Monday business briefing.

Investment and acquisition activity remains brisk across cybersecurity, with AI security attracting particular attention.

San Francisco-based Reach Security raised $50 million in Series B funding to expand its exposure management platform. AI agent security startup Opsin secured $21 million, while Asymptote Labs raised $5.5 million for its AI runtime security technology. AI penetration testing firm ManticoreAI also announced an undisclosed seed round.

On the acquisition front, Proofpoint agreed to buy data and AI security company Varonis for $6.3 billion, potentially creating a combined business serving more than 16,000 enterprises.

Anthropic acquired confidential AI data specialist OPAQUE, while Canadian AI company Cohere agreed to purchase Czech vulnerability management provider AISLE.

Elsewhere, legal technology firm Lineal acquired Swiss digital forensics company Forentec, and Britain’s Bytes Technology Group purchased Microsoft security specialist CyberOne.

The common thread across these deals is growing investment in AI security, data protection, and automated vulnerability management.

Championship rings come with a catch.

The New York Knicks celebrated their first NBA championship in more than half a century by offering employees free championship rings. Unfortunately, the offer was fake, and the real prize was mandatory cybersecurity training.

According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden sent employees a simulated phishing email inviting them to choose between two ring designs. Anyone who clicked the link earned a trip to cybersecurity class instead.

The exercise followed a real security incident in which attackers reportedly used phished employee credentials to hack and extort the organization.

MSG acknowledged that using championship rings as bait was an unfortunate mistake. The company says it’s distributing more than 275 actual rings and pieces of jewelry worth over $3.7 million.

For employees who fell for the phishing test, the championship celebration apparently came with a refresher course in disappointment.

Title: AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack
Context: Background On October 16, Huntress first reported the abuse of a ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to access Microsoft 365 tenants, and since then we have been continuing to...
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Eric Stride and Andrea Hatcher for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

On October 16, Huntress first reported the abuse of a ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to access Microsoft 365 tenants, and since then we have been continuing to investigate threat actor behavior related to this incident.

Now, we're pulling on a different thread: who, or what, was doing the typing during the unauthorized activity we observed. Microsoft has published its own findings, attributing the activity to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent AI framework, to abuse the compromised ConnectWise application credentials and sign in to downstream Microsoft 365 tenants at machine speed. Our telemetry aligns with Microsoft's findings, but does not independently confirm them.

In the activity on the tenants we examined, we observed the tooling change in under a minute between runs and a retry loop appear in the run after a failure. Some actions were tested in one tenant before being run in batches, a pattern we saw three times across two tools.

Taken together, these observations form our working hypothesis: scripted tooling did most of the heavy lifting in this incident, while something adapted the tooling between runs, quickly. That something may very well be an agent. Below, we're providing details about what we saw, and leaving it to the audience to draw their own conclusions.

What we can and cannot see

Our view comes from Entra Sign-in logs and directory audit logs in the Microsoft 365 tenants we monitor, plus the fleet-wide sweeps we ran during the incident window. That gives us the timing, order, and shape of what the actor caused Entra to record. However, it leaves some large gaps:

Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in the Entra audit log, and no victim we know of had Graph activity logging enabled, so the scope and method of any Graph access cannot be seen in the logs available to us.

Application-only audit events carry no source IP address, so we cannot tie some of the activity, such as the credential changes, to a specific IP.

We have no visibility into the actor's own systems, so we cannot see the tooling itself, or whether any model provider sat behind it.

Lastly, we cannot say whether AI was used to plan the operation, develop target lists, or write the tooling.

One day, three modes of operation

Most of what we can see happened on October 15, in a little under 14 hours. Laid out in a single timeline, the activity falls into three distinct behaviors:

Scripted loops

Hands-on operator work (an "operator" being whoever steered the tooling, whether that's a person, automation, or an AI agent)

A stretch where the tooling kept running after the thing it was targeting was already gone

Figure 1: Activity on October 15 in Huntress-monitored tenants, grouped by behavior. Operator-driven means a person, or a model acting for one, was steering the tooling between runs.

How scripts, people, and AI agents look different in logs

The logs Huntress analyzes record behavior and help us figure out what occurred: how fast things happen, what happens after something fails, and how much the requests vary. The logs may show different types of fingerprints depending on if the behavior comes from a script, a person, or an LLM agent. Below is a table of possible behavioral signals between the three, though these are general characteristics and may have substantial overlap.

Signal

Scripted automation

Human operator

LLM agent in the loop

Pacing

Machine-regular, sub-second or fixed intervals

Uneven, with pauses that look like reading output

Steady, gated by model inference

Response to errors

None unless coded, repeats the same failure

Reads the error, adjusts, or gives up

Reads the error and changes approach

Variety of requests

Identical request shape, repeated

Efficient, goes to what it wants

Exploratory, retries with variations

User agent

One fixed string per tool

Varies with the tools the person picks up

Often SDK defaults (python-requests, httpx)

These categories are Huntress analyst heuristics for telling the three apart, not an industry standard. A tricky nuance here is that this isn't a black-or-white determination: no single row completely settles what's primarily behind the attack. For instance, a script can carry a sleep timer and a list of user agents, which could make its behaviors in the logs look more human than it is. One password spray against a single tenant may at first read like a person, but a fixed beat in the timing and a rotating list of user agents would indicate otherwise. When investigating these signals, part of what matters is the mix and whether the behavior changes in response to what just happened. A script repeats itself; a person or an agent adjusts.

Two limits apply to everything in our analysis below:

A person pasting commands from a chatbot into a terminal looks like a person in these logs, because the model never touches the API.

Logs show who ran the tooling, not who wrote it; a model can write a fixed script that looks like any other script.

What we saw

The loops: scripts at scale

The logs showed us that on October 15, between roughly 06:13 and 08:46 UTC, the credential was used against almost 1,000 tenants, one after another, in ascending tenant ID order. That is a loop over a sorted list: one token request per tenant, one to six minutes apart, with the same user agent (Python-urllib/3.12) every time. When the loop stopped partway through the list, it looked like an exhausted list or an interrupted process (as opposed to a concerted decision to stop).

The logs also showed that nine minutes earlier, around 06:04 UTC, about 100 failed token requests had landed within 10 seconds against the first 100 tenants of that same list of 1,000 tenants. Every request failed the same way, and nothing changed between attempts. This is a signature of a thread pool: a fixed set of worker threads pulling tenants off a shared list and firing requests in parallel, each blind to what the others get back. Nothing in the loop reads a response before the next request goes out.

The same thread-pool tool then ran a second time against 100 tenants, using a different application's key, at 13 to 21 attempts per second, and failed the same way. Both runs used application secrets that belong to a single tenant, which cannot authenticate anywhere else, and the tool kept firing regardless. Whoever built it, or at least launched it, did not account for that difference.

Here is what that does and does not tell us: 10 requests a second is faster than anything that reads each response before deciding its next move, whether that is a person or a model working step by step. So this was most likely one script, run at least twice. It does not tell us who or what wrote the script. A model can write a thread pool as easily as a person can, so while this rules out a model making each call, it does not rule out a model writing the tool.

Trial and error

On October 15 between 03:42 and 03:57 UTC, the logs indicated a pattern of trial and error in the unauthorized activity, with the tooling changing in less than a minute between runs. The activity outlined in the logs looked like an attempt to establish persistent access by adding credentials:

A secret was added, removed, and added again.

A certificate was uploaded, but it failed because the thumbprint did not match.

The operator fell back to a secret again before granting, then removing, the Global Administrator role twice.

The same sequence ran in a second tenant 47 seconds later, with both keys added in a single run.

During that window the tooling changed in response to results at least three times. The run after the failed certificate upload added a retry loop, the sequence repeated in a second tenant with both keys in a single run, and when that tenant refused a Global Administrator removal, the actor granted a different role to a sibling principal, and the original service principal was then deleted.

Based on this activity, it's possible that the credential planting and the targeted probe were steered by an operator adapting between runs. However, we can't determine whether that operator was a person, automation, or an LLM model.

The hand-picked targets: pilot, then batch

Between roughly 09:25 and 12:35 UTC on October 15, one sweep touched 17 tenants, with one Graph token request each in a hand-ordered sequence with irregular spacing over three hours. A second sweep at 13:54 UTC ran a fixed probe of six resources per tenant, in sorted order, with four seconds per tenant. Someone appears to have chosen the targets, checked them one at a time, and then handed the list to a script.

Where it started to look like an agent

No single observation here proves anything, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. But several of them pointed in the same direction, and the longer we looked, the harder it became to explain them away as a person at a keyboard or a script left to run.

First, there's the 55-second gap between retries that we described above. The certificate upload that failed on a thumbprint mismatch at 03:48:24 UTC ended that run with no retry. The next run, 55 seconds later, did retry the same error, at 3.5 seconds and then 7.1 seconds, until it worked, and it carried the same retry into the second tenant.

Figure 2: How the tooling changed

So what does this actually tell us about what was going on behind the scenes? Either someone edited the code in under a minute, or a prepared tool had a retry option nobody had used yet. A script left alone does not rewrite itself between runs. A person, a person relaying to a model, or an agent was likely adapting it as an operator. The speed of the change is consistent with an agent loop: read the failure, rewrite the call, run it again.

The retry logic is particularly revealing. Doubling the wait between attempts is textbook defensive error handling. This is something that generated code tends to add unprompted, and in this incident showed up in a tool that had none just a minute earlier. The tooling was also more elaborate than the job required: the 100-tenant burst used a thread pool, where a simple loop over the list would have done the same work.

Another notable pattern that we outlined above: An operator tried an action against one tenant first, then ran it as a batch, again and again. We saw that three times across two sets of tooling. That points to the habits of an operator, not a quirk of one script. Microsoft describes ARTEX as building a graph of the assets it discovers and running parallel breach paths, which has the same shape: probe, learn, and then fan out.

Finally, there is the speed. Our first enumeration activity started around 01:05 UTC, and the credential changes in the first tenant were complete by 03:50 UTC, in line with Microsoft's report of under three hours from targeting to privileged access in multiple environments. Speed alone does not separate an agent from a well-prepared script, but it is the kind of compression Microsoft describes agent frameworks delivering. Some of the user agent strings also look hand-set rather than library defaults. One tool identified itself as python-requests/2.31, where the library sends python-requests/2.31.0 by default, and on October 13 a browser string was missing its standard "(KHTML, like Gecko)" segment. Both fit a model producing user agents from memory, and both fit a person copying them from documentation.

Put together, these factors make up our working hypothesis: scripted tooling is doing the heavy lifting in this incident, with something adapting it between runs, quickly. That something may well be an agent. The next section is about how sure we are, and where the evidence runs out.

What the telemetry can confirm

A working hypothesis is only worth sharing if its limits are clear. Here are ours.

The best evidence against a fully autonomous agent is what happened after 03:57 UTC. The Teams service principal was deleted, and for the next 22 minutes requests using it kept firing every four to eight seconds. These were rejected every time, and subsequent requests didn't change. An agent watching its own output would be expected to stop. A multi-agent framework could keep unattended fan-out tasks running while other agents carry on, which could explain this behavior. So too could a person who launched some background loops and walked away. However we don't know which one played out in this situation.

Another consideration: curl/7.88.1 is the version Debian 12 ships with, and the official python:3.12 container image is built on Debian 12. That points to how the tooling was possibly packaged, since the user agent doesn't align with the system's external fingerprints.

The biggest gap is the missing Graph request logs. They would show query variety, the clearest difference between a script and an agent, and nobody we know of collected them.

So, how sure are we? We are highly confident that an operator, whether a person or an LLM model, adapted the tooling between runs. On our own telemetry alone, we put our confidence that an LLM was involved in the escalation tooling at low to medium. Taking Microsoft's attribution into account, we put it at medium to high.

What would potentially help settle it is evidence we do not hold: the Graph activity logs from a victim that had them enabled, the tooling itself, or traffic from the actor's systems to a model provider's API.

What Microsoft says: Storm-0940 and ARTEX

In its October 21 report Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise credential abuse to Storm-0940, a threat actor they say has been active since 2021. Microsoft asserts that the actor targets organizations across industries for data theft, and has historically gotten in through password spraying and internet-facing applications, then kept access by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

What is new, according to Microsoft, is the tooling. They report that from at least September 2026 the actor used ARTEX, an open-source framework in which LLM-driven agents run a penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction, building a graph of the assets and weaknesses they discover as they go. ARTEX can use any AI model, and Microsoft says it has seen other actors using it in several regions.

How does Microsoft connect that to this incident? The reasoning they've shared points to infrastructure, attributing a large password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 between October 10 and 14 to Storm-0940, and noting that the same IP, and the surrounding range, appear in the ConnectWise advisory. The report does not describe how Microsoft identified ARTEX, or what links the earlier spray to Storm-0940. We have not independently verified either. However, Microsoft may know how to identify this particular tooling, which is why they have mentioned its usage in this campaign.

How our findings line up with Microsoft's report

Our telemetry is consistent with Microsoft's account in several ways.

We saw the same infrastructure (144.172.64[.]128) and user agents (Python-urllib/3.12, curl/7.88.1), and the same sequence: compromised application credentials, then Graph follow-on with credential additions and privileged role changes, including the Teams application assigning itself Global Administrator.

Our telemetry also corroborates the password spray Microsoft attributes to 144.172.64[.]99.

Scale is where we differ, by design. Microsoft counts more than 2,250 tenants and we see only the tenants we protect, so our numbers are only a subset, not a contradiction. We saw python-requests/2.34.2 from 144.172.64[.]99 in the October 10 to 14 password spray, but not azure-toolkit/1.0, and we saw no identity or group changes in the two tenants where we hold directory audit logs.

Why this matters

Whoever, or whatever was behind it, this operation was not polished. Over the course of our investigation we saw:

Secrets added, removed, and added again.

A certificate that failed to upload.

Secrets for one tenant sprayed at a hundred others, where they would never work.

Yet, as we saw in the two tenants where we hold audit logs, it took under three hours from the first enumeration activity to privileged role changes, in line with Microsoft's report across multiple environments, because the stolen application credential did much of the work.

It's clumsy, but it worked. If an agent was in the loop here, it was an early one. It already ran things in parallel, never needed a break, and left defenders a few hours. Tools like this get better quickly: they stop making the mistakes we saw, and they are cheap to point at hundreds of tenants at once. Microsoft makes the same point: agents can work around the clock and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously.

Defenders' visibility is also in flux. In our view, the signals we relied on here (a retry that showed up 55 seconds after a failure, a fixed beat between requests, and user agent strings customized away from the library default) are the first things a better tool will smooth away. Cadence will not be a reliable signal for long. What will hold up is what the activity does, which is where the detections below point.

What defenders can do

Speed is the biggest concern here. This activity moves faster than a person can triage. This is useful detection guidance regardless of the actor:

Alert when a service principal assigns itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator, deletes itself, or when one vendor principal grants a role to a sibling.

Alert on credential additions to high-privilege applications from unexpected sources.

Baseline each vendor application's normal user agent (kiota-dotnet for the ConnectWise applications), source ranges, and cadence. The clearest early signal here was a vendor application behaving differently from its baseline.

Turn on Microsoft Graph activity logs where licensing allows, and keep raw user agent strings and sub-second timestamps. Cadence and retry timing were our most useful signals, and normalization destroys both.

Watch across tenants, not only within one. A trickle in any single tenant can be one campaign running at thousands of attempts per minute across the estate.

We will update this post as ConnectWise, Microsoft, and others share more.
