In a subsequent phase of reconnaissance, attackers deployed additional packet-capture rules to core perimeter firewalls targeting:

UDP port 69 (TFTP): File, communications, firmware and configuration capture

UDP ports 1812 and 1813 (RADIUS and RADIUS-Accounting): Network authentication sniffing

TCP port 389 (LDAP): Active Directory query interception and directory enumeration

Credential Decryption and Initial Re-Entry

The exfiltrated FortiGate configurations contained sensitive credentials stored as reversible ciphertext. We confirmed that the credentials were recoverable by successfully brute-forcing administrative and SSL/VPN passwords from the exfiltrated configuration files.

Using legitimate credentials, the attackers established unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls from known external staging infrastructure (23.240.77[.]233 and 47.18.167[.]159). These sessions granted the attackers authenticated access into internal network-management segments.

Privilege Escalation: CVE-2025-61624

During the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2025-61624 to escalate from FortiOS administrative access to root on the underlying firewall operating system. A FortiOS administrator, including a super_admin, operates within a restricted management command line with no shell access and no direct control over the appliance file system or its running processes. The daemons that implement FortiOS run as root beneath that interface.

The vulnerability allows an authenticated administrative account to read and write arbitrary files as root via path traversal in the FortiOS CLI system.auto-script engine. The auto-script object name is not sanitized, allowing a name containing traversal sequences to place the script body outside the intended directory, at any file system location. The script executes with the privileges of the auto-script engine.

The sanitized event below highlights the creation of the traversal object ../../../../setup used to drop the PEERSTITCH initial-stage loader shown below in Figure 2.

Technical Analysis of the PEERSTITCH Implant

PEERSTITCH is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C and statically linked against glibc. It acts as a one-shot process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons:

/bin/miglogd: The central system and traffic logging daemon

/bin/iked: The IKE/IPsec VPN service daemon handling cryptographic negotiation

Figure 3 shows a flow chart of PEERSTITCH activity, which we will examine in greater detail.

Delivery and Staging Chain

1). Downloader initialization: Exploiting CVE-2025-61624, the attackers pushed ../../../../setup to a select number of firewalls

2). Payload retrieval: The script downloaded five files from hxxp[:]//23.240.77[.]233:8085/ into /data2/template/:

pM.js: Environment preparation script (self-deleting)

a.js (saved as index.js): Emscripten JavaScript runtime module

a.wasm (saved as index.wasm): Compiled WebAssembly binary module

b.js (saved as ipssem.js): Deployment orchestrator script

dd (saved as lldprx): Native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core)

3). Execution: Following an execution delay, ipssem.js launched lldprx with arguments lldprx!index.js!index.wasm!ipssem.js!lldprx!yyyy!pM.js

Injector Execution and Process Parasitization

The lldprx binary performs a single-pass execution sequence:

Process discovery: Iterates through /proc/, parses /proc/<pid>/cmdline and locates the process identifiers (PIDs) for /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked

Memory layout enumeration: Reads /proc/<pid>/maps to extract the base addresses and memory boundaries of both target daemons

Process attachment: Attaches to both running processes using ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE, pid) and halts execution via PTRACE_INTERRUPT

Register state capture: Calls ptrace(PTRACE_GETREGSET, pid) to snapshot all ARM64 general-purpose registers (X0 through X30), the stack pointer (SP) and program counter (PC)

Dynamic shellcode construction: Generates an ARM64 bootstrap stub dynamically. The bootstrap executes an mmap syscall (X8 = 0xDE) requesting 0x4000 (16,384 bytes) of PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE | PROT_EXEC (RWX) memory mapped as MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS

Payload injection: Writes a 1,344-byte injection payload into the newly allocated RWX buffer via /proc/<pid>/mem

Covert IPC and Cross-Daemon Memory Sharing

Instead of using network sockets or disk files, PEERSTITCH creates a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked.

Figure 4 shows a flowchart for PEERSTITCH network traffic.

Passive traffic monitoring: Inside both daemons, the hook code inspects data already passing through the process without redirecting packets. It evaluates string patterns using strstr() for two specific markers:

TCP port marker: 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port)

IP address marker: 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)

Tag extraction and buffering: When a marker is identified, the hook extracts an associated session token or identifier (up to 31 bytes) and writes it into a 16-slot circular ring buffer at offset +0x0F0

Cross-process write: The hook iterates through its forwarding table at offset +0x400 (populated with the counterpart daemon's PID and buffer base address). It invokes open(), lseek() and write() on /proc/<counterpart_pid>/mem, writing the extracted tag directly into the other daemon's memory.

Conditional execution branching: When /bin/iked processes subsequent VPN sessions, its hook inspects its injection buffer. If a corresponding tag exists, the hook takes an alternate return branch (ADRP return path), bypassing default FortiOS security validations.

Memory Patching and Branch Path Modification

To suppress tamper detection and alter default daemon routines, PEERSTITCH applies direct NOP patches (0xAA0003E0, corresponding to MOV X0, X0 on ARM64) to three static offsets within target process memory:

base + 0x106F7B8

base + 0x1072E20

base + 0x109A570

A 20-byte trampoline patch is written to base + 0x135102C to redirect standard execution into the allocated RWX hook buffer. Figure 5 shows a visual memory layout of the 16 KB buffer used by the ARM64 PEERSTITCH payload.

Apache mod_md ACME Reverse Shell Command and Control

Alongside PEERSTITCH, the attackers established a command and control channel by weaponizing the native Apache mod_md (Managing Domains) module on FortiGate firewalls. This module uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol.

The attackers pushed an auto-script object to create ../../tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf, as shown below in Figure 6.

Weaponization Mechanics

1). Rogue certificate authority initialization: The account.json state file demonstrates the initial registration with the attacker's ACME server, explicitly routing ACME directory requests to external infrastructure

2). Challenge orchestration: The order.json file outlines the pending certificate order, mapping the authorization and finalization URLs directly to the attacker's server

3). Command execution via DNS-01 challenge: MDChallengeDns01 was mapped directly to /bin/node. When Apache initiates a certificate validation challenge, it executes Node.js with parameters retrieved from the remote ACME server. The job.json debug log reveals how the attackers exploited this by injecting shell commands (kali@23.240.77[.]233:8084:b -F /tmp/upfile/ssh_config -i) directly into the domain name field of the challenge request, initiating an SSH-based reverse shell.

4). Continuous polling loop: Setting MDRenewMode always forced the Apache daemon to continuously trigger these malicious renewal challenges. Because the DNS-01 challenge was mapped to /bin/node, this polling cycle ensured the continuous re-execution of the injected payload, establishing a persistent outbound reverse-shell communication channel.

Management Impersonation and FortiGate to FortiManager Chained Exploitation

FortiGate to FortiManager (FGFM) communications occur over TCP port 541 using cryptographic trust material requested and validated against appliance serial numbers. The archive exfiltrated during the initial FortiJump compromise contained this material, along with the serial numbers and management relationships of every downstream device.

Following FGFM interactions from external infrastructure over TCP port 541, an administrative account named FortiGateCloud downloaded complete running configurations from multiple managed firewalls. The victim organization operated no FortiManager Cloud tenant, and no such account was provisioned on the affected devices.

We assess with a medium degree of confidence that the attackers issued these commands by impersonating the management platform over FGFM. Two paths were available to them, and the evidence does not distinguish between them:

Exploitation of CVE-2024-26009 to bypass FGFM authentication using the FortiManager's serial number

Direct reuse of the exfiltrated trust material to authenticate as the legitimate FortiManager

Asserting a management identity requires terminating the authentic FortiManager's session. It is possible that the attackers forced this session termination using CVE-2024-26008, consistent with the intermittent tunnel management interface drops described in the Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion section below.

We are aware of other vulnerabilities in which the FortiGateCloud account has been misused to perform unauthorized actions, including:

CVE-2025-59718

CVE-2025-59719

The related single sign-on (SSO) issues tracked under FG-IR-26-060

Each of these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, and the affected firewalls held no such enrollment. We exclude these vulnerabilities from scope for this intrusion. We note that the observed activity reused only the account name and none of the exploitation artifacts associated with those issues.

Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion

The attackers took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts:

Service termination: Executed killall -9 miglogd and killall -9 syslogd to halt local and remote syslog generation prior to executing malicious auto-scripts

Crash log clearing: Issued FortiOS diagnostic command diagnose debug crashlog clear to wipe segmentation fault logs generated during initial memory injection attempts

Configuration rollback: Automatically deleted rogue administrator accounts, rogue VPN groups and auto-script objects (../../../../setup) shortly after execution

Decoy artifact creation: Overwrote /tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf with a common string found in this file (#0 certs managed by ACME\n\n\n) to mask reverse-shell configuration files

Process memory self-deletion: lldprx unlinked its own binary from disk and scanned /proc/ to terminate the staging setup process before exiting

Logging telemetry disruption: Log telemetry showed intermittent drops across the tunnel management interface during periods of malicious activity. We assess with medium confidence that the attackers deliberately induced this degradation to suppress real-time telemetry to central management consoles. This is consistent with the previously described pattern of telemetry suppression, including terminating miglogd and syslogd, clearing crash logs, and rolling back configuration objects. It’s possible that the attackers forced the disconnects using CVE-2024-26008 over TCP port 541. Available logs do not capture the triggered traffic, so we could not confirm the mechanism.

Conclusion

This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks. One compromised appliance yielded the cryptographic keys, credentials and network topology for more than 500 firewalls, including devices protecting client organizations.

The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware. By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring.

For organizations that manage infrastructure on behalf of others, the management platform is the highest-value target on the network. Compromising the management platform is not contained by the boundary of the organization that owns it. That compromise also does not end when the platform is patched.

The cryptographic trust material governing the platform's relationship with every managed device leaves with the attacker and remains valid until it is rotated. Defenders must treat edge management interfaces with the highest level of zero trust isolation. They must also treat the credentials and certificates those interfaces hold as compromised the moment the platform is.

Context: Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal...
Full Text:
In today’s always-connected world, the line between dark and light is blurring.

Well, actually, you’re still protected from finding out what the dark web looks like because you need to download a special browser to access it. But the drama of the dark web can be intriguing. And it’s not all wicked criminal activity either.

Curious about what’s lurking in the shadows of the internet? Keep reading to learn more about the state of the dark web, what it is, and how to access it (safely, of course!).

What is the dark web?

Everyone has their own preconceived notion of what the dark web is. (Of course, with a name as ominous as dark web, it kind of sets the mood, right?) For the sake of this blog, we focused on finding a credible definition that isn’t muddied with preconceptions.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that you can only reach with special tools. Merriam-Webster describes it as a set of sites that search engines don't index and that regular browsers can't open. Reaching them takes specialized software or a specific network setup, and encryption keeps both site owners and visitors anonymous.

(If you were expecting a more sinister-sounding definition for the term dark web, you’re not alone. 😅)

The web, as a whole, can be divided into three parts: the surface web vs. deep web vs. dark web:

Dark web: This is where things get…different. As we said, dark web activity isn't indexed and requires special software or network configuration to access. While it can be a place where people broker illegal activities, it can also be used for legal activities, like anonymously sourcing information.

Surface web: The surface web is everything that’s automatically indexed by search engines. It’s everything that pops up when you Google something (or Bing or whatever search engine), and you don’t need any sort of special software or login to access it.

Deep web: The deep web is sites that are not indexed, but are accessible to the average person, usually through encryption or password protection (or both, both is good!). This includes things like online banking and cloud storage.

What does the dark web look like?

The dark web often looks surprisingly ordinary—with familiar features like About Us sections, pricing pages, and even customer reviews. You’ll see, though, in the screenshots below, that a lot of sites are basic or outdated, often tricky to navigate.

Many of these sites still work like any other ecommerce website. Threat actors advertise, highlight their skills, and market themselves, their expertise, and their services just like any salesperson.

How does the dark web work?

Frankly, the dark web has earned a bad reputation—and unfairly so. At its core, the dark web isn’t inherently evil or mysterious. (Okay, it's a little mysterious.)

It’s simply a collection of websites that require a specific, anonymity-powered web browser to access. Usually, these sites use a .onion domain and are only accessed through the anonymous Tor Browser.

The dark web isn't all crime and chaos—detectives and journalists sometimes access the dark web to do research while maintaining their anonymity. You can play chess on the dark web. At one point in time, you could even navigate to a Tor website and watch a slideshow of cats and kittens submitted by other users.

The dark web isn't any one thing—it's shaped entirely by how people choose to use it.

How to safely access the dark web

Because there are so many different reasons that you might be interested in the dark web, it’s important to know how to access it safely. Here are some tips:

Use a dark web browser: Use the official Tor browser to access the dark web. This is the essential tool for "onion routing" that provides anonymity.

Use a VPN: While Tor provides encryption, using a high-quality virtual private network (VPN) before launching adds an extra layer of privacy by hiding the fact that you are even connecting to the Tor network from your internet service provider (ISP).

Never use personal information: Don’t log into any personal accounts—email, social media, or bank accounts—while using Tor because it immediately de-anonymizes you.

Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal your identity or install malware.

Know what’s legal: Accessing the dark web is completely legal in the US, but engaging in illegal activities (such as buying/selling drugs, weapons, or accessing child pornography) is a serious felony, regardless of anonymity.

Our journey into the dark web

We’re firm believers in the buddy system when it comes to doing scary things like journeying through the dark web. Don't worry, though— we’ve suited up, strapped on our protective gear, and done the risky part for you.

How did we suit up?

First, we booted up our virtual machine (VM) to add an extra layer of security while browsing. Then, we fired up our anonymous Tor Browser. Finally, we disabled JavaScript—a quick but important safeguard against websites that run malicious code.

With these precautions in place, we were ready to access the dark web. We began our journey by navigating to a few .onion directories to find some ~shady~ websites to peruse.

One of the first things we found? A Tor scam list, complete with "safe" browsing recommendations. How… thoughtful.

Who is using the dark web?

There are About Us pages to answer that question.

Chances are, you wouldn’t hire a plumber without doing some research. You’d want to make sure she’s got the experience and skills to leave your pipes in better shape than she found them. So why would anyone hire a hacker without seeing a well-written About Us page?

You might think this requirement would narrow the pool of hackers to choose from, because are hackers really spending their time writing About Us pages? Yes. Yes, they are.

You’ve got to hand it to them: These hackers did a great job at flexing their hacking skills while staying anonymous. It's not exactly LinkedIn, but the info they share gives these folks some credibility (in a strange way).

If you’ve never browsed the dark web before, you probably weren’t expecting to see several websites with About Us pages. It’s eye-opening to see these hackers flaunting their skills and competing with one another to earn new business.

One site was even gracious enough to list the team’s favorite well-known hackers:

It’s kind of sweet, in a weird sort of way.

The takeaway: Threat actors are just like any other entrepreneurs out to make a profit. The difference? They skip the red tape and regulations that everyone else has to follow. This leaves the door wide open for them to advertise whatever services they please—as long as they abide by the Hacker’s Code of Conduct. (More on that later.)

What’s on the dark web?

Product pages, packaged deals, and more.

Now that we know our threat actors, let’s investigate what they can do for us.

Like any good businessperson, hackers aren’t shy about broadcasting what they can do if the price is right. In fact, some are so business-savvy that they provide packages and tiered solutions:

Others simply prefer to put all their services out there for people to pick and choose from:

But then, we stumbled across two different websites that made us raise an eyebrow. Here’s the first site:

And here's the second site:

These two sites look eerily similar to each other except for one thing: on the latter site, the prices for each service are noticeably higher. That’s weird, wouldn’t you say?

The takeaway: Just like any other website where you can purchase products or services, threat actors also have tiered options, promotional packages, and detailed descriptions of their offerings.

One key difference that seems to be standard across dark web websites is that hackers request that their payments be made in cryptocurrencies. Why? Because it’s anonymous.

Our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, nicely sums up why cryptocurrencies are a hacker’s best friend:

"No other technology offers a bad actor the perfect crime: anonymous threats without borders, blackmail and extortion without a financial oversight or governing authority. [...] Unless the bad actors make any unintentional mistake, the inherent design of cryptocurrency makes for a perfect getaway car."

Dark web customer experience and reviews

Threat actors are actually quite concerned with creating a positive customer experience, with features like customer reviews and FAQ on many of the pages we visited.

The takeaway: Just like any other website selling goods and services, threat actors also want to show that they have happy customers and give potential customers all the info they need to make an informed purchase.

Bottom line: The dark web is a business

If a business owner feels she’s been wronged, there are courts for that. The same can be said for hackers. That’s right—threat actors have their very own court system, along with codes of conduct to follow to minimize the chances of landing there themselves.

What happens in “hacker’s court”? The same thing that happens in any other court: Plaintiffs and defendants get together to tell their respective stories in front of a jury before a ruling is made.

We can't stress this enough: Most bad actors today don’t just hack into websites and devices for the fun of it. These are professionals who become experts in their trade and master their skills to earn a paycheck.

They build websites to sell their services, cut their customers special deals, and ask for reviews from satisfied customers. If they’re wronged, they handle it in a civilized manner in hacker’s court. These are organized operations that function just like any other business.

Don’t be afraid of the dark (web)

We hope that this field trip to the dark web has been enlightening. It’s incredible to see just how many parallels exist between anyone with a “normal” day job and dark web threat actors. Many different careers, from marketing and sales to cybersecurity and infosec, have dark-mirror versions of themselves—hackers and scammers running the same playbooks in reverse—on the dark web.

If nothing else, we hope this blog will make you more vigilant against cyberattacks. Hackers are in it for the money. What could destroy your personal records or your business’s reputation is just another payday for a hacker. Think twice before clicking on an email from an unfamiliar sender. Keep your devices updated and install patches as soon as they become available.

Threats can seem overwhelming, but with our in-depth understanding of how threat actors think, we know what to look for. Huntress gives you fully managed endpoint detection and response (EDR), so you've got 24/7 support from security experts ready to respond to threats.

* Special thanks to our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, for his help with writing this blog.

FAQ

Is it legal to look at the dark web?

Yes, exploring the dark web is legal—as long as you aren’t breaking any laws. If you’re just browsing or doing legitimate research, accessing the dark web is fine. If you engage in any criminal act, you’ll be subject to prosecution.

What is the dark web actually used for?

The dark web is a mixed bag. Some people use it for both legitimate purposes, like preserving privacy and free speech, especially in restrictive countries, and, unfortunately, others for shady activities like selling stolen data or illegal goods.

How do I know if I’m on the dark web?

If you're using a specialized browser like Tor to access websites ending with .onion that aren't reachable through regular browsers or search engines, congrats (or maybe not)—you're on the dark web!

Can you be tracked on the dark web?

The dark web offers more anonymity, but it's not exactly an invisibility cloak. With sophisticated methods and one careless click, determined parties can still track your activities, so anonymity isn't guaranteed.

What is a crime on the dark web?

Crimes on the dark web include activities like selling illegal substances, hacking services, and trafficking stolen data. Basically, if it's illegal in the real world, it's illegal on the dark web too—no free passes.

Title: Passkeys Raise the Bar. Here’s Where Attackers Can Still Get In.
Context: The goal is to steer them toward an authentication flow the attacker can exploit
Full Text:
Passkeys are a major step forward in authentication, but protecting a credential is only part of protecting an account. Attackers can still target enrollment, recovery, compromised endpoints, alternative authentication flows, and social engineering.

Recent reporting highlights these gaps. This post examines them and shows how phishing-resistant authentication, identity protection, endpoint protection, security awareness training, and detection work together to close them. The goal is not to weaken the case for passkeys, but rather to show how organizations can make their protection count across the full account lifecycle.

What "passkey-themed phishing" actually means

Passkey-themed phishing is a social engineering attack that uses the passkey as bait, rather than defeating the passkey itself. Attackers impersonate a trusted source, typically IT staff, and urge employees to update or set up a passkey. The goal is to steer them toward an authentication flow the attacker can exploit.

Device code phishing shows how far this approach can reach. Huntress researchers tracked a campaign called EvilTokens that hit 344 organizations across five countries in about 16 days. Device code authentication is the same flow that lets you activate a streaming app on a smart TV by typing a code into your phone. Attackers start that process themselves, then send a convincing email that leads the victim to enter the code on a real Microsoft page. The victim completes MFA correctly, and the attacker walks away with a valid session. No password is stolen, no malware is required, and the attacker does not need to break passkey cryptography. The attacker abuses a legitimate device-code flow to obtain a valid session after the victim authorizes the attacker-controlled client. EvilTokens packaged the technique as a phishing-as-a-service kit with AI-generated lures tailored to each victim's role, which means the pattern can scale.

In another campaign, attackers impersonated IT staff and told employees to update their passkey or sign-in configuration. When Microsoft researchers dug into the incident, they found that the passkey served as the lure, while attackers pursued other authentication flows to get in. One documented attack sequence explicitly involved non-phishing-resistant MFA.

Both campaigns point to the same lesson: attackers look for any legitimate sign-in path that still works in their favor. The passkey may remain secure and untouched. A passkey-themed phishing attack does not mean attackers defeated passkey cryptography. Defenders need to identify the authentication method and policy that actually allowed access, because that is where the fix belongs.

That distinction is where identity threat detection and response (ITDR) becomes relevant. ITDR does not make the passkey itself stronger. It helps defenders identify and contain suspicious activity around a legitimate sign-in.

Enrollment and recovery are security boundaries

An attacker may not need to steal an existing passkey if they can register another credential or exploit a weaker recovery process. The original credential can remain protected while the attacker gets into the account through a separate door.

Closing that door starts with a clear answer to one question: what proof does your organization require before someone adds an authenticator, replaces a lost key, or resets MFA? Those actions deserve strong verification and monitoring.

A compromised endpoint can undermine authentication

SpecterOps' research demonstrates techniques that manipulate Windows WebAuthn interactions, including browser hooks that capture authentication responses or alter challenges. These attacks have specific prerequisites, including local execution or access to the authentication process. That makes them a different class of threat from an ordinary phishing website.

This is why endpoint protection remains necessary after a passkey rollout. Malicious software can target the environment handling authentication without extracting the private key. Protecting the endpoint that handles authentication starts with ensuring that every device signing in to company resources is managed and protected by an active and monitored endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent.

Employees can play a real part in endpoint defense too. This includes things like:

Install updates promptly when your computer or browser asks. Prompt updates close the doors attackers use to get a foothold.

Add browser extensions and software only from your company's approved list.

Lock your screen whenever you step away.

Tell IT when your browser behaves strangely, such as unexpected redirects, new toolbars, or sign-in pages that look slightly off.

Where the passkey lives matters

Passkeys come in two storage models, and each carries a different set of dependencies.

Synced passkeys live in a cloud-backed account, such as a platform keychain or a password manager, and follow the user across their devices. That convenience means the account that stores, synchronizes, and recovers the passkey becomes part of your security perimeter.

Device-bound passkeys live on a single piece of hardware, such as a security key, and stay there. They reduce the dependency on sync accounts, but they require more from your team in the form of key distribution, spare-key management, and replacement processes.

Whichever model you choose for a given group of users, evaluate it together with its enrollment process, recovery process, and endpoint protections. Those surrounding controls determine how much protection the passkey delivers in practice. A practical deployment may use device-bound keys for high-risk roles and synced passkeys for the broader workforce, with managed accounts and strong recovery behind them.

Security awareness training must keep pace

Passkey adoption works best when paired with safe credential handling, strong privilege hygiene, and training on current social engineering tactics. Employees need to be able to recognize fake help-desk calls, urgent enrollment requests, and messages asking them to authorize unfamiliar devices.

Effective training gives people concrete habits:

Use a trusted enrollment route. Open approved account settings directly instead of following unsolicited setup links.

Verify unexpected support requests. Contact IT through an established channel before changing authentication or recovery settings.

Know what you are approving. Stop when an unexpected prompt asks for a device code, biometric verification, or security-key touch.

Protect keys and recovery options. Keep hardware keys under your control, never disclose their PINs, and follow approved storage, spare-key, and recovery procedures.

Report fast, with no blame attached. Make it easy to report suspicious requests, mistaken approvals, and lost keys.

A good security awareness training solution pairs what attackers are doing right now with how people actually learn. That could include things like simulated phishing scenarios that build the instinct to pause in a safe setting before a real phishing email arrives.

Hardware keys remain among the strongest MFA options

Hardware security keys used in FIDO2/WebAuthn mode are among the strongest MFA options available. CISA identifies phishing-resistant MFA as the gold standard. The protocol matters: using a hardware token to generate a one-time code does not provide the same phishing resistance as FIDO authentication.

That distinction makes FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys an excellent choice, and should encourage adoption alongside secure handling, recovery controls, and endpoint protection.

Keep watching after authentication succeeds

Passkeys strengthen the authentication event, but they do not tell defenders whether the session, device, account changes, or follow-on activity are legitimate. ITDR extends protection beyond sign-in by connecting signals such as unusual access, newly registered authentication methods, suspicious cloud activity, and abnormal mailbox or file activity. When those signals indicate compromise, responders can revoke sessions, remove unauthorized authenticators, and investigate persistence.

A successful sign-in is one event in a longer story. An attack may look benign at each layer until defenders ask whether the sign-in makes sense for that person. Is this the device they normally use? Does this authentication flow fit their role and workflow? Defenders can connect those questions to newly registered authentication methods, cloud reconnaissance, and abnormal file or mailbox activity.

For confirmed compromise, effective containment includes revoking sessions and removing unauthorized authentication methods. After cleanup, search for persistence, including inbox rules, OAuth app grants, and forwarding addresses.

A practical passkey deployment checklist

Before rollout, teams need clear answers to these five questions:

How will users enroll a passkey through a trusted route?

What proof is required to recover an account or replace a lost key?

How are the endpoints that handle authentication managed and monitored?

How will employees recognize and report passkey-themed social engineering?

How will the team detect and contain suspicious activity after a successful sign-in?

The Lesson

Passkeys significantly improve account security, but they work best as one layer in a complete identity strategy. Attackers can abuse a legitimate authentication flow to obtain valid sessions while passwords and cryptography stay intact.

Phishing-resistant authentication works best alongside protected enrollment and recovery, identity security, endpoint security, security awareness training, and monitoring that can spot what happens after a successful sign-in. Deploy strong authentication, teach people how to use it safely, and maintain visibility into the activity around it. Protecting the full account lifecycle makes that improvement count.

Title: IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026: AI Is Now the Attacker and the Target
Context: Varonis Threat Labs has also documented this pattern — its SearchLeak research found that a Copilot exploit let an attacker inherit the victim’s full permissions, not because...
Full Text:
Key takeaways

AI-driven attacks rose 56% since last year's Report, with shadow AI incidents more than doubling to 43%.

The majority of AI-related breaches (92%) involved no proper AI access controls, making access and governance gaps the real driver of AI breach costs.

Organizations that applied AI and automation extensively across their security lifecycle cut breach costs by $1.93 million.

What is the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report?

IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026, researched independently by Ponemon Institute, is the security industry's longest-running benchmark for breach economics.

This year's edition studied 602 organizations across 17 industries, drawing on interviews with 3,558 security and C-suite leaders with firsthand knowledge of a breach at their organization between March 2025 and February 2026.

The global average cost of a data breach reached a new record this year — $4.99 million, up 12% from last year.

The rise of machine-speed attacks

The rise of AI has brought about the rise of AI-driven attacks, which increased by 56%. More than one in four organizations that experienced a malicious attack this year said it resulted from AI.

Deepfake impersonation and AI-generated malware were behind most of that volume, and the financial consequence was direct, adding an average of $1 million per breach.

How AI lowered the bar for a convincing attack

Generative AI has lowered the cost, time, and skill required to launch a convincing attack, and attackers are now running them continuously and at scale rather than as isolated attempts.

It's a pattern Varonis Threat Labs has been tracking this year, including Reprompt, a single-click Copilot exploit that silently exfiltrated data, and CoSnitch, which showed how a compromised AI assistant could be turned into its own data leak. Both attacks required a single click to succeed, and neither relied on stolen credentials or custom malware — a sign of how little technical skill a modern AI exploit now demands.

The most expensive attacks target what surrounds the model

Among organizations that reported an AI-related breach, the root cause was rarely the model itself. Instead, it turned out to be the environment around it: compromised APIs, connected applications, and cloud misconfigurations.

The costliest security incidents were inversion attacks, which averaged $6.07 million, and prompt injection attacks, which averaged $5.89 million. These are attacks on trust in the system itself, which pushes remediation past technical recovery into governance and disclosure.

Varonis Threat Labs has also documented this pattern — its SearchLeak research found that a Copilot exploit let an attacker inherit the victim’s full permissions, not because the model was flawed, but because of what it was connected to.

Most AI-related breaches had no AI access controls

This year's report found that 92% of AI-related breaches involved no proper AI access controls, and only 40% of organizations reported using access controls on AI models and data at all. That gap should carry the most weight with security leadership, since it points to the single clearest driver of AI breach costs.

Still, it persists despite identity and access management being reported as one of the most effective cost reducers across breaches overall, suggesting the issue has more to do with execution than awareness.

Governance gaps compound the access control problem

AI governance — covering access controls for models, agents, and applications, plus monitoring for data leaks — was absent at 68% of breached organizations this year (up from 63% last year). Only about a third of organizations with any AI policy had strict approval processes for deploying it, and just 19% reported that governance and security teams actually coordinate with each other.

AI systems have outpaced the access models meant to govern them. But it's access control that determines whether an AI system can reach sensitive data in the first place — which is exactly the gap Varonis’ guidance on least privilege for AI agents is built to close.

Shadow AI incidents more than doubled

Security incidents involving shadow AI — employees using AI tools that were never approved or reviewed — more than doubled to 43% this year (up from 20% last year), and these incidents also got more expensive, averaging $5.39 million compared to $4.63 million last year. Nearly half led to data loss or compromise, and regulators are starting to respond: about one in five shadow AI incidents this year resulted in a reported fine.

Shadow AI is less an AI problem than a visibility problem AI has made urgent. The fix isn’t a policy memo telling employees to stop — it’s visibility into what’s touching sensitive data, approved or not, paired with the ability to act on that in real time.

Critical infrastructure and on-premises data remain high-risk targets

By industry, financial services and energy accounted for 62% of all AI-driven breaches studied, with average costs of $6.29 million and $5.2 million respectively. Both sectors identify and contain breaches roughly four weeks faster than the global average, but their deep interdependence with the rest of the economy means a disruption in one doesn’t stay contained to a single balance sheet.

Breaches involving on-premises data storage also grew this year, now present in 30% of breaches, up from 28% last year and 20% in 2024. Although many organizations still treat on-premises storage as inherently safer than the cloud, this year’s data doesn’t support that belief. On-prem environments place the full burden of patching, physical security, and access management on internal IT with no shared responsibility model to offset it.

AI and automation remain the most effective cost reducer

Combating AI-driven attacks requires AI and automation. Organizations that used both extensively across their security lifecycle shortened breach timelines by 65 days and reduced average costs by $1.93 million compared to those that did not — the strongest cost-reduction signal in this year's report.

But the catch is “extensively.” Only 36% of breached organizations applied these tools across prevention, detection, investigation, and response, and most of that use clustered in detection and investigation.

Half of breached organizations have deployed AI agents in their SOC, yet only 18% have applied them to vulnerability scanning and management — exactly where frontier model capabilities are shifting the advantage toward attackers. Varonis’ own Triage Agent research points to the same conclusion: Agentic AI delivers the most value when it’s applied across the full investigation lifecycle, not merely one stage of it.

What this means for security teams building AI programs

Taken together, these findings point to one conclusion: control over where AI systems run, how they process data, and who can access them has become a baseline security requirement.

More than half of organizations now plan to invest in AI security and governance tools following a breach — an 88% increase from last year — and 85% plan to increase security spending specifically in response to frontier AI model threats.

How Varonis helps close the AI access control gap

The report’s clearest signal is also its most actionable: access control, not model sophistication, is what separates costly AI breaches from contained ones. Varonis addresses that gap directly, treating AI security as data security, so access decisions account for both what an AI system can do and what sensitive data it can reach:

Varonis Atlas continuously discovers every AI model, agent, and tool in your environment — including shadow AI — and enforces real-time policy through an inline AI Gateway, closing the visibility gap behind this year’s doubling in shadow AI incidents.

Agent intent-based access control compares what an agent was asked to do against what it actually reaches for, enforcing least privilege at runtime rather than only at provisioning — directly addressing the 92% access-control gap behind this year’s costliest AI breaches.

The Varonis Data Security Platform discovers and classifies sensitive data, maps blast radius, and automatically remediates excessive and stale permissions, so access controls are grounded in what data an identity — human or AI — can actually reach.

Varonis automatically executes more than 200 million remediation actions every month, giving security teams the automated, continuous enforcement this report shows most organizations still lack.

Title: ROMULUS Malware Server Leverages ClickFix to Deliver Multiple Payloads
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Cybercriminals have started to adapt campaigns that deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims, cybersecurity researchers have warned.

As detailed in a blog post published on October 14, security analysts at Vedere Labs, a part of Forescout Research, discovered the server hosting panel ROMULUS while investigating an incident.

They found that the exact same malware delivered by a separate ClickFix campaign was also connected to another server linked to the incident being investigated.

The new server was discovered to be hosting a panel called ROMULUS. Further analysis revealed this to be a new multi-payload shared ClickFix delivery platform.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

And because ClickFix relies on the real, trusted user of the machine to run the commands, action often bypasses any security protections that may be in place to stop unauthorized action.

ClickFix Able to be Deployed at Scale

The newly uncovered ROMULUS platform appears to be capable of deploying a range of attack routes to deliver different forms of malware. Researchers also note that ROMULUS is a reusable delivery backend rather than a single hard-coded malware server, suggesting it is being used at scale.

In total, Forescout analysts identified a total of six different servers running ROMULUS, something they said could indicate that this infrastructure is being run as a toolkit for a wide-range of cybercriminals to use to distribute their attacks.

ROMULUS is also notable for using an unusual method to help disguise its operations. One delivery route was observed to distribute LegionLoader, a multi-pronged malware delivery platform, through encrypted archives containing an executable artificially inflated to approximately 842 MiB, potentially exceeding file-size limits imposed by security scanning and analysis tools.

Researchers believe that this operation shows how ClickFix is evolving beyond a simple social engineering technique into an entry point for malware operations, while attackers are also diversifying their delivery infrastructure, disguising malicious activity and making threats harder to detect.

The identity of the operator behind the platform and common ownership of the final malware families are unknown. But it is noted that this ROMULUS platform is separate to RomulusLoader, a form of malware identified by researchers at Proofpoint earlier in 2026.

Title: Break the silence: Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS government organizations
Context: This was the first vulnerability exploit we observed in UAT-6275’s malware delivery
Full Text:
This research was conducted jointly with Julian-Ferdinand Vögele of Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Details of the joint research and presentation are available here.

Cisco Talos identified UAT-6275 (TAG-193 by Recorded Future) activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Recovered artifacts show additional interest in water resources and energy. This focus is consistent with intelligence collection and may reflect the regional effects of the Russia–Ukraine war.

In activity observed from June 2025 through August 2026, Talos identified four infection-chain types that use macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and a crafted WinRAR archive exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The recovered payloads include several custom reverse shells that provide interactive remote access.

Three publicly accessible staging directories and GitHub repository history exposed payload builds, tool inventories, and changes to command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. These operational security lapses gave us direct visibility into the group's recent activity.

The files recovered from the exposed infrastructure suggest preparation for post-compromise operations and potential activity against Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.

Talos assesses with medium confidence that UAT-6275 has a Kazakhstan nexus, based on infrastructure access, language artifacts, sample submissions, working hours analysis, and regional targeting interests.

Background

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group jointly investigated UAT-6275 activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The investigation uncovered three publicly accessible staging directories and a previously unreported GitHub repository used to host malicious scripts and payloads. These exposed assets provided visibility into the threat actor's malware development, infrastructure changes and preparations for additional intrusion activity.

Talos tracks this activity as UAT-6275, while Recorded Future tracks it as TAG-193. It overlaps with Silent Lynx (first reported by Seqrite) and sits within a broader set of campaigns connected to YoroTrooper, which we first reported in 2023. Subsequent research on Tomiris (Kaspersky), ShadowSilk (Group-IB), Cavalry Werewolf (BI.ZONE), and Hydra Saiga (VMRay) identified overlapping indicators across these reported clusters. We assess that UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper likely belong to the same broader activity cluster. However, we continue to track them separately because we have not observed direct indicator or toolset overlap between the two.

This post summarizes our joint Virus Bulletin 2026 white paper, “Break the silence: tracking Silent Lynx through exposed infrastructure” which contains the full technical analysis and indicators of compromise (IOCs).

Victimology

UAT-6275's targeting is concentrated in Central Asia and the wider CIS region. Across the reviewed campaigns, observed victims and lure themes span nine countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus.

Figure 1. Regional targeting.

Government and diplomatic affairs

UAT-6275 targets government institutions responsible for diplomacy, economic development, agriculture, and environmental management. These organizations hold information that can inform bilateral negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions.

Our network flow analysis identified activity involving a Tajik government entity shortly after treaty discussions with Kazakhstan in March 2026 and a Belarusian government entity ahead of a bilateral meeting in April. This timing may indicate an interest in regional diplomatic developments.

The decoy documents we recovered also suggest an interest in diplomatic relations, international trade, and aviation. Examples include a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Figure 2. Lure document masquerading as a Russian diplomatic congratulatory letter to the Armenian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Water security and resource management

The group’s interest in regional resources spans environmental management and energy. Talos observed activity involving an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, consistent with earlier reporting on Silent Lynx targeting water resource organizations across Central Asia.

Energy-themed decoys included a cooperation proposal between Turkmenistan’s state oil company, Turkmennebit, and Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery, used in an August 2025 sample. The refinery supplies petroleum products to Kazakhstan and later shut down after a Ukrainian drone strike in August 2026, with repairs expected to take up to six months. These ties suggest a possible intelligence interest in regional fuel supplies and the war’s implications for Kazakhstan’s energy security.

Figure 3. Decoy impersonating Turkmennebit and proposing cooperation with Orsk Oil Refinery management.

Campaign timeline

Since Seqrite first reported Silent Lynx in January 2025, we have identified at least eight campaigns across the region through May 2026. These include malware delivery targeting Russia, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan; a credential-harvesting site impersonating Azerbaijan’s State Agency for Public Service; and lures referencing the China–Central Asia Summit and Russian energy infrastructure. In 2026, we also observed activity involving government entities in Tajikistan, Armenia, and Belarus, as well as Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative in May.

Figure 4. Campaign timeline.

Infrastructure and malware delivery

Talos identified three publicly accessible staging directories containing malware and tools of UAT-6275. One sample led to the previously unreported GitHub repository, where the group hosted PowerShell scripts and payloads. Its commit history allowed us to track infrastructure changes and malware development.

The group relies on lightweight reverse shells, including Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell, to issue commands on compromised systems.

We also recovered Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for FortiWeb CVE-2025-25257 from UAT-6275 infrastructure. These findings suggest interest in expanding the group’s operational capabilities.

Four infection chains

UAT-6275 used malicious documents, executable downloaders, and shortcuts to deliver malware, and later incorporated a WinRAR exploit. Talos categorized the recovered samples into four infection chains, A – D, based on how they retrieve and execute their payloads.

Figure 5. First observations of four UAT-6275 infection chains, June 2025 – April 2026.

The first Chain A samples, observed in June 2025, used macro-enabled Word documents to download and execute a second-stage binary. In July 2025, we observed Chain B downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as standalone Windows executables. These downloaders retrieved reverse-shell payloads and created scheduled tasks for persistence.

We first observed Chain C in October 2025. A malicious shortcut launches PowerShell to retrieve and execute a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Later samples also downloaded PickleShell and placed it in the Windows Startup folder for persistence.

Figure 6. Chain C retrieves a GitHub-hosted PowerShell script; later samples also deploy PickleShell to the Startup folder.

In April 2026, we identified a RAR archive that exploited CVE-2025-8088 in WinRAR to place PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder (Chain D). The payload runs at the next user sign-in. This was the first vulnerability exploit we observed in UAT-6275’s malware delivery.

Figure 7. Chain D exploits CVE-2025-8088 to place PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder for execution at the next sign-in.

Kazakhstan nexus assessment

Talos assesses with medium confidence that UAT-6275 has a Kazakhstan nexus. Supporting evidence includes Russian-language artifacts, apparent malware-testing submissions from Kazakhstan shortly after compilation, and operator activity consistent with UTC+5 working hours.

Figure 8. Timing of 77 GitHub commits in UTC+3 and UTC+5, with 09:00–18:00 local working hours shaded.

Looking ahead

UAT-6275’s sustained activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest the group will continue pursuing access to government organizations across Central Asia and the CIS. Its interest in environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure reflects the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management.

Defenders in these sectors should monitor unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads from public services such as GitHub, alongside scheduled tasks and Startup-folder changes. Keeping archive utilities patched can help reduce exposure to the exploit-assisted delivery observed in this campaign.

For further details on this research and our accompanying presentation, see “Break the Silence: Tracking Silent Lynx Through Exposed Infrastructure” on Virus Bulletin’s website, as well as Recorded Future’s related blog post.

Coverage

The following ClamAV signatures detect and block this threat:

Win.Backdoor.PickleShell-10060602-0

Win.Backdoor.Chvost-10060603-0

Win.Malware.Generic-10060604-0

Win.Malware.LAPLAS-10060605-0

Win.Malware.LAPLAS-10060606-0

Win.Proxy.Generic-10060628-0

The following Snort rules cover this threat:

Snort 2: 1:11192, 1:15306, 1:46983, 1:47398

Snort 3: 1:46983, 4:16

Title: AI Agents Won’t Go Rogue, They’ll Inherit Overprivileged Access
Context: After the first block, the agent tried a workaround: The agent found no other path, stopped, and reported back: The agent, the task, and the persistence were the same
Full Text:
What you will learn

Here's how an AI agent inherits your admin rights, edits the policy that blocked it and finishes the task anyway, and how zero standing privilege and just-in-time (JIT) access limit what agents can do on your behalf.

The agent found out who it was working for.

Our core belief at Delinea is that organizations need to secure agent access alongside human access. Our teams are adding capabilities to the Delinea Platform that put this belief into practice. One of these capabilities enables runtime authorization policies to determine whether a human or an agent is acting.

To test that capability, I wrote a policy that enables a human to write to a database and stops the agent working for that human from changing anything in the same database.

The policy worked. The test also showed me how far an agent will go to finish a task.

To secure agents, you must make sure the humans behind them have zero standing privilege; meaning no one holds admin rights until a task requires them.

Why I ran the "human or agent" test

Engineering teams now give AI agents such as Claude Code access to production systems, including source code repositories, databases and cloud infrastructure.

An agent reads a repository, connects to a database and runs commands that nobody typed. Most access controls were built for people, and they make one decision: whether a user can connect. Once the connection opens, the user can run any command the database credential permits.

That model breaks down for agents. An agent that needs to read sales data does not need to change it, even when the person who launched the agent needs to do both.

Delinea runtime authorization enforces policy per action, not only per connection. A gateway sits between the user and the database, inspects each action and checks it against policy before the action reaches the database. The gateway can apply one set of rules to a human and a different set to the agent that human launched.

I wanted to see that work with Claude Code against a live Postgres database, so I set up a test environment.

The test

Before the test, I wrote a policy for the database. The policy had three rules:

Users must request just-in-time (JIT) access.

Agents can read but cannot write.

Humans can read and write.

I pointed Claude Code at a Postgres database behind the Delinea gateway and gave it a one-line task:

The agent requested access, and an approval workflow approved the request automatically. The agent then ran several SELECT statements to find the sales table and return the last five orders. The gateway checked each action against the policy. The reads worked.

Then I asked for a write:

The gateway blocked the write, as my policy required. The agent diagnosed the failure:

The database credential held full insert privilege, so Postgres would have accepted the write. The gateway blocked the write before the statement reached Postgres.

When I ran the same insert myself, outside Claude Code, the write succeeded. Postgres inserted two rows, and a follow-up query returned the new order:

The database and the gateway did not change. Only the identity changed. Delinea runtime authorization checks each action at the gateway and bases each decision on the policy defined for that identity.

The part I didn’t plan for

I also ran the same test while logged in to Delinea as an administrator. I was over-privileged, as admins tend to be.

The gateway recognized Claude Code and blocked the first write. Then the agent did what a persistent engineer would do. The agent investigated the denial, identified the responsible policy, and began editing it so the write would go through.

The agent could edit the policy because the agent acted on my behalf. As an administrator, I had the right to edit policies, so the agent had that right too. My policy limited what the agent could do in the database. Nothing limited what the agent could do as an administrator.

The agent had no hidden agenda. I had told the agent to insert an order, and the agent was trying to finish the task.

What the agent did

The agent reasoned in a straight line from “I was blocked” to “the block is a policy” to “I can edit the policy.” Each step was sensible. None of the steps was malicious. Together, the steps led the agent from the database to the policy that protects that database.

The same agent without admin rights

In the recorded run, I was not logged in as an administrator. After the first block, the agent tried a workaround:

The agent found no other path, stopped, and reported back:

The agent, the task, and the persistence were the same. Only my authority changed.

What the two runs show

1. Agents inherit your authority

An agent acting on your behalf can do what you can do. If you are an administrator, the agent is an administrator too. The agent will use the permissions needed to complete the job.

2. Persistence is the feature, and the risk

Agents are useful because they keep going. An agent diagnoses a failure and tries another way. The same behavior turns a denial into an obstacle to route around. In the recorded run, the agent rewrote its write after the first block and then searched for another access path.

3. Editing policy is a privilege

The right to edit a policy is a privilege, like the right to write to a database. If an agent acts for an identity that holds this privilege, the agent can remove the rule that blocked it.

What to do

Run agents from identities that cannot edit policy. In the test, the agent had its own identity, and the policy treated the agent differently from me. The agent still carried my admin rights because the agent acted on my behalf.

Grant admin rights only when needed. An administrator who holds policy rights all day passes those rights to every agent the administrator runs. Request admin rights just-in-time, for the task that needs them.

Keep access JIT and scoped. In the test, the agent had no standing access. The agent requested access before connecting.

Make denial the end of the road. Write policy at the action level, and give agent identities no other path to the resource. A control that works only if the agent gives up will eventually fail.

Log the attempts. Across both runs, the agent hit a denial, rewrote the write, searched for another access path and edited the policy. Each step belongs in your logs.

Secure the human behind the agent

Runtime authorization gave me what I wanted. Agents could read, humans could write, and the gateway decided each action. The admin run showed the other half of the story.

To secure agents, make sure the humans behind them have zero standing privilege

Policy-based authorization is only as strong as the weakest identity that can edit the policy. The agent didn’t break the control. The agent borrowed the most powerful credential in the room and turned it on the control.

Run the test yourself

Before you connect an agent to production, check whether the agent's identity can edit its own policy. To run this test on your own resources, request a demo.

Title: How Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection Spots Attacker Intent Early
Context: The malware arrives only after the attacker is in control
Full Text:
Imagine this: There’s an active attack but no alert. Nothing looks wrong. Every login is valid. Every tool is trusted. Every command is one your team has run before. This invisible attack chain is how many attackers work today, and they can take control of a domain in minutes and encrypt an environment while evading traditional detections.

It’s what happens between the login and the ransom note that’s the modern cyber battlefield. Attackers work in the open, scouting the network, raising their privileges, and moving between systems to weaken defenses and remove recovery options. Each action uses tools and permissions that look like normal administration. The malware arrives only after the attacker is in control.

At Arctic Wolf, we see this pattern in our incident response (IR) work time and time again. Abuse of external remote access tools drove 65% of our non-business email compromise (BEC) cases, up from 24% a few years ago. Ransomware drove 44% of the incident response cases as reported in the 2026 Arctic Wolf Threat Report, which means defensive measures didn’t stop the payload from executing in those cases.

The window to detect an attacker between login and payload is closing fast, with the time between initial access and handoff to a ransomware group happening in a matter of minutes. With AI speeding up attacks and timelines shrinking, security teams need to catch attackers earlier.

Today we’re introducing Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection, a next-generation endpoint solution built to disrupt attacks mid-flight with AI-powered intent detection.

Why Earlier Matters

The Arctic Wolf VP of Incident Response Kerri Shafer-Page puts it plainly: “In cases where defenders interrupt the attack before detonation, the difference in cost, downtime, and recovery complexity is dramatic.” That seems straightforward, but knowing an earlier response leads to a better outcome is different from being able to achieve it.

The first minutes of an attack tend to decide everything that follows. What happens in those first minutes after initial access can determine whether an incident becomes a breach. Yet many organizations alert on everything and lack the capacity to watch or respond to those alerts.

Recovery also gets harder as time passes. Ransomware operators now target backup infrastructure and identity services directly. Once those are gone, organizations face a choice between paying and rebuilding.

Endpoint detection and response (EDR) is a well-established technology that delivers rich detection. As we respond to AI-driven attacks, we need a way to bring that capability forward in the attack chain.

We’re aligned with Gartner’s recent observation that “to stay ahead of AI-augmented attacks, enterprises are increasingly moving beyond reactive monitoring toward preemptive controls, specifically capabilities that can deny, deceive, and disrupt adversaries.”1

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is designed to help organizations make that shift. It identifies malicious intent early in the attack lifecycle and works to disrupt attacks automatically before they cause significant damage. It strengthens what your endpoint tools already do without relying on static policies.

It also runs alongside your existing endpoint protection platform (EPP) and EDR tools, including third-party platforms and Aurora® Endpoint Security. You keep what you have and add a layer that reads intent.

How Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection Predicts the Attack Story

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is powered by a custom-trained small language model that predicts and maps endpoint activity through a causal graph. That lets it detect intent as soon as a process or file begins to behave unexpectedly.

Because the causal graph keeps context over time, it can spot intent even when individual actions look benign. Consider a sequence like this: a user pastes a command from a web page into a terminal, remote access software your IT team might also use gets installed, a script bundles files into an archive, and then the archive uploads to cloud storage. Each step has a legitimate twin, but together they tell a clear story.

We don’t raise an alert on any one of those steps. Each activity is a chapter in a larger story, and Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection evaluates how each chapter relates to the others as it predicts how the whole story will end.

The small language model and agentic workflows do that evaluation. They separate legitimate business operations from emerging threats. When Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection confirms malicious intent, it’s designed to disrupt the activity and reverse the entire attack chain rather than just the final step.

The Activities That Define the Story

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection also graphs the low-level events that generate too much noise for other tools, which helps surface early signals of malicious intent. It groups those signals by how attacks actually unfold rather than by a generic framework.

Getting in. Attackers start with tricks that persuade a user to run something or with tools that look like normal IT work. It watches for the signs of both.

Staying hidden. Attackers work to slip past execution controls and weaken the defenses around them. It tracks those moves as they happen.

Taking what matters. Attackers collect credentials and data on the way to a payoff. It follows that activity from first touch to exit.

Doing damage. Encryption and destruction come last, along with efforts to block recovery. It’s built to interrupt before they land.

Credential theft keeps growing. Credential-harvesting malware now siphons stolen logins from infected devices at enormous scale. A stolen login lets an attacker skip the exploit. Spotting information stealers early shuts that door.

Rolling Back to a Pre-attack State

Stopping an attack is half the job. Cleanup is the other half. When Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection confirms malicious intent, it reverses the attack chain and returns the endpoint to a pre-attack state. That reduces manual remediation and saves your team time, all with minimal impact on endpoint performance.

Join the Beta

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is available now in beta for Arctic Wolf customers. If you want to see intent-based detection in your environment, enroll today at arcticwolf.com/aatp-beta.

Full Text:
While many supermarkets in France are still grappling with food stock disruptions due to a cyber-attack that targeted refrigeration controllers on October 11, the scope of the incident could be larger than previously observed.

Recent developments suggest that the incident does not only impact Danfoss refrigeration controllers, but also temperature regulation devices from Dixell Electronics, an Italian brand owned by American heating and cooling equipment provider Copeland.

Notably, French local media France 3 reported that an E. Leclerc supermarket in the Tarn region, in the south-west of France, experienced disruptions to its refrigeration systems, despite using Dixell equipment instead of Danfoss.

French national newspaper Le Monde also reported a supermarket near Bordeaux, where attackers reportedly changed freezer settings from −22°C to 150°C. A technician observed several settings being altered per second, suggesting automation.

A security advisory published by the French national Computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) on October 12 specifically named Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series as well as Dixell xweb and Copeland xweb as “affected systems.”

Fears of Deliberate Industrial Sabotage

Speaking to Infosecurity, Amir Preminger, CTO of industrial security provider Claroty, said refrigeration controllers are a prime target, not just for supermarkets but also cold-storage facilities, warehouses, pharmaceuticals, chemical manufacturing and more, that often go overlooked by security teams.

“Industrial control systems such as refrigeration controllers are often assumed to be on safely isolated networks, however, our research found many of these devices are directly exposed to the public internet. While this convenience significantly reduces maintenance costs by allowing engineers to troubleshoot issues remotely, it also lowers the barrier to entry for attackers,” he said.

Preminger assessed that while the attack did not necessarily require sophisticated skills, the targeting was a clear deliberate attempt to cause damage.

“I don’t think it’s sophisticated,” he said. “However, you cannot cause a defrost by mistake by typing the wrong parameter. You need to initiate the defrost. Somebody needed to guide the exploit, the campaign to have that impact.”

He compared the apparent tactic with an incident at a food-processing facility in Israelin 2025. In that case, an attacker inside the facility’s network manipulated a refrigeration compressor and caused it to defrost. While the impact was similar, Preminger did not claim the incidents involved the same group.

He argued that the broader concern was that refrigeration controllers were exposed to the internet. Preminger said such exposed Danfoss devices could be found outside of France too, including in Israel and the US, but he did not know what software versions those devices were running or whether they were vulnerable.

He also cautioned that patching alone does not make internet exposure safe. His advice was to keep critical devices off the public internet and restrict access through measures such as corporate virtual private networks (VPNs) or even access point name (APN) gateways.

He also urged operators to segment their networks, inventory their equipment, and know who can access each device. “Gate your devices, segment your devices. That’s the first frontier,” he said.

Why Supermarket Fridges Are Connected to the Internet

Supermarket fridges are generally connected to the internet to comply with legislation, which, in Europe, requires them to maintain timestamped monitoring of temperatures to strengthen food safety and to install an alarm system in case of an abnormal rise in temperature.

This connection also allows for remote maintenance.

“This is an essential system for the proper preservation of food products,” emphasized Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Coopérative U, in a post on X.
